chapters.title: The Old Sea-dog at the Admiral Benbow
paragraphs: It was Squire Trelawney, Dr. Livesey, and the rest of the gentlemen who asked me to write down the whole story of Treasure Island, beginning to end — to hold nothing back but where the island lies, and that only because there is treasure still buried there. So I take up my pen in the year 17—, and go back to when my father kept the Admiral Benbow inn, and the brown old seaman with the sabre scar across his face first came to lodge under our roof.

I remember him as if it were yesterday, plodding up to the inn door with his sea-chest hauled behind him on a barrow — a tall, strong, heavy man, nut-brown, his tarry pigtail hanging over the shoulder of a grubby blue coat, his hands cracked and scarred with black, broken nails, and that sabre scar across one cheek, a dirty, livid white. I can still see him glancing round the cove and whistling to himself, then suddenly breaking into the old sea-song he would sing so often afterward:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

— in that high, cracked old voice that seemed to have been worn and broken at the capstan bars. Then he rapped on the door with a stick like a handspike that he carried, and when my father appeared he gruffly called for a glass of rum. When it came he drank it slowly, like a man who knew his liquor, lingering on the taste, his eyes still roving over the cliffs and up at our signboard.
“This is a handy cove,” he said at last, “and a pleasant spot for a tavern. Much custom, mate?”
My father told him no — very little, worse luck.

“Well then,” said he, “this is the berth for me. Here, matey,” he called to the man with the barrow, “bring her alongside and help up my chest. I’ll be staying a while,” he went on. “I’m a plain man — rum and bacon and eggs is what I want, and that headland up there to watch for ships. What to call me? You can call me captain. Oh, I see what you’re after — there.” And he flung three or four gold pieces down on the doorstep. “Tell me when I’ve drunk through that,” said he, with a look as fierce as any commander’s.

And indeed, ragged as his clothes were and rough as he talked, he looked nothing like a common hand who sailed before the mast — more like a mate or skipper used to being obeyed, or to hitting out. The man with the barrow told us the coach had set him down the morning before at the Royal George; that he had asked what inns there were along the coast; and that, hearing ours well spoken of and described as lonely, he had picked it over the rest for his lodging. That was all we ever learned about our guest.

He was a silent man by habit. All day he prowled the cove or the cliffs with a brass spyglass; all evening he sat in the corner of the parlour by the fire, drinking rum and water, very strong. Mostly he would not answer when spoken to — only glance up sharp and fierce and snort through his nose like a foghorn — and we and our regulars soon learned to leave him be. Every day, coming back from his walk, he would ask whether any seafaring men had passed along the road. At first we thought he asked for want of company of his own sort; in the end we saw it was the opposite — he wanted to avoid them. When a sailor did stop at the Admiral Benbow — as one did now and then, taking the coast road to Bristol — the captain would peer at him through the curtained door before coming into the parlour, and he was always quiet as a mouse while any such man was present. To me, at least, it was no mystery, for in a way I shared his fears. He had taken me aside one day and promised me a silver fourpenny on the first of every month if I would only keep my “weather-eye open for a seafaring man with one leg” and tell him the moment such a man appeared. Often enough, when the first of the month came round and I asked for my wages, he would only snort at me and stare me down; but before the week was out he was always sure to think better of it, bring me my fourpenny piece, and repeat his order to watch for “the seafaring man with one leg.”

I hardly need tell you how that figure haunted my dreams. On stormy nights, when the wind shook the four corners of the house and the surf roared in the cove and up the cliffs, I would see him in a thousand shapes, with a thousand devilish faces. Sometimes the leg was cut off at the knee, sometimes at the hip; sometimes he was a monstrous thing that had only ever had the one leg, set in the middle of his body. To watch him leap and run and chase me over hedge and ditch was the worst nightmare of all. So, one way and another, I paid pretty dear for my monthly fourpence, in the coin of these hideous dreams.

But frightened as I was by the idea of the one-legged sailor, I feared the captain himself far less than anyone else who knew him. There were nights he took more rum and water than his head could carry, and then he would sit singing his wicked old sea-songs, heeding nobody; but other nights he would call for drinks all round and force the whole trembling room to listen to his stories or join the chorus of his song. Many a time I have heard the house shaking with “Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum,” every neighbour joining in for dear life, in terror, each singing louder than the next to escape notice. For in these fits he was the most overbearing company you ever saw: he would slap the table for silence; he would fly into a rage at a question, or at no question at all, deciding the company was not following his tale; and he would let no one leave the inn until he had drunk himself sleepy and staggered off to bed.

It was his stories that frightened people most. Dreadful stories — hangings, walking the plank, storms at sea, the Dry Tortugas, and wild deeds and places on the Spanish Main. By his own telling he must have spent his life among some of the wickedest men ever let loose on the ocean, and the language he told it in shocked our plain country folk almost as much as the crimes he described. My father was forever sure the inn would be ruined — that people would stop coming to be bullied and crushed and sent shivering to bed — but I really believe his presence did us good. People were frightened at the time, yet looking back they rather liked it; it was a fine bit of excitement in a quiet country life. There was even a knot of younger men who claimed to admire him, calling him a “true sea-dog” and a “real old salt” and the like, and saying it was men like him that made England feared at sea.

In one way, though, he did fairly threaten to ruin us, for he stayed on week after week, and then month after month, until the money he had put down was long gone, and still my father never plucked up the heart to insist on more. If ever he hinted at it, the captain snorted through his nose so loudly it was almost a roar, and stared my poor father out of the room. I have seen him wringing his hands after such a rebuff, and I am sure the worry and the fright he lived in did much to hasten his early and unhappy death.

All the while he lodged with us the captain never changed his clothes, except to buy a few stockings from a pedlar. One side of his hat-brim came down, and he let it hang from that day on, for all the bother it gave him in a wind. I remember his coat, which he patched himself upstairs in his room until, toward the end, it was nothing but patches. He never wrote a letter or got one, and he spoke to nobody but the neighbours — and to them, mostly, only when the rum was in him. The great sea-chest none of us had ever seen open.

He was crossed only once, and that was near the end, when my poor father was far gone in the decline that carried him off. Dr. Livesey came late one afternoon to see the patient, took a little dinner from my mother, and went into the parlour to smoke a pipe while he waited for his horse to be brought down from the hamlet — we had no stable at the old Benbow. I followed him in, and I remember the contrast: the neat, bright doctor, his hair powdered snow-white, his black eyes quick, his manner pleasant, against the clumsy country people, and above all against that filthy, hulking, bleary scarecrow of a pirate of ours, slumped far gone in rum with his arms on the table. Suddenly the captain struck up his everlasting song:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

At first I had taken “the dead man’s chest” to mean that very box of his upstairs in the front room, and the thought had got tangled in my nightmares with the one-legged sailor. But by now we had all long stopped paying the song any mind; that night it was new to no one but Dr. Livesey, and I could see it did not please him, for he glanced up a moment, quite angry, before going on with what he was saying to old Taylor the gardener about a new cure for rheumatism. Meanwhile the captain warmed to his own music, and at last slapped the table in the way we all knew meant silence. Every voice stopped at once — all but the doctor’s, who went on as before, clear and kind, drawing briskly at his pipe between every word or two. The captain glared at him a while, slapped the table again, glared harder, and at last burst out with a vile, low oath: “Silence, there, between decks!”

“Were you speaking to me, sir?” said the doctor; and when the ruffian, with another oath, told him he was, “I have only one thing to say to you, sir,” the doctor replied: “that if you keep on drinking rum, the world will soon be rid of a very dirty scoundrel.”
The old fellow’s fury was terrible. He sprang up, drew and snapped open a sailor’s clasp-knife, and, balancing it open on his palm, threatened to pin the doctor to the wall.

The doctor never so much as stirred. He spoke to him just as before, over his shoulder, in the same tone — pitched a little high, so the whole room could hear — perfectly calm and steady: “If you do not put that knife back in your pocket this instant, I promise you, on my honour, you shall hang at the next assizes.”
Then came a battle of looks between them, but the captain soon gave in, put away his weapon, and sat back down, growling like a beaten dog.

“And now, sir,” the doctor went on, “since I know there is such a man in my district, you may count on it that I shall keep an eye on you day and night. I am not a doctor only — I am a magistrate; and if I catch one breath of complaint against you, even for a rudeness like tonight’s, I shall see to it you are hunted down and turned out of here. Let that be enough.”
Soon after, Dr. Livesey’s horse came to the door and he rode away; but the captain held his tongue that evening, and for many evenings to come.

chapters.title: Black Dog Appears and Disappears
paragraphs: It was not long after this that the first of the strange events occurred — the ones that finally rid us of the captain, though not, as you will see, of his affairs. It was a bitter winter, with long hard frosts and heavy gales, and from the first it was plain my poor father had little chance of seeing the spring. He sank day by day, and my mother and I had the whole inn on our hands, busy enough without sparing much thought for our unwelcome guest.

It was early one January morning — a pinching, frosty morning — the cove all grey with hoar-frost, the ripples lapping softly on the stones, the sun still low and only touching the hilltops and shining far out to sea. The captain had risen earlier than usual and gone off down the beach, his cutlass swinging under the broad skirts of the old blue coat, his brass spyglass under his arm, his hat tilted back on his head. I remember his breath trailing like smoke behind him as he strode away, and the last sound I heard of him as he rounded the big rock was a loud, indignant snort, as though his mind were still running on Dr. Livesey.

Well, mother was upstairs with father, and I was laying the breakfast table for the captain’s return, when the parlour door opened and in stepped a man I had never set eyes on before. He was a pale, waxy creature, short two fingers on the left hand, and though he wore a cutlass he did not look much of a fighter. I always kept an eye out for seafaring men, one leg or two, and I remember this one puzzled me: he was not quite sailorly, and yet there was a smack of the sea about him all the same.
I asked what he would have, and he said rum; but as I went to fetch it he sat down on a table and waved me closer. I stopped where I was, napkin in hand.
“Come here, sonny,” said he. “Come a bit nearer.”
I took a step toward him.
“Is this table here set out for my mate Bill?” he asked, with a kind of leer.
I told him I knew no mate Bill — the table was for a man staying with us whom we called the captain.

“Well,” said he, “my mate Bill might well be called the captain, like as not. He has a cut on one cheek, and a mighty pleasant way with him, especially in drink, has my mate Bill. Let us say, for argument’s sake, that your captain has a cut on one cheek — and let us say, if you like, that it is the right cheek. Ah, there you are. Now — is my mate Bill in this house?”
I told him he was out walking.
“Which way, sonny? Which way is he gone?”

And when I had pointed out the rock, and told him how and how soon the captain was likely to be back, and answered a question or two more, “Ah,” said he, “this’ll be as good as a drink to my mate Bill.”

The look on his face as he said it was anything but pleasant, and I had my own reasons to think the stranger was mistaken, even if he meant what he said. But it was no business of mine, I thought, and besides it was hard to know what to do. The stranger kept lurking just inside the inn door, peering round the corner like a cat watching a mouse. Once I stepped out into the road myself, but he called me straight back, and when I did not move fast enough to suit him, a horrible change came over that waxy face and he ordered me in with an oath that made me jump. The moment I was back he turned smooth again, half fawning, half sneering, patted my shoulder and told me I was a good lad and he had taken quite a fancy to me. “I have a son of my own,” he said, “the very spit of you, and he is all the pride of my heart. But the great thing for boys is discipline, sonny — discipline. Now, if you had sailed with Bill, you’d not have stood there to be spoken to twice — not you. That was never Bill’s way, nor the way of them as sailed with him. And here, sure enough, is my mate Bill, with a spyglass under his arm, bless his old heart. You and me’ll just step back into the parlour, sonny, and get behind the door, and we’ll give Bill a little surprise — bless his heart, I say again.”

With that the stranger backed into the parlour with me and put me behind him in the corner, both of us hidden by the open door. I was very uneasy and alarmed, as you may imagine, and it did nothing for my nerves to see that the stranger was plainly frightened himself. He freed the hilt of his cutlass and loosened the blade in its sheath, and the whole time we waited he kept swallowing as if he had what we used to call a lump in the throat.
At last in strode the captain, slammed the door behind him without a glance to either side, and marched straight across the room to where his breakfast was waiting.
“Bill,” said the stranger, in a voice he seemed to force loud and bold.

The captain spun on his heel and faced us. All the brown had drained from his face; even his nose had gone blue. He had the look of a man seeing a ghost, or the devil, or something worse, if worse there is; and upon my word, I felt sorry to watch him turn, in a moment, so old and sick.
“Come, Bill — you know me; you know an old shipmate, surely, Bill,” said the stranger.
The captain gave a sort of gasp.
“Black Dog!” said he.

“And who else?” said the other, easier now. “Black Dog as ever was, come to see his old shipmate Billy at the Admiral Benbow inn. Ah, Bill, Bill, we have seen a deal of life, us two, since I lost these two talons,” — and he held up his maimed hand.
“Now look here,” said the captain. “You’ve run me to ground; here I am; well then — out with it; what is it?”

“That’s you, Bill,” said Black Dog. “You’re in the right of it, Billy. I’ll have a glass of rum from this dear child I’ve taken such a liking to, and we’ll sit down, if you please, and talk straight, like old shipmates.”

When I came back with the rum, the two were already seated on either side of the captain’s breakfast — Black Dog next the door, sitting sideways so as to keep one eye on his old shipmate and one, I thought, on his line of retreat.
He told me to go out and leave the door standing wide. “None of your keyholes for me, sonny,” he said; and I left the two of them together and slipped back to the bar.
For a long time, though I certainly did my best to listen, I could make out nothing but a low murmur; but at last the voices rose, and I could pick up a word or two, mostly oaths, from the captain.
“No, no, no, no — and there’s an end of it!” he cried once; and again, “If it comes to swinging, let all swing, says I.”

Then all at once came a great burst of oaths and other noise — chair and table went over together, a clash of steel followed, then a cry of pain, and the next moment I saw Black Dog in full flight and the captain hard after him, both with drawn cutlasses, Black Dog streaming blood from the left shoulder. Right at the door the captain aimed one last tremendous slash, which would surely have split him to the backbone had it not caught on the big signboard of the Admiral Benbow. You can see the notch on the lower edge of the frame to this day.

That blow ended the fight. Once out on the road, Black Dog, wound and all, showed a wonderful clean pair of heels and was over the brow of the hill in half a minute. The captain, for his part, stood staring at the signboard like a man dazed. Then he passed his hand over his eyes again and again, and at last turned back indoors.
“Jim,” said he, “rum.” And as he spoke he swayed a little, and caught himself with one hand against the wall.
“Are you hurt?” cried I.
“Rum,” he said again. “I must get away from here. Rum! Rum!”

I ran for it, but I was so shaken by all that had happened that I broke a glass and jammed the tap, and while I was still fumbling I heard a heavy fall in the parlour, and running in, found the captain stretched full length on the floor. At the same moment my mother, alarmed by the shouting and the fighting, came hurrying down to help. Between us we lifted his head. He was breathing very loud and hard, but his eyes were shut and his face a dreadful colour.
“Dear, deary me,” cried my mother, “what a disgrace on the house — and your poor father lying sick upstairs!”

Meanwhile we had no notion how to help the captain, nor any thought but that he had got his death-wound in the scuffle with the stranger. I fetched the rum, sure enough, and tried to get it down his throat, but his teeth were clenched and his jaws as strong as iron. It was a blessed relief when the door opened and Doctor Livesey came in, on his visit to my father.
“Oh, doctor,” we cried, “what are we to do? Where is the man hurt?”

“Hurt? Rubbish!” said the doctor. “No more hurt than you or I. The man has had a stroke, just as I warned him. Now, Mrs. Hawkins, run up to your husband and, if you can, tell him nothing of this. For my part, I must do my best to save this fellow’s three-times-worthless life. Jim, fetch me a basin.”

When I got back with the basin the doctor had already slit the captain’s sleeve and laid bare his great sinewy arm, tattooed in several places. “Here’s luck,” “A fair wind,” and “Billy Bones his fancy” were lettered very neat and clear along the forearm; and up near the shoulder was a sketch of a gallows with a man hanging from it — done, I thought, with great spirit.

“Prophetic,” said the doctor, touching the picture with his finger. “And now, Master Billy Bones — if that is your name — we’ll have a look at the colour of your blood. Jim,” he said, “are you afraid of blood?”
“No, sir,” said I.
“Well then,” said he, “you hold the basin.” And with that he took his lancet and opened a vein.

A great deal of blood was taken before the captain opened his eyes and looked round him, bleary. First he made out the doctor, with an unmistakable scowl; then his eye fell on me, and he looked relieved. But all at once his colour changed, and he struggled to sit up, crying, “Where’s Black Dog?”

“There is no Black Dog here,” said the doctor, “except the one on your own back. You have been drinking rum, and you have had a stroke, exactly as I told you; and I have just this minute, much against my will, hauled you headfirst out of the grave. Now, Mr. Bones—”
“That’s not my name,” he broke in.

“Much I care,” said the doctor. “It’s the name of a buccaneer I’ve heard of, and I shall call you by it for short. Here is what I have to say to you: one glass of rum won’t kill you, but if you take one you’ll take another, and another, and I stake my wig that if you don’t break off short you’ll die — do you understand? Die. And go to your own place, like the man in the Bible. Come now, make the effort. I’ll help you to your bed this once.”
Between us, with no end of trouble, we got him upstairs and laid him on his bed, where his head fell back on the pillow as if he were near to fainting.
“Now, mind you,” said the doctor, “I clear my conscience — the name of rum, for you, is death.”
And with that he set off to see my father, drawing me along by the arm.

“This is nothing,” he said the moment he had shut the door. “I have drawn blood enough to keep him quiet a while; he should lie a week where he is — that is best for him and for you — but another stroke would settle him.”

chapters.title: The Black Spot
paragraphs: About noon I came to the captain’s door with some cooling drinks and his medicine. He was lying much as we had left him, only propped a little higher, and he looked both weak and worked-up.

“Jim,” he said, “you’re the only one here worth anything, and you know I’ve always been good to you. Never a month but I gave you your silver fourpenny. And now, mate, you see I’m pretty low, and deserted by all; so, Jim, you’ll bring me one mug of rum — won’t you, matey?”
“The doctor—” I began.

But he broke in, cursing the doctor in a feeble voice but heartily. “Doctors is all swabs,” he said; “and that one there — what does he know about seafaring men? I’ve been in places hot as pitch, with mates dropping round me of Yellow Jack, and the good land heaving like the sea with earthquakes — what does the doctor know of country like that? I lived on rum, I tell you. It’s been meat and drink to me, and man and wife besides; and if I can’t have my rum now I’m a poor old hulk on a lee shore. My blood’ll be on you, Jim, and on that swab of a doctor.” And he ran on cursing a while. “Look, Jim, how my fingers won’t keep still,” he went on, pleading now. “I can’t hold ’em steady, not I. I’ve not had a drop this whole blessed day. That doctor’s a fool, I tell you. If I don’t get a dram of rum, Jim, I’ll have the horrors — I’ve seen some of ’em already. I saw old Flint, there in the corner behind you, plain as print; and if I get the horrors, I’m a man that’s lived rough, and I’ll raise Cain. Your own doctor said one glass wouldn’t hurt me. I’ll give you a golden guinea for a mug, Jim.”

He was growing more and more excited, and it frightened me for my father, who was very low that day and needed quiet; besides, the doctor’s words, now thrown back at him, had reassured me, and I was rather offended at being offered a bribe.
“I want no money of yours,” said I, “only what you owe my father. I’ll bring you one glass, and not another.”
When I brought it to him he snatched it greedily and drank it off.
“Aye, aye,” said he, “that’s a sight better, sure enough. And now, matey, did that doctor say how long I’m to lie here in this old berth?”
“A week at least,” said I.

“Thunder!” he cried. “A week! I can’t do that — they’d have the black spot on me by then. The lubbers are casting about to get word of me this very minute — lubbers that couldn’t keep what they had, and now want to grab what is another man’s. Is that seamanly behaviour, now, I ask you? But I’m a saving soul. I never wasted good money of mine, nor lost it either; and I’ll trick ’em again. I’m not afraid of ’em. I’ll shake out another reef, matey, and leave ’em standing.”

As he spoke he had hauled himself up off the bed with great difficulty, gripping my shoulder so hard I nearly cried out, and dragging his legs like dead weight. His words, bold as they were in meaning, made a sad contrast with the feeble voice that carried them. He paused once he had got himself sitting on the edge.
“That doctor’s done for me,” he muttered. “My ears are singing. Lay me back.”
Before I could do much to help, he had dropped back to where he had been, and lay a while in silence.
“Jim,” he said at length, “you saw that seafaring man today?”
“Black Dog?” I asked.

“Ah — Black Dog,” said he. “He’s a bad one; but there’s worse behind him that put him on. Now, if I can’t get clear no way, and they tip me the black spot, mind you — it’s my old sea-chest they’re after. You get on a horse — you can ride, can’t you? Well then, you get on a horse and go to — yes, I will! — to that everlasting swab of a doctor, and tell him to pipe all hands, magistrates and such, and he’ll lay ’em aboard at the Admiral Benbow — all old Flint’s crew, every man and boy of ’em that’s left. I was first mate, I was — old Flint’s first mate — and I’m the only one as knows the place. He gave it me at Savannah, when he lay a-dying, like as I might now, you see. But you’ll not breathe a word unless they tip me the black spot, or unless you see that Black Dog again, or a seafaring man with one leg, Jim — him above all.”
“But what is the black spot, captain?” I asked.
“A summons, mate. I’ll tell you if they bring it. But you keep your weather-eye open, Jim, and I’ll share with you, fair halves, upon my honour.”

He rambled on a little longer, his voice growing weaker; but soon after I had given him his medicine — which he took like a child, with the remark, “If ever a sailor needed drugs, it’s me” — he fell at last into a heavy, swoon-like sleep, and I left him so. What I should have done if all had gone well I do not know. Most likely I should have told the doctor the whole story, for I was in mortal fear the captain might regret his confidences and make an end of me. But as it fell out, my poor father died quite suddenly that evening, and that pushed everything else aside. Our natural grief, the neighbours’ visits, the arranging of the funeral, and all the inn’s work to be carried on in the meantime kept me so busy that I had scarcely time to think of the captain, far less to be afraid of him.

He did get downstairs the next morning, to be sure, and ate his meals as usual, though little, and took, I am afraid, more than his share of rum, helping himself at the bar, scowling and snorting, with nobody daring to cross him. The night before the funeral he was as drunk as ever, and it was shocking, in that house of mourning, to hear him bawling out his ugly old sea-song; but weak as he was, we all went in fear of him, and the doctor had been called away suddenly to a case many miles off and never came near the house after my father’s death. I have said the captain was weak, and indeed he seemed to grow weaker rather than mend. He hauled himself up and down stairs, and went from the parlour to the bar and back, and now and then put his nose out of doors to smell the sea, holding to the walls for support as he went and breathing hard and fast like a man climbing a steep hill. He never spoke to me directly, and it is my belief he had as good as forgotten what he had confided; but his temper was flightier, and — allowing for his bodily weakness — more violent than ever. He had an alarming new way, when drunk, of drawing his cutlass and laying it bare on the table before him. Yet for all that, he took less notice of people, and seemed shut up in his own thoughts, and rather wandering. Once, for instance, to our great surprise, he struck up a different tune — a kind of country love-song he must have learned in his youth, before he took to the sea.

So things went until, the day after the funeral — about three o’clock of a bitter, foggy, frosty afternoon — I was standing a moment at the door, full of sad thoughts of my father, when I saw someone coming slowly along the road. He was plainly blind, for he tapped ahead of him with a stick and wore a great green shade over his eyes and nose; and he was bent, as if with age or weakness, and wrapped in a huge old tattered sea-cloak with a hood that made him look positively deformed. I never in my life saw a more dreadful-looking figure. He stopped a little short of the inn and, raising his voice in an odd sing-song, called out to the air in front of him: “Will any kind friend tell a poor blind man, who has lost the precious sight of his eyes in the gracious defence of his native country, England — and God bless King George! — where, or in what part of the country, he may now be?”
“This is the Admiral Benbow, at Black Hill Cove, my good man,” I told him.
“I hear a voice,” said he — “a young one. Give me your hand, my kind young friend, and lead me inside.”

I held out my hand, and the horrible, soft-spoken, eyeless creature gripped it in a moment like a vice. I was so startled that I tried to pull away, but with one motion of his arm the blind man dragged me close.
“Now, boy,” said he, “take me in to the captain.”
“Sir,” said I, “upon my word I dare not.”
“Oh,” he sneered, “that’s it, is it? Take me in straight, or I’ll break your arm.”
And as he spoke he gave it a wrench that made me cry out.
“Sir,” said I, “it is for your own sake. The captain is not what he used to be. He sits with a drawn cutlass. Another gentleman—”

“Come, now — march,” he cut in; and I never heard a voice so cruel and cold and ugly as that blind man’s. It cowed me more than the pain, and I began to obey him at once, walking straight in at the door and toward the parlour, where our sick old buccaneer sat, dazed with rum. The blind man clung to me, gripping me in one iron fist and leaning more of his weight on me than I could well carry. “Lead me straight up to him, and when I’m in sight, call out, ‘Here’s a friend for you, Bill.’ If you don’t, I’ll do this” — and he gave me a twist that I thought would have made me faint. Between this and that, I was so utterly terrified of the blind beggar that I forgot my dread of the captain, and as I opened the parlour door I called out the words he had ordered, in a trembling voice.

The poor captain looked up, and at one glance the rum went clean out of him and left him staring sober. His face showed not so much terror as mortal sickness. He made a movement to rise, but I do not believe he had the strength left in his body.

“Stay where you are, Bill,” said the beggar. “Blind I may be, but I can hear a finger stir. Business is business. Put out your left hand. Boy — take him by the wrist and bring his left hand over to my right.”
We both obeyed him to the letter, and I saw him pass something from the hollow of the hand that held his stick into the captain’s palm, which closed on it at once.

“And now that’s done,” said the blind man; and with the words he suddenly let go of me and, with astonishing speed and sureness, skipped out of the parlour and into the road, where, as I still stood frozen, I could hear his stick go tap-tap-tapping off into the distance.

It was some time before either of us came to his senses; but at last, and about at the same moment, I let go his wrist, which I was still holding, and he drew in his hand and looked sharply at the palm.
“Ten o’clock!” he cried. “Six hours — we’ll beat ’em yet,” and he sprang to his feet.
Even as he did, he reeled, put his hand to his throat, stood swaying a moment, and then, with an odd sound, fell his whole height face-first to the floor.

I ran to him at once, calling for my mother. But all haste was useless. The captain had been struck dead by a thundering stroke. It is a strange thing to account for, since I had certainly never liked the man — though of late I had begun to pity him — but the moment I saw he was dead, I burst into a flood of tears. It was the second death I had known, and the grief of the first was still fresh in my heart.

chapters.title: The Sea-chest
paragraphs: Of course I lost no time in telling my mother everything I knew — I should perhaps have told her long before — and we saw at once that we were in a tight and dangerous spot. Some of the man’s money, if he had any, was surely owed to us; but it wasn’t likely the captain’s old shipmates — above all the two I had seen, Black Dog and the blind beggar — would hand over their loot to pay a dead man’s debts. The captain’s own order, to ride off at once for Dr. Livesey, would have left my mother alone and unprotected, which was out of the question. In fact it seemed impossible for either of us to stay much longer in the house at all: a coal falling in the grate, the very tick of the clock, set our nerves jumping. The neighbourhood seemed to us full of approaching footsteps; and between the captain’s dead body on the parlour floor and the thought of that loathsome blind beggar lurking near and ready to come back, there were moments when, as the saying goes, I fairly jumped out of my skin with terror. Something had to be settled fast, and at last it struck us to set out together and seek help in the nearby hamlet. No sooner thought than done: bareheaded as we were, we ran out into the gathering dusk and the frosty fog.

The hamlet lay only a few hundred yards off, though out of sight, on the far side of the next cove; and what cheered me most, it was the opposite way from where the blind man had come and, I supposed, gone back. We weren’t many minutes on the road, though now and then we stopped, clinging to each other, and listened. But there was no strange sound — only the low wash of the ripple and the croaking of the creatures in the wood.

It was already candle-light when we reached the hamlet, and I’ll never forget how it heartened me to see the yellow glow in the doors and windows — though that, as it turned out, was the most help we’d get from that quarter. For — you’d think men would be ashamed of it — not one soul would come back with us to the Admiral Benbow. The more we told of our trouble, the tighter they clung, man, woman, and child, to the shelter of their houses. The name of Captain Flint, strange as it was to me, was well enough known to some of them and carried a great weight of dread. A few of the men who had been at field-work beyond the Admiral Benbow remembered, besides, having seen several strangers on the road, and, taking them for smugglers, having bolted home; and one at least had seen a little lugger in what we called Kitt’s Hole. For that matter, anyone who had been a comrade of the captain’s was enough to scare them witless. The long and short of it was that, though we could find several willing enough to ride to Dr. Livesey’s, which lay another way, not one would help us guard the inn.

They say cowardice is catching; but argument, on the other hand, is a great emboldener — and so, when each had had his say, my mother made them a speech. She would not, she declared, lose money owed to her fatherless boy. “If none of the rest of you dare,” said she, “Jim and I dare. Back we’ll go, the way we came, and small thanks to you big, hulking, chicken-hearted men. We’ll have that chest open, if it kills us. And I’ll thank you for the loan of that bag, Mrs. Crossley, to carry home our lawful money in.”

Of course I said I’d go with my mother, and of course they all cried out at our recklessness; but even so, not a man would come along. All they would do was give me a loaded pistol in case we were attacked, promise to have horses saddled if we were chased on the way back, and send one lad ahead to the doctor’s to fetch armed help.

My heart was thumping hard as the two of us set out into the cold night on this dangerous errand. A full moon was just rising, glowing red through the upper edges of the fog, and that hurried us the more, for plainly, before we got out again, all would be bright as day and our going exposed to any watcher’s eye. We slipped along the hedges, swift and silent, and saw and heard nothing to add to our fears — until, to our relief, the door of the Admiral Benbow had shut behind us.

I shot the bolt at once, and we stood a moment panting in the dark, alone in the house with the dead captain’s body. Then my mother fetched a candle from the bar, and hand in hand we went into the parlour. He lay where we had left him, on his back, eyes open, one arm flung out.

“Draw down the blind, Jim,” whispered my mother; “they might come and watch from outside. And now,” she said when I had done it, “we’ve to get the key off that — and who’s to touch him, I’d like to know!” — and she gave a kind of sob as she spoke.

Down I went on my knees at once. On the floor by his hand lay a little round of paper, blackened on one side. I had no doubt it was the black spot; and picking it up, I found on the other side, in a good clear hand, this short message: “You have till ten tonight.”

“Then he had till ten, Mother,” said I — and the words were scarcely out when our old clock started striking. The sound made us both jump horribly; but it was good news after all, for the hour was only six.
“Now, Jim,” she said, “that key.”

I felt through his pockets one by one. A few small coins, a thimble, some thread and big needles, a twist of pigtail tobacco bitten off at the end, his clasp-knife with the crooked handle, a pocket compass, and a tinderbox — that was all they held, and I began to lose heart.
“Maybe it’s round his neck,” said my mother.

Choking down a strong disgust, I tore open his shirt at the neck, and there, sure enough, on a bit of tarry string — which I cut through with his own knife — we found the key. At this success we took fresh hope and hurried straight upstairs to the little room where he had slept so long, and where his box had stood since the day he came.
From the outside it was like any other seaman’s chest, the initial “B” burned into the lid with a hot iron, the corners knocked and battered by long, rough handling.
“Give me the key,” said my mother; and though the lock was very stiff, she had it turned and the lid thrown back in a moment.

A strong reek of tobacco and tar rose from inside, but on top there was nothing to see except a suit of very good clothes, carefully brushed and folded. They had never been worn, my mother said. Under that the jumble began — a quadrant, a tin cup, several sticks of tobacco, two pairs of very handsome pistols, a bar of silver, an old Spanish watch and some other trinkets of little worth and mostly foreign make, a brass-mounted pair of compasses, and five or six odd West Indian shells. I’ve often wondered since why he carried those shells about with him through his wandering, guilty, hunted life.

So far we had found nothing of value but the silver and the trinkets, and neither was any use to us. Underneath lay an old boat-cloak, whitened with sea-salt from many a harbour bar. My mother tugged it aside impatiently, and there before us lay the last things in the chest: a bundle wrapped in oilcloth, like papers, and a canvas bag that gave out, at a touch, the chink of gold.

“I’ll show these rogues I’m an honest woman,” said my mother. “I’ll have my due, and not a farthing over. Hold Mrs. Crossley’s bag.” And she set to counting out the captain’s debt from the sailor’s bag into the one I held.

It was a long, awkward business, for the coins were of every country and size — doubloons and louis d’ors, guineas and pieces of eight, and I don’t know what besides, all jumbled together at random. The guineas, too, were the scarcest, and it was only with those that my mother knew how to reckon her count.

When we were about halfway through I suddenly laid my hand on her arm, for in the still frosty air I had caught a sound that brought my heart into my mouth — the tap-tap-tapping of the blind man’s stick on the frozen road. It came nearer and nearer while we sat holding our breath. Then it struck sharp on the inn door, and we heard the handle turn and the bolt rattle as the wretch tried to get in; and then, within and without, a long silence. At last the tapping began again and — to our unspeakable joy and relief — died slowly away until we could hear it no more.

“Mother,” said I, “take the lot and let’s be off” — for I felt sure the bolted door must have looked suspicious and would bring the whole hornet’s nest down on us, though how glad I was I had bolted it, no one could know who had never met that terrible blind man.

But my mother, frightened as she was, would not hear of taking a fraction more than her due, and was just as stubbornly unwilling to take less. It was not seven o’clock yet, not by a long way, she said; she knew her rights and would have them — and she was still arguing the point with me when a low whistle sounded a good way off on the hill. That was enough, and more than enough, for the two of us.
“I’ll take what I’ve got,” she said, springing up.
“And I’ll take this, to round off the count,” said I, snatching up the oilskin packet.

The next moment we were both groping down the stairs, leaving the candle by the empty chest; and the moment after we had opened the door and were in full flight. We hadn’t started a second too soon. The fog was lifting fast; already the moon shone clear on the high ground to either side, and only in the very bottom of the hollow and round the tavern door did a thin veil still hang to hide the first steps of our escape. Far short of halfway to the hamlet, just past the foot of the hill, we’d have to break out into the moonlight. And that wasn’t all, for now there came to our ears the sound of several running feet, and looking back toward it we saw a light tossing to and fro and still coming on fast — one of the newcomers carried a lantern.
“Jim, my dear,” my mother said all at once, “take the money and go on without me. I feel I’m going to faint.”

This, I thought, was surely the end of us both. How I cursed the neighbours’ cowardice; how I blamed my poor mother for her honesty and her greed, for her earlier recklessness and her present weakness! By good luck we were just at the little bridge, and I helped her, swaying as she was, to the edge of the bank, where, sure enough, she gave a sigh and sank against my shoulder. I don’t know where I found the strength, and I’m afraid I did it roughly, but I managed to drag her down the bank and a little way under the arch. Farther I couldn’t get her, for the bridge was too low to let me do more than crawl beneath it. So there we had to stay — my mother almost wholly in view, and both of us within earshot of the inn.

chapters.title: The Last of the Blind Man
paragraphs: My curiosity, in a way, proved stronger than my fear, for I couldn’t stay where I was, but crept back up to the bank, where, hiding my head behind a clump of broom, I had a clear view of the road in front of our door. I was scarcely in place when the enemy began to arrive — seven or eight of them, running hard, their feet beating out of step along the road, the man with the lantern a few paces ahead. Three of them ran together, hand in hand, and even through the mist I made out that the middle one of the three was the blind beggar. The next instant his voice proved me right.
“Down with the door!” he cried.

“Aye, aye, sir!” answered two or three, and they rushed at the Admiral Benbow, the lantern-bearer behind them; and then I saw them pause and heard words exchanged in a lower tone, as if surprised to find the door open. But the pause was short, for the blind man gave his orders again, his voice higher and louder, as if he were ablaze with eagerness and rage.
“In, in, in!” he shouted, cursing them for hanging back.
Four or five obeyed at once, two staying out on the road with the dreadful beggar. There was a pause, then a cry of surprise, then a voice shouting from inside the house: “Bill’s dead.”
But the blind man only swore at them again for their delay.
“Search him, some of you lazy lubbers, and the rest of you up and fetch the chest,” he cried.

I could hear their feet clattering up our old stairs till the house must have shaken with it. Right after came fresh shouts of astonishment; the window of the captain’s room was flung open with a bang and a jingle of broken glass, and a man leaned out, head and shoulders, into the moonlight, calling down to the blind beggar on the road below.
“Pew,” he cried, “they’ve been here before us. Someone’s turned the chest out top to bottom.”
“Is it there?” roared Pew.
“The money’s there.”
The blind man cursed the money.
“Flint’s fist, I mean,” he cried.
“We don’t see it anywhere,” the man called back.
“Here — you below — is it on Bill?” the blind man cried again.
At that another fellow — the one, most likely, who had stayed down to search the captain’s body — came to the inn door. “Bill’s been gone through already,” said he; “nothing left.”

“It’s these people of the inn — it’s that boy. I wish I’d put his eyes out!” cried the blind man, Pew. “They were here no time ago — they had the door bolted when I tried it. Scatter, lads, and find ’em.”
“Sure enough, they left their light burning here,” said the man at the window.
“Scatter and find ’em! Turn the house out!” Pew shouted again, hammering the road with his stick.

Then came a great uproar all through our old inn — heavy feet pounding back and forth, furniture overturned, doors kicked in, till the rocks themselves rang with it — and the men came out again, one after another, onto the road, and swore that we were nowhere to be found. And just then the same whistle that had startled my mother and me over the dead captain’s money rang once more, clear through the night, but this time twice over. I had taken it before for the blind man’s trumpet, so to speak, calling his crew to the attack; but now I learned it was a signal from the hillside toward the hamlet — and, by its effect on the buccaneers, a warning of danger coming.
“That’s Dirk again,” said one. “Twice! We’ll have to shift, mates.”

“Shift, you skulker!” cried Pew. “Dirk was a fool and a coward from the start — never mind him. They must be close by; they can’t be far; you’ve as good as got your hands on it. Scatter and hunt them out, you dogs! Oh, curse my soul,” he cried, “if only I had eyes!”

The appeal seemed to tell, for two of the fellows began poking here and there among the lumber — half-heartedly, I thought, and with half a mind on their own danger all the while — while the rest stood undecided in the road.

“You’ve your hands on thousands, you fools, and you hang back! You’d be as rich as kings if you could find it, and you know it’s here, and you stand there skulking. Not one of you dared face Bill, and I did it — a blind man! And I’m to lose my chance because of you — to stay a poor, crawling beggar, cadging for rum, when I might be riding in my coach! If you’d the pluck of a weevil in a biscuit you’d catch them yet.”
“Hang it, Pew, we’ve got the doubloons!” grumbled one.
“They might have hid the cursed thing,” said another. “Take the Georges, Pew, and quit your squalling.”

Squalling was the word for it: Pew’s rage flew so high at these objections that at last, his temper getting clean the better of him, he struck out at them left and right in his blindness, and his stick came down hard on more than one of them.
These, in their turn, cursed the blind villain back, threatened him with frightful words, and tried in vain to catch the stick and wrench it out of his hand.

That quarrel was the saving of us; for while it still raged, another sound came over the top of the hill on the hamlet side — the tramp of galloping horses. Almost at the same moment a pistol-shot, flash and bang, came from along the hedge. Plainly that was the last warning of danger, for the buccaneers turned on the instant and ran, scattering every way — one toward the sea along the cove, one slantwise across the hill, and so on — until in half a minute there was no sign of them left but Pew. Him they had deserted, whether in sheer panic or to pay him back for his foul words and blows I can’t say; but there he stayed behind, tapping up and down the road in a frenzy, groping and calling for his mates. At last he took a wrong turn and ran a few steps past me, toward the hamlet, crying, “Johnny, Black Dog, Dirk,” and other names, “you won’t leave old Pew, mates — not old Pew!”
Just then the noise of the horses topped the rise, and four or five riders came in sight in the moonlight and swept down the slope at full gallop.

At that Pew saw his mistake, turned with a scream, and ran straight for the ditch, into which he tumbled. But he was up again in a second and made another dash, utterly bewildered now, right under the nearest of the oncoming horses.

The rider hauled at his reins to spare him, but it was no good. Pew went down with a cry that rang up into the night, and the four hooves trod him under and swept on. He toppled onto his side, slid slowly onto his face, and lay still for good.

I sprang to my feet and hailed the riders. They were reining up, in any case, horrified at the accident; and I soon saw who they were. One, trailing behind the rest, was the lad who had gone from the hamlet to Dr. Livesey’s; the others were revenue officers he had met on the road and had had the sense to bring straight back. Word of the lugger in Kitt’s Hole had reached Supervisor Dance and sent him out our way that night — and to that my mother and I owed our lives.

Pew was dead — stone dead. As for my mother, when we had carried her up to the hamlet, a little cold water and smelling-salts soon brought her round, and she was none the worse for her fright, though she still kept lamenting the rest of the money. Meanwhile the supervisor rode on as hard as he could for Kitt’s Hole; but his men had to dismount and grope down the dell, leading and sometimes half-carrying their horses, in constant fear of an ambush, so it was no wonder that by the time they reached the Hole the lugger was already under way, though still close in. He hailed her. A voice answered, telling him to get out of the moonlight or he’d take some lead, and at the same moment a bullet whistled past his arm. Soon after, the lugger rounded the point and was gone. Mr. Dance stood there, as he put it, “like a fish out of water,” and all he could do was send a man off to B—— to warn the cutter. “And that,” said he, “is about as good as nothing. They’ve got clean away, and there’s an end of it. Only,” he added, “I’m glad I trod on Master Pew’s corns” — for by now he had heard my story.

I went back with him to the Admiral Benbow, and you can’t imagine a house in such a wreck; the very clock had been thrown down by these fellows in their furious hunt for my mother and me; and though they had carried off nothing but the captain’s money-bag and a little silver from the till, I could see at a glance we were ruined. Mr. Dance could make nothing of the scene.
“So they got the money, you tell me? Then what on earth were they hunting for, Hawkins? More of the same, I suppose?”
“No, sir — not money, I think,” I replied. “In fact, sir, I believe I’ve the thing here in my breast pocket; and to tell the truth, I’d like to see it put somewhere safe.”
“Quite right, my boy, to be sure,” said he. “Hand it over and I’ll keep it safe for you, if you like.”
“I was thinking, perhaps, Dr. Livesey—” I began.

“Perfectly right,” he broke in, cheerful as you please — “perfectly right; a gentleman and a magistrate. And come to think of it, I might as well ride round there myself and report to him, or to the squire. Master Pew’s dead, when all’s said; not that I’m sorry for it, but he’s dead, you see, and folk will use it against an officer of His Majesty’s revenue if they can. So I’ll tell you what, Hawkins — if you like, I’ll take you along.”
I thanked him warmly for the offer, and back we went to the hamlet, where the horses were waiting. By the time I’d explained my plan to mother, the whole party was already mounted.
“Dogger,” said Mr. Dance, “you’ve a good horse; take this lad up behind you.”
The moment I was up behind, gripping Dogger’s belt, the supervisor gave the word, and off the whole party went at a jolting trot along the road to Dr. Livesey’s.

chapters.title: The Captain’s Papers
paragraphs: We rode hard the whole way, until we pulled up before Dr. Livesey’s door. The front of the house was all dark.
Mr. Dance had me get down and knock, and Dogger held out a stirrup for me to climb down by. Almost at once the maid opened the door.
“Is Dr. Livesey in?” I asked.
No, she told us — he’d been home in the afternoon, but had since walked up to the hall to dine and pass the evening with the squire.
“Then up there we go, boys,” said Mr. Dance.

This time, the distance being short, I didn’t remount but ran at Dogger’s stirrup-leather to the lodge gates and on up the long, leafless, moonlit avenue to where the white line of the hall buildings looked out on either side over great old gardens. Here Mr. Dance dismounted and, taking me with him, was let into the house at a word.

The servant led us down a matted passage and showed us at the end into a great library, all lined with bookcases topped with busts, where the squire and Dr. Livesey sat with pipes in hand on either side of a bright fire.

I had never seen the squire so close before. He was a tall man, over six feet, and broad to match, with a bluff, rough-and-ready face, weathered and reddened and lined by his long travels. His eyebrows were very black and quick to move, which gave him a look of some temper — not bad-natured, you’d say, but hasty and high.
“Come in, Mr. Dance,” said he, very grand and gracious.
“Evening, Dance,” said the doctor with a nod. “And a good evening to you too, friend Jim. What fair wind blows you our way?”

Stiff and upright, the supervisor delivered his report like a schoolboy reciting a lesson; and you should have seen the two gentlemen lean in and trade glances, too caught up in surprise and interest to remember their pipes. At the part where my mother turned back to the inn, Dr. Livesey slapped his thigh outright, and the squire shouted “Bravo!” and snapped his long pipe against the grate. Well before the tale was done, Mr. Trelawney — the squire’s name, you’ll remember — was up and pacing the room, while the doctor, as though to listen the closer, had taken off his powdered wig, so that he sat there looking very odd indeed with his own cropped black head.
At last Mr. Dance finished the story.

“Mr. Dance,” said the squire, “you are a very fine fellow. And as for riding that black, vicious scoundrel down, I call it an act of virtue, sir — like treading on a cockroach. This lad Hawkins is a trump, I see. Hawkins, will you ring that bell? Mr. Dance must have some ale.”
“So, Jim,” said the doctor, “it’s you that has the very thing they were hunting, is it?”
“It’s here, sir,” I said, and put the oilskin packet into his hands.
The doctor turned it over, as if his fingers itched to open it; but instead of that he put it quietly away in his coat pocket.

“Squire,” said he, “once Dance has had his ale he’ll have to be off, of course, on the King’s business; but I mean to keep young Hawkins here to sleep under my roof, and, by your leave, I’d say we send up the cold pie and let the boy get his supper.”
“Have it your way, Livesey,” said the squire. “The boy’s earned a sight better than cold pie.”
So in came a great pigeon pie, set out on a side-table, and I ate my fill, for I was famished as a hawk, while Mr. Dance got another round of praise and was at last sent off about his business.
“And now, squire,” said the doctor.
“And now, Livesey,” said the squire in the same breath.
“One at a time, gentlemen, one at a time,” laughed Dr. Livesey. “I take it you’ve heard of this Flint?”

“Heard of him!” cried the squire. “Heard of him, you say! Why, he was the bloodthirstiest buccaneer that ever put to sea. Blackbeard was a mere child beside Flint. The Spaniards stood in such mortal dread of him that, I tell you, sir, there were days I was half proud he was an Englishman. I saw his topsails with my own eyes, off Trinidad, and the rum-soaked coward of a captain I sailed under turned tail — turned tail, sir, and ran back into Port of Spain.”
“I’ve heard of him too, mind you, back in England,” said the doctor. “But here’s the point: did the man have money?”
“Money!” cried the squire. “Did you hear the story? What were these villains after but money? What do they care for but money? What would they risk their rascally hides for but money?”

“That we shall soon find out,” said the doctor. “But you’re so confoundedly hot and full of exclamations that I can’t get a word in. What I want to know is this: suppose I have here in my pocket some clue to where Flint buried his treasure — will that treasure come to much?”

“Come to much, sir!” cried the squire. “It will come to this: if we have the clue you talk of, I’ll fit out a ship in Bristol dock, take you and young Hawkins here along, and have that treasure if it takes me a year to find it.”
“Very good,” said the doctor. “Then, if Jim agrees, we’ll open the packet” — and he laid it before him on the table.
The bundle was sewn up, and the doctor had to fetch his instrument case and cut the stitches with his medical scissors. Inside were two things — a book and a sealed paper.
“First we’ll try the book,” said the doctor.

The squire and I both peered over his shoulder as he opened it, for Dr. Livesey had kindly waved me round from the side-table, where I’d been eating, to share the fun of the search. On the first page were only a few scraps of writing, the sort a man might make with a pen for idleness or practice. One was the same as the tattoo — “Billy Bones his fancy”; then “Mr. W. Bones, mate,” “No more rum,” “Off Palm Key he got itt,” and other snatches, mostly single words and past making out. I couldn’t help wondering who had “got itt,” and what “itt” was that he got — a knife in the back, as like as not.
“Not much to be learned there,” said Dr. Livesey, turning on.

The next ten or twelve pages were filled with an odd run of entries. There was a date at one end of each line and a sum of money at the other, as in an ordinary account-book, but instead of any explanation, only a varying number of crosses between the two. On the 12th of June 1745, for instance, a sum of seventy pounds had plainly fallen due to someone, with nothing but six crosses to say why. In a few cases a place-name was added — “Offe Caraccas” — or a bare entry of latitude and longitude, like “62o 17′ 20″, 19o 2′ 40″.”

The record ran over close to twenty years, the separate sums growing larger as time went on, and at the very end a grand total had been worked out — after five or six false additions — with these words set under it: “Bones, his pile.”
“I can make neither head nor tail of it,” said Dr. Livesey.

“The thing’s as clear as daylight,” cried the squire. “This is the black-hearted hound’s account-book. These crosses stand for the ships or the towns they sank and plundered. The sums are the scoundrel’s own share, and where he feared things might get muddled, you see he added a word to make it plain. ‘Offe Caraccas’ — there was some poor vessel boarded off that coast. God help the souls that manned her — coral long ago.”
“Just so!” said the doctor. “There’s the good of having travelled. Just so! And you’ll notice the sums swell as the man climbed in rank.”
There was little else in the book but a few compass-bearings of places noted on the blank leaves toward the end, and a table for turning French, English, and Spanish money into a common value.
“A thrifty man!” cried the doctor. “Not one to be cheated.”
“And now,” said the squire, “for the other.”

The paper had been sealed in several places with a thimble for a seal — the very thimble, perhaps, I had found in the captain’s pocket. The doctor opened the seals with great care, and out fell the map of an island, with latitude and longitude, soundings, the names of hills and bays and inlets, and every particular needed to bring a ship to safe anchorage off its shores. It was about nine miles long and five across, shaped — you might say — like a fat dragon standing up, with two fine landlocked harbours and a hill in the middle marked “The Spy-glass.” There were several notes of a later date, but above all three crosses in red ink — two on the north of the island, one in the southwest — and beside this last, in the same red ink and a small neat hand very unlike the captain’s shaky scrawl, the words: “Bulk of treasure here.”
On the back the same hand had added this further note:
Tall tree, Spy-glass shoulder, bearing a point to the N. of N.N.E.
Skeleton Island E.S.E. and by E.
Ten feet.
The bar silver lies in the northern cache; you’ll strike it by following the line of the eastern hummock, ten fathoms to the south of the black crag with the face on it.
The weapons are easily come at in the sand-hill, north point of the northern inlet cape, bearing east and a quarter north. J.F.
That was all; but brief and, to me, unintelligible as it was, it filled the squire and Dr. Livesey with delight.

“Livesey,” said the squire, “you’ll give up this wretched practice at once. Tomorrow I set off for Bristol. In three weeks’ time — three weeks! — two weeks — ten days — we’ll have the best ship, sir, and the choicest crew in England. Hawkins shall come as cabin-boy. You’ll make a famous cabin-boy, Hawkins. You, Livesey, are ship’s doctor; I’m admiral. We’ll take Redruth, Joyce, and Hunter. We’ll have fair winds, a quick passage, and not the least trouble finding the spot — and money to spare, to roll in, to skip across the water like stones ever after.”
“Trelawney,” said the doctor, “I’ll go with you, and I’ll wager Jim will too, and do credit to the venture. There’s only one man I’m afraid of.”
“And who’s that?” cried the squire. “Name the dog, sir!”

“You,” said the doctor, “for you can’t hold your tongue. We’re not the only ones who know of this paper. The fellows who attacked the inn tonight — bold, desperate blades, no doubt of it — and the rest who stayed aboard that lugger, and more, I dare say, not far off, are every man of them bent, through thick and thin, on getting that money. Not one of us must go about alone till we’re at sea. Jim and I will stick together meanwhile; you’ll take Joyce and Hunter when you ride to Bristol; and from first to last, not one of us must breathe a word of what we’ve found.”
“Livesey,” returned the squire, “you’re forever in the right of it. From now on I’ll be as silent as the grave.”

chapters.title: I Go to Bristol
paragraphs: It was longer than the squire had reckoned before we were ready for sea, and none of our first plans — not even Dr. Livesey’s, of keeping me at his side — worked out as intended. The doctor had to go to London to find a physician to take over his practice; the squire was hard at it in Bristol; and I stayed on at the hall in the charge of old Redruth, the gamekeeper — near enough a prisoner, but brimful of sea-dreams and the most delicious daydreams of strange islands and adventures. For hours together I pored over the map, every detail of which I had by heart. Sitting by the fire in the housekeeper’s room, I came at that island in my fancy from every quarter; I roamed every acre of it; I climbed a thousand times to the tall hill they call the Spy-glass and from its top looked out on the most marvellous, ever-shifting views. Sometimes the isle swarmed with savages we fought, sometimes with dangerous beasts that hunted us; but in all my imaginings nothing fell out half so strange and tragic as our real adventures were to be.

So the weeks went by, until one fine day a letter came addressed to Dr. Livesey, with this note added: “To be opened, in his absence, by Tom Redruth or young Hawkins.” Obeying that, we found — or rather I found, the gamekeeper being a poor hand at anything but print — the following great news:
Old Anchor Inn, Bristol, March 1, 17—.
Dear Livesey — Since I don’t know whether you are at the hall or still in London, I am sending this to both places at once.
The ship is bought and fitted out. She lies at anchor, ready for sea. You never pictured a sweeter schooner — a child could sail her — two hundred tons; her name, HISPANIOLA.

I got her through my old friend Blandly, who has shown himself a perfect marvel from start to finish. The admirable fellow positively slaved on my behalf — and so, I may say, did everyone in Bristol, the moment they caught wind of the port we sail for: treasure, that is.
“Redruth,” said I, breaking off from the letter, “Dr. Livesey won’t like this. The squire’s been talking, after all.”
“And who’s got a better right?” growled the gamekeeper. “A pretty state of things if the squire mayn’t talk for Dr. Livesey, I should think.”
At that I gave up trying to comment and read straight on:

Blandly himself found the HISPANIOLA, and by the cleverest handling got her for a mere trifle. There’s a set of men in Bristol monstrously set against Blandly. They go so far as to claim that this honest creature would do anything for money, that the HISPANIOLA was his own, and that he sold her to me at a scandalous price — the most transparent slanders. Not one of them, though, dares deny the merits of the ship.
So far there wasn’t a hitch. The workpeople — riggers and the rest — were annoyingly slow, to be sure, but time mended that. It was the crew that gave me trouble.

I wanted a good twenty men — against natives, buccaneers, or the hateful French — and I had no end of bother scraping up so much as half a dozen, until the most extraordinary stroke of luck threw the very man I needed in my way.

I was standing on the dock when, by the merest chance, I fell into talk with him. He turned out to be an old sailor who kept a public house, knew every seafaring man in Bristol, had lost his health ashore, and wanted a good berth as cook to get back to sea. He had hobbled down that morning, he said, just to get a smell of the salt.

I was wonderfully touched — so would you have been — and out of sheer pity I signed him on the spot as ship’s cook. Long John Silver, they call him, and he has lost a leg; but I counted that a recommendation, since he lost it in his country’s service, under the immortal Hawke. He draws no pension, Livesey. Think what an abominable age we live in!

Well, sir, I thought I’d found only a cook, but it was a whole crew I had turned up. Between us, Silver and I rounded up in a few days a company of the toughest old salts you could imagine — no beauties to look at, but men, by their faces, of the most unbreakable spirit. I tell you, we could take on a frigate.
Long John even weeded out two of the six or seven I’d already engaged. He showed me in a moment that they were just the fresh-water swabs we had most to fear in a serious venture.

I am in the most magnificent health and spirits — eating like a bull, sleeping like a log — and yet I shan’t know a happy moment till I hear my old tarpaulins tramping round the capstan. To sea, ho! Hang the treasure! It’s the glory of the sea that has turned my head. So come post-haste, Livesey; don’t waste an hour, if you care for me.
Let young Hawkins go straight to see his mother, with Redruth to guard him, and then let the pair of you come full speed to Bristol. — John Trelawney.

Postscript. — I forgot to tell you that Blandly — who, by the by, is to send a consort after us if we’re not back by the end of August — has found an excellent fellow for sailing master: a stiff man, which I’m sorry for, but in every other way a treasure. Long John Silver dug up a thoroughly able man for mate, one named Arrow. And I have a boatswain who pipes, Livesey, so things shall be done man-o’-war fashion aboard the good ship HISPANIOLA.

I forgot to mention that Silver is a man of means; I know for a fact he keeps a banker’s account that has never once been overdrawn. He leaves his wife to run the inn; and as she is a woman of colour, a pair of old bachelors like you and me may be forgiven for guessing that it is the wife, quite as much as his health, that sends him roving again. — J.T.
P.P.S. — Hawkins may spend one night with his mother. — J.T.

You can imagine the state that letter threw me into. I was half wild with delight; and if ever I scorned a man, it was old Tom Redruth, who could do nothing but grumble and lament. Any of the under-gamekeepers would gladly have changed places with him; but that wasn’t the squire’s pleasure, and the squire’s pleasure was as good as law to them all. No one but old Redruth would have dared so much as grumble.

Next morning he and I set out on foot for the Admiral Benbow, where I found my mother in good health and good spirits. The captain, who had so long made everything wretched, was gone where the wicked cease from troubling. The squire had had the whole place put to rights, the public rooms and the sign repainted, and some furniture added — above all a fine armchair for mother behind the bar. He had also found her a boy as apprentice, so she shouldn’t lack help while I was away.

It was the sight of that boy that first brought home my situation to me. Until that moment I had thought only of the adventures ahead, never of the home I was leaving; and now, at the sight of this clumsy stranger who was to take my place beside my mother, I had my first fit of tears. I’m afraid I led the boy a dog’s life, for being new to the work he gave me a hundred chances to correct him and put him down, and I wasn’t slow to take them.

The night passed, and the next day, after dinner, Redruth and I were on the road again. I said goodbye to mother, and to the cove where I’d lived since I was born, and to the dear old Admiral Benbow — though, since the repainting, no longer quite so dear. One of my last thoughts was of the captain, who had so often tramped the beach in his cocked hat, with his sabre-scarred cheek and his old brass telescope. Next moment we’d rounded the corner, and home was out of sight.

The mail coach picked us up about dusk at the Royal George on the heath. I was wedged between Redruth and a stout old gentleman, and in spite of the swift motion and the cold night air I must have dozed from the very start, and then slept like a log up hill and down dale through stage after stage; for when I was woken at last it was by a punch in the ribs, and I opened my eyes to find us standing still before a big building in a city street, with the day already broad about us.
“Where are we?” I asked.
“Bristol,” said Tom. “Get down.”

Mr. Trelawney had taken lodgings at an inn well down the docks, to oversee the work on the schooner. There we now had to walk, and our way — to my great delight — ran along the quays past a huge throng of ships of every size and rig and nation. On one, sailors were singing at their work; on another, men were aloft high over my head, hanging to lines no thicker, it seemed, than a spider’s thread. Though I’d lived by the shore all my life, I felt I had never been near the sea before. The smell of tar and salt was new to me. I saw the most wonderful figureheads, every one of which had been far across the ocean. I saw, too, many old sailors with rings in their ears and whiskers curled in ringlets and tarry pigtails, rolling along in their swaggering, clumsy sea-walk; and if I had seen as many kings or archbishops I couldn’t have been more delighted.
And I was going to sea myself — to sea in a schooner, with a piping boatswain and pigtailed singing sailors — to sea, bound for an unknown island, to hunt for buried treasure!

While I was still lost in that lovely daydream, we came all at once in front of a big inn and met Squire Trelawney, got up from head to foot like a sea-officer in stout blue cloth, stepping out the door with a smile on his face and a capital imitation of a sailor’s roll.
“Here you are!” he cried. “And the doctor came down from London last night. Bravo — the ship’s company’s complete!”
“Oh, sir,” I cried, “when do we sail?”
“Sail!” says he. “We sail tomorrow!”

chapters.title: At the Sign of the Spy-glass
paragraphs: When I’d finished my breakfast, the squire gave me a note addressed to John Silver, at the sign of the Spy-glass, and told me I’d find the place easily by following the line of the docks and keeping a sharp lookout for a little tavern with a big brass telescope for a sign. I set off overjoyed at the chance to see more of the ships and seamen, and threaded my way through a great crowd of people and carts and bales — for the dock was now at its busiest — until I found the tavern in question.

It was a cheerful enough little place. The sign was freshly painted, the windows had neat red curtains, the floor was clean-sanded. There was a street on either side and an open door on each, which let plenty of light into the big, low room, for all the clouds of tobacco smoke.
Most of the customers were seafaring men, and the talk ran so loud that I lingered in the doorway, half afraid to step inside.

As I waited, a man came out of a side room, and at one glance I felt sure it must be Long John. His left leg was cut off close to the hip, and under the left shoulder he carried a crutch, which he worked with wonderful skill, hopping about on it like a bird. He was very tall and strong, with a face as broad as a ham — plain and pale, but shrewd and smiling. Indeed, he seemed in the best of spirits, whistling as he moved among the tables, with a merry word or a clap on the shoulder for his more favoured guests.

Now, to tell the truth, from the very first mention of Long John in the squire’s letter a fear had taken hold of me that he might turn out to be the very one-legged sailor I’d watched for so long at the old Benbow. But one look at the man before me settled it. I had seen the captain, and Black Dog, and the blind man Pew, and I thought I knew what a buccaneer looked like — a very different creature, to my mind, from this clean, good-humoured landlord.
I screwed up my courage then and there, stepped inside, and went right up to where the man stood propped on his crutch, in talk with a customer.
“Mr. Silver, sir?” I asked, holding out the note.
“Yes, my lad,” said he; “that’s my name, sure enough. And who might you be?” Then, catching sight of the squire’s letter, he seemed to me to give something almost like a start.
“Oh!” said he, quite loud, putting out his hand. “I see. You’re our new cabin-boy. Glad to see you, I am.”
And he took my hand in his big, firm grip.

Just then one of the customers over at the far side got up suddenly and made for the door. It was close beside him, and he was out in the street in a moment. But his haste had caught my eye, and I knew him at a glance — the tallow-faced man, short two fingers, who had been the first to come to the Admiral Benbow.
“Oh,” I cried, “stop him! It’s Black Dog!”
“I don’t care two coppers who he is,” cried Silver, “but he’s not paid his score. Harry, run and nab him.”
One of the others, the one nearest the door, sprang up and gave chase.
“Were he Admiral Hawke himself, he’d settle his score,” cried Silver; then, dropping my hand, he asked, “Now, what name did you give him? Black what?”
“Black Dog, sir,” said I. “Hasn’t Mr. Trelawney spoken to you of the buccaneers? He was one of that crew.”
“What?” cried Silver. “In my house! Ben, run and lend Harry a hand. So he was one of those swabs, was he? Was that you drinking with him, Morgan? Step up here.”
The man he called Morgan — an old, grey-haired, mahogany-faced sailor — shuffled forward rather sheepishly, working his wad of tobacco.
“Now then, Morgan,” said Long John, very stern, “you never set eyes on that Black — Black Dog — before now, did you?”
“Not I, sir,” said Morgan, with a salute.
“You didn’t know his name, now, did you?”
“No, sir.”

“By thunder, Tom Morgan, it’s as well for you!” the landlord burst out. “If you’d been mixed up with the likes of him, you’d never have set foot in my house again, you may take your oath on that. And what was he saying to you?”
“I couldn’t rightly tell you, sir,” Morgan answered.

“Is that a head you’ve got on your shoulders, or a blessed dead-eye?” cried Long John. “Couldn’t rightly tell, eh! Maybe you couldn’t rightly tell who it was you were talking to, neither? Come on — what was he gabbing about? Voyages, captains, ships? Out with it! What was it?”
“We was talkin’ about keel-hauling,” Morgan answered.
“Keel-hauling, were you? And a mighty fitting subject, too, you may lay to it. Get back to your seat for a lubber, Tom.”

And then, as Morgan rolled back to his place, Silver added to me in a confidential whisper that I found very flattering: “He’s an honest enough man, Tom Morgan — only stupid. And now,” he ran on aloud, “let’s see — Black Dog? No, the name’s strange to me, it is. And yet — I’ve a notion I’ve — yes, I’ve laid eyes on the swab. He used to come in here with a blind beggar, so he did.”
“He did indeed, you may take my word for it,” said I. “And I knew the blind man as well — Pew, his name was.”

“It was!” cried Silver, quite excited now. “Pew! That was the name, sure as fate. Ah, he had a sharkish look about him, he did! If we run this Black Dog to earth, now, there’ll be news for Captain Trelawney! Ben’s a fine runner; few seamen run better than Ben. He ought to overhaul him, hand over hand, by the powers! Talked of keel-hauling, did he? I’ll keel-haul him!”

All the while he was jerking out these phrases, he was stumping up and down the tavern on his crutch, banging the tables with his hand, and putting on such a show of feeling as would have satisfied an Old Bailey judge or a Bow Street runner. My suspicions had been thoroughly roused again at finding Black Dog at the Spy-glass, and I watched the cook closely. But he was too deep, too quick, and too clever for me; and by the time the two men came back out of breath, owning they’d lost the track in the crowd and been scolded like thieves, I’d have gone bail for the innocence of Long John Silver.

“See here now, Hawkins,” said he, “here’s a cruel hard thing for a man like me, isn’t it now? There’s Captain Trelawney — what’s he to think? Here I have this confounded son of a Dutchman sitting in my own house, drinking my own rum! Then you come and tell me plain what he is; and here I let him give us all the slip right under my blessed deadlights! Now, Hawkins, you do me justice with the cap’n. You’re only a lad, but you’re as smart as paint — I saw that the moment you came in. Now here it is: what could I do, on this old timber I hobble about on? When I was an able-bodied master mariner I’d have come up alongside him, hand over hand, and brought him to in a brace of shakes — but now —”
And then, all of a sudden, he broke off, and his jaw dropped as if he’d just remembered something.
“My score!” he burst out. “Three goes of rum, and shiver my timbers if it hadn’t gone clean out of my head!”
And dropping onto a bench, he laughed till the tears ran down his cheeks. I couldn’t help joining in, and we laughed together, peal upon peal, till the whole tavern rang with it.

“Why, what a precious old sea-calf I am!” he said at last, wiping his face. “You and me ought to get on, Hawkins, for hang me if I shouldn’t be rated ship’s boy myself.
