But come now, stand by to go about — this won’t do. Duty’s duty, messmates. I’ll clap on my old cocked hat and step along with you to Captain Trelawney to report this business. For mind you, it’s serious, young Hawkins; and neither you nor me’s come out of it with what you might call credit. Nor you neither, says you — not smart, neither of us. But split my sides! That was a good one about my score.”
And he started laughing again, so heartily that, though I didn’t see the joke as he did, I was once more forced to join in his mirth.

On our little walk along the quays he made himself the most interesting of companions, telling me about the various ships we passed — their rig, tonnage, and nation — explaining the work going on (how one was unloading, another taking in cargo, a third making ready for sea), and now and then giving me some little story of ships or seamen, or repeating a nautical phrase till I had it by heart. I began to see that here was one of the best of all possible shipmates.
When we reached the inn, the squire and Dr. Livesey were sitting together, finishing a quart of ale with toast in it, before going aboard the schooner on a tour of inspection.

Long John told the whole story, first to last, with great spirit and perfect truthfulness. “That’s how it was, now, wasn’t it, Hawkins?” he’d say every now and then, and I could always back him to the hilt.
The two gentlemen were sorry Black Dog had got away, but we all agreed there was nothing to be done; and after he’d been complimented, Long John took up his crutch and left.
“All hands aboard by four this afternoon!” the squire shouted after him.
“Aye, aye, sir,” called the cook from the passage.
“Well, squire,” said Dr. Livesey, “I don’t, as a rule, put much faith in your finds; but I’ll say this — John Silver suits me.”
“The man’s a perfect trump,” the squire declared.
“And now,” the doctor added, “Jim may come aboard with us, mayn’t he?”
“To be sure he may,” says the squire. “Take your hat, Hawkins, and we’ll have a look at the ship.”

chapters.title: Powder and Arms
paragraphs: The Hispaniola lay some way out, and we passed under the figureheads and round the sterns of many other ships, their cables now grating beneath our keel, now swinging over our heads. At last we came alongside, and as we stepped aboard we were met and saluted by the mate, Mr. Arrow — a brown old sailor with earrings and a squint. He and the squire were thick as thieves, but I soon noticed things were not so easy between Mr. Trelawney and the captain.
This last was a sharp-faced man who seemed put out by everything aboard, and was soon to tell us why; for we’d hardly got down into the cabin when a sailor came after us.
“Captain Smollett, sir, asking to speak with you,” said he.
“I’m at the captain’s orders, always. Send him in,” said the squire.
The captain, close on his man’s heels, came straight in and shut the door behind him.
“Now then, Captain Smollett — what is it you have to say? All well, I trust; everything shipshape and seaworthy?”
“Well, sir,” said the captain, “I’d best be plain with you, even if it gives offence. This cruise is not to my liking; nor are the men; nor is my officer. That’s the whole of it, short and sweet.”
“Perhaps, sir, you don’t like the ship either?” asked the squire, very angry, as I could see.
“As to that, sir, I can’t say — I’ve not seen her tried,” said the captain. “A clever craft, by her looks; more than that I’ll not venture.”
“And perhaps, sir, you don’t like your employer, into the bargain?” says the squire.
But here Dr. Livesey broke in.

“Hold on,” said he, “hold on. No good comes of questions like that but bad blood. The captain has said either too much or too little, and I’m bound to ask him to explain himself. You don’t, you say, like this cruise. Now — why not?”

“I was engaged, sir, on what they call sealed orders, to sail this ship wherever that gentleman should bid me,” said the captain. “So far, well and good. But now I find every man before the mast knows more than I do. I don’t call that fair — do you?”
“No,” said Dr. Livesey, “I don’t.”

“Next,” said the captain, “I learn we’re going after treasure — and I hear it from my own crew, mind you. Now, treasure is ticklish work; I’ve no liking for treasure voyages on any terms, and least of all when they’re meant to be secret and the secret — begging your pardon, Mr. Trelawney — has been told to the parrot.”
“Silver’s parrot?” asked the squire.

“It’s a manner of speaking,” said the captain. “Blabbed, I mean. It’s my belief neither of you gentlemen knows what he’s about; but I’ll tell you how I see it — it’s life or death, and a close-run thing.”
“That’s all clear, and likely enough true,” replied Dr. Livesey. “We take the risk, but we’re not so much in the dark as you suppose. Next, you say you don’t like the crew. Aren’t they good seamen?”
“I don’t like them, sir,” returned Captain Smollett. “And if it comes to that, I think I ought to have had the choosing of my own hands.”
“Perhaps you ought,” the doctor allowed. “My friend should, perhaps, have taken you with him; but the slight, if it was one, wasn’t meant. And you don’t like Mr. Arrow?”
“I don’t, sir. He’s a good seaman, I believe, but too free with the crew to make a good officer. A mate ought to keep to himself — and not go drinking with the men before the mast.”
“Do you mean he drinks?” cried the squire.
“No, sir,” said the captain; “only that he’s too familiar.”
“Well now, the long and short of it, captain?” asked the doctor. “Tell us what you want.”
“Well, gentlemen — are you set on going through with this cruise?”
“Set like iron,” answered the squire.

“Very good,” said the captain. “Then, since you’ve heard me out so patiently on things I can’t prove, hear a few words more. They’re stowing the powder and the arms in the fore hold. Now, there’s a good place under the cabin — why not put them there? That’s the first point. Next, you’re bringing four of your own people, and I’m told some of them are to be berthed forward. Why not give them the berths here by the cabin? That’s the second.”
“Anything more?” asked Mr. Trelawney.
“One thing more,” said the captain. “There’s been too much blabbing already.”
“Far too much,” the doctor agreed.

“I’ll tell you what I’ve heard with my own ears,” the captain went on: “that you have a map of an island; that there are crosses on it marking where treasure lies; and that the island lies —” and then he named the latitude and longitude, exactly.
“I never told that,” cried the squire, “to a living soul!”
“The hands know it, sir,” returned the captain.
“Livesey, then it must have been you, or Hawkins,” cried the squire.

“It hardly matters now who it was,” replied the doctor. And I could see that neither he nor the captain set much store by Mr. Trelawney’s protests — nor did I, to be honest, loose a talker as he was; though in this one case I do believe he was right, and that nobody had given away the island’s position.
“Well, gentlemen,” the captain continued, “I don’t know who holds this map; but I make it a condition it’s kept secret even from me and Mr. Arrow. Otherwise I must ask you to let me resign.”

“I see,” said the doctor. “You want us to keep the thing dark, and to make a fort of the stern of the ship, manned with my friend’s own people and stocked with all the arms and powder aboard. In other words — you fear a mutiny.”

“Sir,” said Captain Smollett, “meaning no offence, I won’t have words put in my mouth. No captain alive would be right to put to sea at all if he had grounds to say that. As for Mr. Arrow, I believe him perfectly honest; some of the men the same; all of them may be, for what I know. But I’m answerable for the ship’s safety and for the life of every soul aboard her. I see things going, as I think, not quite as they should. And I ask you to take certain precautions — or to let me resign my berth. That’s all.”

“Captain Smollett,” the doctor began with a smile, “did you ever hear the fable of the mountain and the mouse? You’ll forgive me, I’m sure, but you put me in mind of it. When you came in here, I’ll stake my wig, you meant a deal more than this.”
“Doctor,” said the captain, “you’re a shrewd one. When I came in here I meant to be discharged. I’d no notion Mr. Trelawney would hear a word of it.”

“And no more I would have,” cried the squire. “Had Livesey not been here, I’d have seen you to the devil first. As it is, I’ve heard you out. I’ll do as you ask — but I think the worse of you for it.”
“As you please, sir,” said the captain. “You’ll find me a man that does his duty.”
And with that he took his leave.
“Trelawney,” said the doctor, “against all my expectations, I do believe you’ve got two honest men aboard with you — that man, and John Silver.”
“Silver, by all means,” cried the squire; “but as for that insufferable humbug, I call his conduct unmanly, unsailorly, and downright un-English.”
“Well,” says the doctor, “we shall see.”
When we came up on deck, the men had already begun shifting the arms and powder, heaving and yo-ho-ing at the work, while the captain and Mr. Arrow stood by overseeing them.

The new arrangement suited me very well. The whole schooner had been overhauled; six berths had been knocked together aft, out of what had been the after-part of the main hold, and this set of cabins was joined to the galley and forecastle only by a railed-off passage on the port side. The plan had been for the captain, Mr. Arrow, Hunter, Joyce, the doctor, and the squire to have these six berths. Now Redruth and I were to get two of them, and Mr. Arrow and the captain were to sleep on deck in the companion, which had been widened on both sides until you might almost have called it a round-house. Still very low, of course, but with room to swing two hammocks, and even the mate seemed pleased with it. Even he, perhaps, had had his doubts about the crew — but that’s only a guess, for, as you’ll hear, we hadn’t long the benefit of his opinion.
We were all hard at work, the powder and berths still being shifted about, when the last man or two — Long John with them — came off from shore in a boat.
The cook came up the side as nimbly as a monkey, and the moment he saw what was afoot, “So ho, mates!” says he. “What’s all this?”
“We’re shifting the powder, Jack,” one answers.
“Why, by the powers,” cried Long John, “shift it now and we’ll lose the morning tide!”
“My orders!” said the captain, short. “You can go below, my man. The hands will be wanting their supper.”
“Aye, aye, sir,” answered the cook; and touching his forelock, he vanished at once toward his galley.
“That’s a good man, captain,” said the doctor.

“Very likely, sir,” replied Captain Smollett. “Easy with that, men — easy now,” he went on, to the fellows shifting the powder; and then, suddenly noticing me examining the swivel-gun we carried amidships, a long brass nine-pounder, “Here, you, ship’s boy,” he cried, “out of that! Off with you to the cook, and find some work.”
And as I made off, I caught him saying, loud enough for all, to the doctor: “No favourites aboard my ship.”
I can tell you, I was entirely of the squire’s mind, and hated the captain heartily.

chapters.title: The Voyage
paragraphs: All that night we were in a great bustle, getting things stowed in their places, with boatload after boatload of the squire’s friends — Mr. Blandly and the like — coming off to wish him a good voyage and a safe return. We never had a night at the Admiral Benbow that gave me half the work, and I was dog-tired when, a little before dawn, the boatswain piped and the crew set to the capstan-bars. Tired as I was — twice as tired, I’d not have left the deck, it was all so new and fascinating to me: the short, sharp orders, the shrill of the whistle, the men hurrying to their places by the dim light of the ship’s lanterns.
“Now, Barbecue, give us a song,” cried one voice.
“The old one,” cried another.
“Aye, aye, mates,” said Long John, who stood by with his crutch under his arm, and struck up at once the tune and words I knew so well:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest—”
And then the whole crew came in on the chorus:
“Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”
And on the third “Ho!” they drove the bars round with a will.

Even at that stirring moment it carried me back to the old Admiral Benbow in a flash, and I seemed to hear the dead captain’s voice joining the chorus. But soon the anchor was up and dripping at the bows, soon the sails began to draw, and the land and the shipping went sliding by on either hand; and before I could lie down for an hour’s sleep, the HISPANIOLA had begun her voyage to the Isle of Treasure.

I shan’t tell the voyage in detail. It went well enough. The ship proved a good one, the crew were capable seamen, and the captain knew his business through and through. But before we made the length of Treasure Island, two or three things happened that have to be set down.

Mr. Arrow, to begin with, turned out even worse than the captain had feared. He had no authority among the men, who did as they liked with him. And that wasn’t the worst, for after a day or two at sea he took to coming on deck with bleared eye, flushed cheeks, a stammering tongue, and every other mark of drink. Time and again he was ordered below in disgrace. Sometimes he fell and cut himself; sometimes he lay all day in his little bunk at the side of the companion; sometimes, for a day or two, he’d be nearly sober and do his work after a fashion.

Meanwhile we could never make out where he got the liquor. That was the ship’s great riddle. Watch him as we might, we couldn’t solve it; and if we asked him to his face, he’d only laugh, if he were drunk, and if he were sober swear solemnly that he never touched anything but water.

He was useless as an officer and a bad example to the men; and plainly, at this rate, he’d soon be the death of himself; so no one was much surprised — nor very sorry — when, one dark night with a heavy sea running, he vanished altogether and was never seen again.
“Overboard!” said the captain. “Well, gentlemen, that spares us the bother of clapping him in irons.”

But there we were, without a mate, and one of the men had of course to be promoted. The boatswain, Job Anderson, was the likeliest aboard, and though he kept his old rank, he served after a fashion as mate. Mr. Trelawney had been to sea, and his knowledge made him useful — he’d often stand a watch himself in easy weather. And the coxswain, Israel Hands, was a careful, crafty, seasoned old hand who could be trusted at a pinch with almost anything.
He was a great crony of Long John Silver’s, and that brings me round to speak of our ship’s cook — Barbecue, as the men called him.

Aboard ship he slung his crutch from a lanyard round his neck, to keep both hands as free as he could. It was a sight to see him jam the foot of the crutch against a bulkhead and, propped there, riding every roll of the ship, get on with his cooking as steady as a man ashore. Stranger still to watch him cross the deck in the heaviest weather. He’d rigged a line or two — “Long John’s earrings,” the men called them — to help him over the widest stretches, and he’d swing himself from hold to hold, now using the crutch, now trailing it by its lanyard, as fast as another man could walk. Even so, some of the men who had sailed with him before were sorry to see him brought so low.

“He’s no common man, is Barbecue,” the coxswain told me. “He was well schooled in his young days, and can talk like a book when he’s a mind to; and brave — why, a lion’s nothing beside Long John! I’ve seen him grapple four men and crack their heads together, and him with no weapon at all.”

The whole crew respected him, and some of them obeyed him. He had a knack of speaking to each man and doing every one some little kindness. To me he was tireless in his kindness, always glad to see me in the galley, which he kept as bright as a new pin, the dishes hung up polished, and his parrot in a cage in one corner.

“Come along, Hawkins,” he’d say, “come and have a yarn with John. There’s nobody more welcome than yourself, my son. Sit you down and hear the news. Here’s Cap’n Flint — I call my parrot Cap’n Flint, after the famous buccaneer — here’s Cap’n Flint foretelling a roaring success to our voyage. Weren’t you, Cap’n?”
And the parrot would rattle off, “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!” so fast you wondered it didn’t run out of breath, until John dropped his handkerchief over the cage.

“Now that bird,” he’d say, “is maybe two hundred years old, Hawkins — they live pretty near forever, mostly; and if anything’s seen more wickedness, it must be the devil himself. She’s sailed with England — the great Cap’n England, the pirate. She’s been to Madagascar, and Malabar, and Surinam, and Providence, and Portobello. She was there at the fishing-up of the wrecked plate-ships. That’s where she learned ‘Pieces of eight’ — and small wonder, three hundred and fifty thousand of ’em, Hawkins! She was at the boarding of the Viceroy of the Indies, out of Goa, she was; and to look at her you’d take her for a babe. But you’ve smelt powder — haven’t you, Cap’n?”
“Stand by to go about!” the parrot would scream.

“Ah, she’s a handsome craft, she is,” the cook would say, and feed her sugar from his pocket; and then the bird would peck at the bars and swear away past all believing for wickedness. “There,” John would add, “you can’t touch pitch and not be mucked, lad. Here’s my poor old innocent bird swearing blue fire, and none the wiser for it, you may lay to that. She’d swear the same, you might say, before a chaplain.” And John would touch his forelock with that solemn air of his that made me think he was the best of men.

Meanwhile the squire and Captain Smollett were still on distant terms. The squire made no secret of it — he despised the captain. The captain, for his part, never spoke unless spoken to, and then sharp and short and dry, with not a word wasted. He owned, when pushed into a corner, that he seemed to have been wrong about the crew — that some were as smart as he’d wish to see, and all had behaved well enough. As for the ship, he’d taken a downright fancy to her. “She’ll lie a point nearer the wind than a man has any right to ask of his own wedded wife, sir. But,” he’d add, “all I say is, we’re not home yet, and I don’t like the cruise.”
At that the squire would turn away and stump up and down the deck with his chin in the air.
“A trifle more of that man,” he’d say, “and I shall burst.”

We had some heavy weather, which only showed off the qualities of the HISPANIOLA. Every man aboard seemed well content, and they’d have been hard to please otherwise, for it’s my belief no ship’s company was ever so coddled since Noah first put to sea. Double grog on the least excuse; duff on odd days — if the squire heard, say, that it was any man’s birthday; and always a barrel of apples standing open in the waist for anyone to help himself who had a mind.
“Never knew good come of it yet,” the captain said to Dr. Livesey. “Spoil your forecastle hands and you make devils of them. That’s my belief.”
But good did come of the apple barrel, as you’ll hear; for if it hadn’t been for that, we’d have had no warning at all, and might every one of us have died by treachery.
This is how it came about.

We had run up into the trades to get the wind of the island we were bound for — I’m not allowed to be plainer — and now we were running down for it, a sharp lookout kept day and night. By the longest reckoning it was about the last day of our outward run; some time that night, or by noon next day at the latest, we should sight Treasure Island. We were heading south-southwest with a steady breeze on the beam and a quiet sea. The HISPANIOLA rolled along steadily, now and again dipping her bowsprit with a puff of spray. Everything was drawing, high and low; and every soul was in the best of spirits, for we were now so near the end of the first part of our adventure.

Now, just after sundown, with all my work done and my way to my berth before me, it came into my head that I’d like an apple. I ran up on deck. The watch were all forward, looking out for the island; the man at the helm was watching the set of the sail and whistling softly to himself; and that was the only sound, except the swish of the sea against the bows and along the sides.

I climbed right into the apple barrel and found there was scarcely an apple left; but sitting there in the dark, what with the wash of the water and the rocking of the ship, I had either dropped asleep or was just on the edge of it when a heavy man sat down close by with rather a thump. The barrel shook as he leaned his shoulders against it, and I was on the point of jumping up when the man began to speak. It was Silver’s voice; and before I’d heard a dozen words I would not have shown myself for the whole world, but lay there shaking and listening, in the last extreme of fear and curiosity — for from those dozen words I understood that the lives of every honest man aboard hung on me alone.

chapters.title: What I Heard in the Apple-Barrel
paragraphs: “No, not I,” said Silver. “Flint was cap’n; I was quartermaster, on account of my timber leg. The same broadside that took my leg, old Pew lost his sight in. It was a trained surgeon that took it off me — college man and all, Latin by the bucketful and the rest of it; but he was hanged like a dog and dried in the sun with the others, at Corso Castle. Roberts’ men, those were, and it all came of changing the names of their ships — Royal Fortune and such. Now, what a ship’s been christened, christened let her stay, says I. So it was with the Cassandra, that brought us all home safe from Malabar after England took the Viceroy of the Indies; and so it was with the old Walrus, Flint’s ship, that I’ve seen running red with blood and near sinking with the weight of gold.”
“Ah!” cried another voice — the youngest hand aboard, and plainly full of admiration — “Flint was the flower of the flock!”

“Davis was a man too, by all accounts,” said Silver. “I never sailed with him; England first, then Flint — that’s my history; and now here on my own hook, in a manner of speaking. I put by nine hundred from England, and two thousand after Flint. That’s not bad for a hand before the mast — every penny safe in the bank. It’s not the earning that does it now, it’s the saving, you may lay to that. Where’s all of England’s men now? I couldn’t tell you. Where’s Flint’s? Why, most of ’em aboard here, and glad enough to get their duff — some of ’em were begging before that. Old Pew, after he’d lost his sight — and you’d think he’d have known shame — went through twelve hundred pound in a year, like a lord in Parliament. And where’s he now? Dead, and under hatches; but for the two years before that, shiver my timbers, the man was starving! He begged, and he stole, and he cut throats, and starved even so, by the powers!”
“Well, it’s not much use, after all,” said the young seaman.

“It’s no use to fools, you may lay to it — that, nor anything,” cried Silver. “But see here: you’re young, but you’re as smart as paint. I saw that the moment I laid eyes on you, and I’ll talk to you like a man.”

You can imagine how I felt, hearing this abominable old rogue use on another the very same flattering words he had used on me. I think, if I could have, I’d have killed him through the barrel. Meanwhile he ran on, never dreaming he was overheard.

“Here’s the truth of it about gentlemen of fortune. They live rough, and they run the risk of the gallows, but they eat and drink like fighting-cocks, and when a cruise is done they’ve hundreds of pounds in their pockets where other men have hundreds of farthings. Most of it goes on rum and a good spree, and back to sea in their shirts. But that’s not my course. I lay it all by — a little here, a little there, and never too much in any one place, for fear of being suspected. I’m fifty, mark you; once I’m back from this cruise, I set up for a real gentleman. Time enough, says you. Ah, but I’ve lived easy meanwhile — never denied myself anything my heart fancied, slept soft and ate dainty all my days, except when I was at sea. And how did I begin? Before the mast, like you!”
“Well,” said the other, “but the rest of your money’s gone now, isn’t it? You’ll not dare show your face in Bristol after this.”
“Why, where do you suppose it is?” asked Silver, with a jeer.
“At Bristol, in banks and such,” his companion answered.

“It was,” said the cook, “it was, when we weighed anchor. But my old missis has the whole of it by now. And the Spy-glass is sold — lease, goodwill, rigging and all — and the old girl’s gone off to meet me. I’d tell you where, for I trust you, but it’d set the other mates jealous.”
“And can you trust your missis?” asked the other.

“Gentlemen of fortune,” returned the cook, “mostly trust one another precious little, and right they are too, you may lay to it. But I have a way with me, I have. When a mate slips his cable — one that knows me, I mean — he won’t be in the same world as old John for long after. There was some feared Pew, and some feared Flint; but Flint his own self was feared of me. Feared, and proud of it he was. The roughest crew afloat, Flint’s were; the devil himself would have thought twice about shipping with them. Well now, I tell you, I’m no boaster, and you saw for yourself how easy I keep company; but in the days I was quartermaster, ‘lambs’ wasn’t the word for Flint’s old buccaneers. Ah, you can feel safe aboard old John’s ship.”
“Well, I’ll tell you straight,” the lad replied, “I didn’t like the job by half a quarter till I’d had this talk with you, John; but there’s my hand on it now.”
“A brave lad, and smart with it,” said Silver, wringing the boy’s hand so hard the whole barrel shook; “a finer figurehead for a gentleman of fortune I never clapped eyes on.”

By now I had begun to take the meaning of their words. By a “gentleman of fortune” they plainly meant nothing more nor less than a common pirate, and the little scene I’d overheard was the last act in the corrupting of one of the honest hands — perhaps the last one left aboard. But on that point I was soon set at ease, for at a low whistle from Silver a third man strolled up and sat down with them.
“Dick’s straight,” said Silver.

“Oh, I knew Dick was straight,” returned the coxswain, Israel Hands. “He’s no fool, isn’t Dick.” He turned his quid and spat. “But look here,” he went on, “here’s what I want to know, Barbecue — how much longer are we to stand off and on like a blessed bumboat? I’ve had near enough of Cap’n Smollett; he’s bullied me long enough, by thunder! I want to get into that cabin, I do. I want their pickles and their wines and all.”

“Israel,” said Silver, “your head was never worth much, and isn’t now. But you can hear, I reckon; your ears are big enough, anyway. So here’s my word: you’ll berth forward, you’ll live hard, you’ll talk soft, and you’ll keep sober till I give the signal — and you may lay to that, my son.”
“Well, I’m not saying no, am I?” growled the coxswain. “What I’m saying is, when? That’s all I’m asking — when?”

“When! By the powers!” cried Silver. “Well, since you must have it, I’ll tell you when. The very last moment I can stretch it to — that’s when. Here’s a first-rate seaman, Cap’n Smollett, sailing the blessed ship for us. Here’s this squire and doctor with a map and the rest — and where it is, I don’t know, do I? No more do you, says you. Well then, I mean to have this squire and doctor find the stuff for us, and help us get it aboard, by the powers. Then we’ll see. If I could be sure of the lot of you, you sons of double Dutchmen, I’d let Cap’n Smollett sail us halfway home again before I struck.”
“Why, aren’t we all seamen aboard here?” said the lad Dick.

“We’re all forecastle hands, you mean,” snapped Silver. “We can steer a course — but who’s to set one? That’s where all you fine fellows come to grief, first and last. If I had my way, I’d let Cap’n Smollett work us back at least into the trades, so we’d have no blessed miscalculations and a spoonful of water a day. But I know your sort. I’ll settle with the pair of ’em at the island, the minute the money’s aboard — and a pity it is. But there’s no contenting you till you’re drunk. Split my sides, it’s a sick heart I have, sailing with the likes of you!”
“Easy all, Long John,” cried Israel. “Who’s crossing you?”

“Why, how many tall ships, do you think, have I seen boarded and taken? And how many brisk lads strung up to dry in the sun at Execution Dock?” cried Silver. “And all of it from this same hurry, and hurry, and hurry. You hear me? I’ve seen a thing or two at sea, I have. If you’d only lay your course, and a point to windward, you’d ride in carriages, you would. But not you! I know you. You’ll have your skinful of rum tomorrow, and go to the gallows.”

“Everybody knew you for a kind of chaplain, John; but there’s others could hand and steer as well as you,” said Israel. “They liked their bit of fun, they did. They weren’t so stiff and dry; they took their fling, like jolly companions all.”
“So?” says Silver. “And where are they now? Pew was that sort, and he died a beggar. Flint was, and he died of rum at Savannah. Ah, a sweet crew they were, to be sure! Only — where are they?”
“But,” asked Dick, “when we do lay ’em by the heels, what’s to be done with ’em?”

“Now there’s a man after my own heart!” cried the cook in admiration. “That’s what I call business. Well, what’s your notion? Maroon ’em ashore? That would have been England’s way. Or cut ’em down like so much pork? That was Flint’s way, or Billy Bones’s.”
“Billy was the man for that,” said Israel. “‘Dead men don’t bite,’ he’d say. Well, he’s dead himself now; he knows the rights of it now; and if ever a rough hand came to port, it was Billy.”

“Right you are,” said Silver, “rough and ready. But mark me: I’m an easy man — quite the gentleman, says you; but this time it’s serious. Duty’s duty, mates. I vote death. When I’m in Parliament and riding in my coach, I don’t want any of these sea-lawyers turning up at home unlooked-for, like the devil at prayers. Wait, is what I say; but when the time comes — why, let her rip!”
“John,” cries the coxswain, “you’re a man!”

“You’ll say so, Israel, when you’ve seen,” said Silver. “Only one thing I claim — I claim Trelawney. I’ll wring his calf’s head off his shoulders with these two hands. Dick!” he added, breaking off, “just jump up, like a good lad, and fetch me an apple, to wet my pipe.”

You can fancy the terror I was in! I’d have leaped out and run if I’d had the strength, but my limbs and my heart both failed me. I heard Dick begin to get up, and then someone seemed to stop him, and the voice of Hands broke in: “Oh, stow that! Don’t go sucking at that bilge-water, John. Let’s have a go of the rum.”
“Dick,” said Silver, “I’ll trust you. There’s a gauge set on the keg, mind. Here’s the key — fill a pannikin and fetch it up.”
Terrified as I was, I couldn’t help thinking that this must have been how Mr. Arrow came by the strong drink that destroyed him.

Dick was gone only a little while, and while he was away Israel spoke straight into the cook’s ear. It was no more than a word or two I could catch, yet I gathered something of importance; for, besides other scraps to the same purpose, I heard this whole sentence plainly: “Not another man of them will join.” So there were still faithful men aboard.

When Dick came back, the three of them took the pannikin turn and turn about and drank — one “To luck,” another “Here’s to old Flint,” and Silver himself, in a kind of singsong, “Here’s to ourselves, and hold your luff; plenty of prizes and plenty of duff.”

Just then a sort of brightness fell into the barrel, and looking up I saw the moon had risen and was silvering the mizzen-top and shining white on the belly of the foresail; and almost in the same moment the lookout’s voice shouted, “Land ho!”

chapters.title: Council of War
paragraphs: There was a great rush of feet across the deck. I could hear people tumbling up from the cabin and the forecastle; and, slipping out of my barrel in an instant, I dived behind the foresail, doubled back toward the stern, and came out on the open deck just in time to join Hunter and Dr. Livesey in the rush to the weather bow.

There all hands were already gathered. A belt of fog had lifted almost the moment the moon appeared. Away to the southwest we saw two low hills, a couple of miles apart, and rising behind one of them a third, higher hill whose peak was still wrapped in fog. All three looked sharp and conical.

So much I saw, as if in a dream, for I hadn’t yet got over my horrible fright of a minute before. And then I heard Captain Smollett giving orders. The HISPANIOLA was brought a couple of points nearer the wind and now sailed a course that would just clear the island to the east.
“Now then, men,” said the captain, once all was sheeted home, “has any of you ever laid eyes on that land ahead?”
“I have, sir,” said Silver. “I watered there once, aboard a trader I cooked in.”
“The anchorage is on the south, behind a little island, I take it?” asked the captain.

“Yes, sir — Skeleton Island, they call it. It was a great haunt of pirates once, and a hand we had aboard knew all their names for it. That hill to the north they call the Foremast Hill; there’s three in a row running south — fore, main, and mizzen, sir. But the main — the big one, with the cloud on it — they mostly call the Spy-glass, on account of the lookout they kept there while they lay in the anchorage cleaning; for it’s there they careened their ships, sir, begging your pardon.”
“I’ve a chart here,” says Captain Smollett. “Tell me if this is the place.”

Long John’s eyes fairly burned in his head as he took the chart; but one glance at the freshness of the paper told me he was bound for a disappointment. This wasn’t the map we’d found in Billy Bones’s chest, but an exact copy, complete in every particular — names and heights and soundings — save only for the red crosses and the written notes. Sharp as his vexation must have been, Silver had the self-command to hide it.

“Yes, sir,” said he, “this is the spot, right enough, and very prettily drawn out too. Who might have done it, I wonder? The pirates were too ignorant, I reckon. Aye, here it is — ‘Capt. Kidd’s Anchorage’ — the very name my shipmate gave it. There’s a strong current sets along the south, then turns north up the west coast. You did right, sir,” says he, “to haul your wind and keep to windward of the island — leastways if you meant to run in and careen, and there’s no better place for that in these waters.”
“Thank you, my man,” says Captain Smollett. “I’ll ask your help again later. You may go.”

I was struck by the coolness with which John owned to knowing the island, and I confess I was half-frightened when I saw him moving closer to me. He didn’t know, of course, that I’d overheard his council from the apple barrel; and yet by now I had taken such a horror of his cruelty, his double-dealing, and his power that I could scarcely keep from shuddering when he laid his hand on my arm.

“Ah,” says he, “this here’s a sweet spot, this island — a sweet spot for a lad to come ashore on. You’ll bathe, and climb trees, and hunt goats, you will; and you’ll go up those hills as nimble as a goat yourself. Why, it makes me young again. I was near forgetting my timber leg, I was. It’s a fine thing to be young and have your ten toes, you may lay to that. When you’ve a mind to go exploring, you just ask old John, and he’ll put up a snack for you to carry along.”
And with the friendliest clap on my shoulder, he swung himself off forward and went below.

Captain Smollett, the squire, and Dr. Livesey were in talk together on the quarter-deck, and anxious as I was to tell my story, I dared not break in on them openly. While I was still hunting in my mind for some likely excuse, Dr. Livesey called me over. He’d left his pipe below, and being a slave to tobacco, meant to send me for it; but the moment I was near enough to speak without being overheard, I burst out, “Doctor, let me speak. Get the captain and squire down to the cabin, and then send for me on some pretence. I have terrible news.”
The doctor’s face changed a little, but in a moment he had himself in hand again.
“Thank you, Jim,” said he, quite loud, “that was all I wanted to know,” as if he’d put a question to me.

And with that he turned on his heel and went back to the other two. They talked a little among themselves, and though none of them started, or raised his voice, or so much as whistled, it was plain Dr. Livesey had passed on my message; for the next thing I heard was the captain giving an order to Job Anderson, and all hands being piped on deck.

“My lads,” said Captain Smollett, “I’ve a word to say to you. This land we’ve sighted is the place we’ve been making for. Mr. Trelawney — a very open-handed gentleman, as we all know — has just put me a question or two; and since I was able to tell him that every man aboard had done his duty, high and low, as well as I could ever ask, why, he and I and the doctor are going below to the cabin to drink your health and luck, and grog will be served out for you to drink ours. I’ll tell you what I think of it: I think it’s handsome of him. And if you think as I do, you’ll give a good sea-cheer for the gentleman that does it.”
The cheer went up — of course it did; but it rang out so full and hearty that I confess I could hardly believe these same men were plotting for our blood.
“One more cheer for Cap’n Smollett!” cried Long John when the first had died down.
And that one was given with a will too.
On the back of it the three gentlemen went below; and not long after, word came forward that Jim Hawkins was wanted in the cabin.

I found the three of them seated round the table, a bottle of Spanish wine and a dish of raisins before them, the doctor smoking away with his wig in his lap — and that, I knew, was a sign he was upset. The stern window stood open, for it was a warm night, and you could see the moon shining on the ship’s wake behind.
“Now, Hawkins,” said the squire, “you have something to tell us. Out with it.”

I did as I was bid, and as briefly as I could, gave the whole of Silver’s conversation. No one broke in till I’d done, nor did any of the three so much as stir, but they kept their eyes on my face from first to last.
“Jim,” said Dr. Livesey, “take a seat.”

And they sat me down at the table beside them, poured me a glass of wine, heaped my hands with raisins, and all three, one after another and each with a bow, drank to my health, and their service, for my luck and my courage.
“Well, captain,” said the squire, “you had the right of it, and I was wrong. I’m an ass, I own it, and I’m at your orders.”

“No more an ass than I, sir,” returned the captain. “I never knew a crew that meant mischief but showed signs of it beforehand, for any man with an eye in his head to read and act on. But this crew,” he added, “has me beaten.”
“Captain,” said the doctor, “by your leave — that’s Silver’s doing. A very remarkable man.”
“He’d look remarkably well from a yard-arm, sir,” returned the captain. “But this is talk, and talk leads nowhere. I see three or four points, and with Mr. Trelawney’s leave I’ll name them.”
“You, sir, are the captain. Yours is the word,” says Mr. Trelawney, grand as you please.

“First point,” began Mr. Smollett. “We must go on, because we can’t turn back. Give the word to put about and they’d rise on the instant. Second point, we have time on our side — at least till the treasure’s found. Third point, there are faithful hands left. Now, sir, it must come to blows sooner or later; and what I say is, let’s take time by the forelock, as they say, and fall on them some fine day when they least look for it. Can we count, I take it, on your own household men, Mr. Trelawney?”
“As upon myself,” declared the squire.
“Three, then,” reckoned the captain; “and ourselves makes seven, counting Hawkins here. Now, what about the honest hands?”
“Most likely Trelawney’s own men,” said the doctor — “the ones he picked up for himself before he fell in with Silver.”
“No,” said the squire. “Hands was one of mine.”
“I did think I could trust Hands,” the captain added.
“And to think they’re every one of them Englishmen!” the squire broke out. “Sir, I’ve half a mind to blow the ship sky-high.”

“Well, gentlemen,” said the captain, “the best I can offer isn’t much. We must lie low, by your leave, and keep a sharp lookout. It’s hard on a man, I know. It would be pleasanter to come straight to blows. But there’s no help for it till we know our men. Lie low and whistle for a wind — that’s my view.”
“Jim here,” said the doctor, “can help us more than anyone. The men aren’t shy of him, and Jim’s a sharp-eyed lad.”
“Hawkins, I put prodigious faith in you,” added the squire.

This left me feeling pretty desperate, for I felt altogether helpless; and yet, by an odd chain of chances, it really was through me that safety came in the end. Meanwhile, talk as we might, only seven out of twenty-six were men we could count on; and of those seven, one was a boy — so that the grown men on our side stood six against their nineteen.

chapters.title: How I Began My Shore Adventure
paragraphs: When I came on deck next morning, the island looked altogether different. The breeze had dropped away entirely, and we had made a good deal of headway in the night, so that we now lay becalmed about half a mile off the low eastern shore. Grey woods covered much of the land. The even grey was broken here and there by streaks of yellow sandbank in the lower parts, and by many tall pines that overtopped the rest, some standing alone, some in clumps; but the general colour was uniform and dreary. Above the woods the hills ran up in bare spires of rock. All were oddly shaped, and the Spy-glass — three or four hundred feet the tallest on the island — was the strangest of all, rising sheer on nearly every side and then cut off short at the top, like a pedestal made to set a statue on.

The HISPANIOLA was rolling her scuppers under in the ocean swell. The booms snatched at the blocks, the rudder banged from side to side, and the whole ship creaked and groaned and jumped like a factory at work. I had to cling hard to a backstay, and the world spun dizzily before me; for though I was a fair enough sailor under way, this lying still and being rolled about like a bottle was a thing I never could stomach without a qualm, above all in the morning on an empty belly.

Perhaps it was that — perhaps it was the look of the island, with its grey, melancholy woods, its wild stone spires, and the surf we could both see and hear thundering and foaming on the steep beach — but at any rate, though the sun shone bright and hot, and the shore birds fished and cried all round us, and you'd think anyone would be glad to make land after so long at sea, my heart sank, as the saying goes, into my boots; and from that first look on, I loathed the very thought of Treasure Island.

We had a dreary morning's work ahead of us, for there wasn't a breath of wind, and the boats had to be lowered and manned and the ship warped three or four miles round the corner of the island and up the narrow channel to the haven behind Skeleton Island. I volunteered for one of the boats, where of course I had no business at all. The heat was stifling, and the men grumbled savagely over the labour. Anderson had charge of my boat, and instead of keeping the crew in order he grumbled as loudly as the worst of them.
“Well,” he said, with an oath, “it's not forever.”
I thought that a very bad sign; for up to that day the men had gone about their work briskly and willingly, but the mere sight of the island had loosened the bonds of discipline.

All the way in, Long John stood by the steersman and conned the ship. He knew the channel like the back of his hand, and though the man heaving the lead found everywhere more water than the chart gave, John never once hesitated.
“There's a strong scour with the ebb,” he said, “and this channel's been dug out, you might say, with a spade.”

We brought up just where the anchor was marked on the chart, about a third of a mile from either shore — the mainland on one hand, Skeleton Island on the other. The bottom was clean sand. The splash of our anchor sent up clouds of birds wheeling and crying over the woods, but in under a minute they had settled again and all was silent once more.

The place was entirely landlocked, smothered in woods, the trees coming right down to the high-water mark; the shores mostly flat, and the hilltops standing round at a distance like an amphitheatre, one here, one there. Two little rivers — or rather two swamps — drained into this pond, as you might call it; and the foliage about that part of the shore had a kind of poisonous brightness to it. From the ship we could see nothing of the house or the stockade, both quite buried among the trees; and but for the chart on the companion, we might have thought ourselves the first ever to anchor there since the island rose out of the sea.

Not a breath of air stirred, nor any sound but the surf booming half a mile off along the beaches and against the outer rocks. A queer, stagnant smell hung over the anchorage — sodden leaves and rotting tree-trunks. I saw the doctor sniffing and sniffing at it, like a man tasting a bad egg.
“I don't know about treasure,” he said, “but I'll stake my wig there's fever here.”

If the men's behaviour had been alarming in the boats, it grew downright threatening once they were aboard again. They sprawled about the deck, growling together; the slightest order met with a black look and was obeyed grudgingly and carelessly. Even the honest hands must have caught the contagion, for there wasn't one man aboard to set another right. Mutiny, plainly, hung over us like a thundercloud.

And it wasn't only we of the cabin party who saw the danger. Long John was hard at work, going from knot to knot of men, spending himself in good counsel — and for sheer example no man could have bettered him. He fairly outdid himself in eagerness and civility, all smiles to everyone. Let an order be given and John would be up on his crutch in a moment with the cheeriest “Aye, aye, sir!” in the world; and when there was nothing else to do, he kept up one song after another, as if to cover the sullenness of the rest.
Of all the gloomy features of that gloomy afternoon, this open anxiety on Long John's part seemed the worst.
We held a council in the cabin.

“Sir,” said the captain, “if I venture another order, the whole crew will be down on us at the run. Here's how it stands, you see. I get a rough answer, don't I? Well, if I answer back, the pikes will be out in two shakes; if I don't, Silver will see there's something behind it, and the game's lost. Now, we've just one man we can rely on.”
“And who is that?” asked the squire.

“Silver, sir,” returned the captain. “He's as eager as you or I to smother this down. It's only a fit of temper; he'd soon coax them out of it, given the chance — and what I propose is to give him the chance. Let's allow the men an afternoon ashore. If they all go, why, we'll fight the ship. If none of them go, then we hold the cabin, and God defend the right. And if some go — mark my words, sir — Silver will bring them back aboard as meek as lambs.”

So it was settled. Loaded pistols were served out to all the trusty men; Hunter, Joyce, and Redruth were let into the secret, and took it with less surprise and better spirit than we'd looked for; and then the captain went up on deck and spoke to the crew.

“My lads,” said he, “it's been a hot day, and we're all tired and out of sorts. A turn ashore will do nobody harm — the boats are still in the water; take the gigs, and as many as please may go ashore for the afternoon. I'll fire a gun half an hour before sundown.”

I do believe the silly fellows thought they'd be barking their shins on treasure the moment they landed, for they came out of their sulks in an instant and gave a cheer that woke the echo in a distant hill and set the birds flying and squalling round the anchorage once more.

The captain was too shrewd to stay in the way. He whisked himself out of sight in a moment, leaving Silver to make up the party — and I fancy it was as well he did. Had he stayed on deck, he could no longer have pretended not to understand the situation. It was as plain as day. Silver was the captain now, and a mighty mutinous crew he had under him. The honest hands — and I was soon to see there were such aboard — must have been dull fellows indeed. Or rather, I suppose the truth was this: that all hands had been soured by the ringleaders' example, only some more and some less; and a few, being decent men at bottom, could be neither led nor driven any further. It is one thing to loaf and skulk, and quite another to seize a ship and murder a parcel of innocent men.
At last, however, the party was made up. Six men were to stay aboard, and the other thirteen, Silver among them, set about embarking.

And then it was that the first of the wild notions came into my head — the notions that did so much, in the end, to save our lives. If Silver had left six men aboard, plainly our party couldn't seize and fight the ship; and since only six were left, plainly the cabin party had no present need of me. It struck me at once to slip ashore. In a twinkling I was over the side and curled up in the bows of the nearest boat, and almost at the same moment she shoved off.

No one took any notice of me, except the bow oar, who said, “Is that you, Jim? Keep your head down.” But Silver, from the other boat, looked sharply across and called to know if that was me; and from that moment I began to wish I hadn't come.

The crews raced for the beach; but the boat I was in, having a start and being both lighter and better manned, shot well ahead of her consort, and her bow had run in among the shore-side trees, and I had caught a branch and swung myself out and plunged into the nearest thicket, while Silver and the rest were still a hundred yards behind.
“Jim, Jim!” I heard him shouting.
But you may be sure I paid no heed; jumping, ducking, and crashing through the brush, I ran straight before my nose until I could run no more.

chapters.title: The First Blow
paragraphs: I was so pleased at having given Long John the slip that I began to enjoy myself and to look about with some interest at the strange land I was in.

I had crossed a marshy stretch full of willows and bulrushes and odd, outlandish swamp-trees, and now came out on the edge of an open piece of rolling, sandy country about a mile long, dotted with a few pines and a great many twisted trees, not unlike oaks in growth but pale in the leaf, like willows. On the far side of the open ground rose one of the hills, its two strange, craggy peaks shining bright in the sun.

Now, for the first time, I felt the joy of exploring. The isle was uninhabited; I had left my shipmates behind, and nothing lived ahead of me but dumb beasts and birds. I wandered this way and that among the trees. Here and there were flowering plants I didn't know; here and there I saw snakes, and one lifted its head from a ledge of rock and hissed at me with a noise rather like a spinning top. Little did I guess he was a deadly enemy, and that the noise was the famous rattle.

Then I came to a long thicket of those oak-like trees — live oaks, or evergreen oaks, I heard afterward they should be called — that grew low along the sand like brambles, their boughs oddly twisted, their leaves close-packed like thatch. The thicket ran down from the crown of one of the sandy knolls, spreading and growing taller as it went, until it reached the edge of the broad, reedy fen through which the nearest of the little rivers soaked its way into the anchorage. The marsh steamed in the strong sun, and the outline of the Spy-glass quivered through the haze.

All at once a sort of stir began among the bulrushes; a wild duck flew up with a quack, then another, and soon over the whole face of the marsh a great cloud of birds hung screaming and wheeling in the air. I judged at once that some of my shipmates must be coming along the edge of the fen. Nor was I wrong, for soon I heard the far-off, low murmur of a human voice, which, as I kept listening, grew steadily louder and nearer.
This put me into a great fright, and I crawled in under cover of the nearest live oak and crouched there, listening, as silent as a mouse.

Another voice answered, and then the first — which I now knew for Silver's — took up the talk again and ran on a long while in a stream, only now and then broken in upon by the other. By the sound, they must have been talking earnestly, almost fiercely; but no clear word reached me.
At last the speakers seemed to pause, and perhaps to sit down, for not only did they come no nearer, but the birds themselves began to settle and drop back to their places in the swamp.

And now I began to feel I was shirking my duty — that since I'd been so rash as to come ashore with these desperadoes, the least I could do was to overhear them at their councils; and that my plain duty was to creep as close as I could, under cover of the crouching trees.
I could fix the speakers' direction well enough, both by their voices and by the behaviour of the few birds still hanging in alarm above the intruders' heads.

Crawling on all fours, I worked steadily but slowly toward them, until at last, lifting my head to a gap in the leaves, I could look down into a little green hollow beside the marsh, thickly screened with trees, where Long John Silver and one of the crew stood face to face, in talk.
The sun beat full on them. Silver had flung his hat down beside him on the ground, and his great, smooth, fair face, all shining with the heat, was turned up to the other man's in a kind of appeal.

“Mate,” he was saying, “it's because I think the world of you — gold dust, you are, and you may lay to that! If I hadn't taken to you like pitch, do you suppose I'd be here warning you? It's all up — you can't make it nor mend it; it's to save your neck I'm speaking, and if one of the wild ones knew it, where would I be, Tom — tell me that, where would I be?”

“Silver,” said the other — and I noticed he was not only red in the face but spoke as hoarse as a crow, his voice shaking too, like a stretched rope — “Silver,” says he, “you're old, and you're honest, or have the name for it; and you've money, which is more than most poor sailors; and you're brave, or I'm much mistaken. And you'll tell me you'll let yourself be led off by that pack of swabs? Not you! As God sees me, I'd sooner lose my hand. If I turn against my duty—”

And there, all at once, a noise cut him short. I had found one honest hand — and here, in the same moment, came word of another. Far out across the marsh there rose, all of a sudden, a sound like a cry of rage, then another on its heels, and then one long, horrible, drawn-out scream. The rocks of the Spy-glass flung it back a dozen times; the whole army of marsh-birds rose again, darkening the sky, with a single whirr; and long after that death-yell still rang in my brain, silence had settled back over everything, and only the rustle of the descending birds and the boom of the far-off surf stirred the languor of the afternoon.
Tom had leaped at the sound like a horse at the spur; but Silver never batted an eye. He stood where he was, balanced lightly on his crutch, watching his companion like a snake about to strike.
“John!” said the sailor, putting out his hand.
“Hands off!” cried Silver, and sprang back a full yard — quick and sure, it seemed to me, as a trained acrobat.
“Hands off, then, if you will, John Silver,” said the other. “It's a black conscience that can make you afraid of me. But in heaven's name, tell me — what was that?”
“That?” said Silver, smiling away, but warier than ever, his eye shrunk to a pinpoint in that broad face, yet glittering like a crumb of glass. “That? Oh, I reckon that'll be Alan.”
And at that, poor Tom blazed up like a hero.

“Alan!” he cried. “Then God rest him for a true seaman! And as for you, John Silver — long you've been a mate of mine, but you're no mate of mine now. If I die like a dog, I'll die doing my duty. You've killed Alan, have you? Then kill me too, if you can. But I defy you.”

And with that the brave fellow turned his back square on the cook and set off walking for the beach. But he wasn't to go far. With a cry John caught at a branch of a tree, snatched the crutch from under his arm, and sent that clumsy missile whistling through the air. It struck poor Tom point-first, and with stunning force, square between the shoulders. His hands flew up, he gave a sort of gasp, and down he went.

Whether he was much hurt or little, no one could ever tell. Likely enough, by the sound, his back was broken on the spot. But he was given no time to come round. Silver, nimble as a monkey even without leg or crutch, was on top of him the next instant, and had twice buried his knife to the haft in that defenceless body. From my hiding place I could hear him panting aloud as he struck the blows.

I don't rightly know what it is to faint, but I do know that for the next little while the whole world went swimming away from me in a whirling mist — Silver, the birds, the tall Spy-glass peak, all going round and round and topsy-turvy before my eyes, and every kind of bell ringing and far-off voices shouting in my ears.

When I came to myself again, the monster had pulled himself together, crutch under his arm and hat on his head. Just before him Tom lay still on the turf; but the murderer paid him no heed, wiping his blood-stained knife the while on a wisp of grass. Everything else was as before — the sun still beating pitilessly on the steaming marsh and the tall mountain peak — and I could scarcely make myself believe that murder had really been done, and a man's life cruelly cut short, a moment since before my eyes.

But now John put his hand in his pocket, drew out a whistle, and blew several measured blasts that carried far across the heated air. I couldn't, of course, tell what the signal meant, but it woke all my fears at once. More men would come. I might be found. They had already killed two of the honest hands; after Tom and Alan, might I not be next?

At once I set about backing out, crawling away as fast and as silently as I could manage toward the more open part of the wood. As I went, I could hear hails passing to and fro between the old buccaneer and his comrades, and the sound of danger gave me wings. The moment I was clear of the thicket I ran as I never ran before, hardly caring which way I went so long as it took me from the murderers; and as I ran, fear grew and grew on me until it turned to a kind of frenzy.

Indeed, could anyone have been more utterly lost than I was? When the gun fired, how should I dare go down to the boats among those fiends, still reeking from their crime? Wouldn't the first of them who saw me wring my neck like a snipe's? Wouldn't my very absence prove to them my alarm, and so my fatal knowledge? It was all over, I thought. Goodbye to the HISPANIOLA; goodbye to the squire, the doctor, and the captain! Nothing was left me but to starve, or to die by the hands of the mutineers.

All this while, as I say, I kept running, and without noticing it had drawn near the foot of the little two-peaked hill, into a part of the island where the live oaks stood more widely apart and looked more like forest trees in their bearing and their size. Among them rose a few scattered pines, some fifty, some nearer seventy feet high. The air, too, smelt fresher here than down by the marsh.
And here a fresh alarm brought me up short, with a thumping heart.

chapters.title: The Man of the Island
paragraphs: From the side of the hill — steep and stony just there — a spurt of gravel was dislodged and came rattling and bounding down through the trees. My eyes turned that way by instinct, and I saw a figure leap, quick as thought, behind a pine-trunk. What it was — bear, man, or monkey — I couldn't for the life of me tell. It looked dark and shaggy; more than that I didn't know. But the terror of this new apparition held me rooted.

I was cut off now, it seemed, on both sides: behind me the murderers, before me this lurking thing. And straightaway I began to prefer the dangers I knew to the one I didn't. Silver himself seemed less terrible set against this creature of the woods; so I turned on my heel, and, with a sharp look back over my shoulder, started to retrace my steps toward the boats.

At once the figure showed itself again and, fetching a wide circle, began to head me off. I was tired, at all events; but had I been as fresh as when I rose that morning, I could see it was hopeless to match such an adversary for speed. From trunk to trunk the creature flitted like a deer, running upright on two legs, like a man, yet unlike any man I'd ever seen, for it stooped almost double as it ran. Still, a man it was — of that I could no longer doubt.

I began to call to mind what I'd heard of cannibals, and was within an ace of shouting for help. But the mere fact that he was a man, wild as he was, had somewhat steadied me, and my fear of Silver began to come back in proportion. I stood still, then, casting about for some way of escape; and as I did so, the thought of my pistol flashed on me. Once I remembered I wasn't defenceless, courage glowed up again in my heart, and I set my face squarely toward this man of the island and walked briskly at him.

By now he was hidden again behind another tree-trunk; but he must have been watching me close, for the moment I moved his way he came out and took a step to meet me. Then he hung back, drew away, came forward once more, and at last, to my wonder and confusion, threw himself on his knees and held out his clasped hands in entreaty.
At that I stopped again.
“Who are you?” I asked.
“Ben Gunn,” he answered, his voice as hoarse and creaky as a rusty lock. “I'm poor Ben Gunn, I am; and I've not spoke with a Christian soul these three years.”

I could see now that he was a white man like myself, and even pleasant-featured. His skin, wherever it showed, was scorched by the sun; even his lips were black, and his pale eyes looked startling in so dark a face. Of all the beggars I'd ever seen or imagined, he was the king for rags. He was clad in shreds of old ship's canvas and old sea-cloth, this strange patchwork held together by the most assorted, mismatched fastenings — brass buttons, bits of stick, loops of tarry rope-yarn. About his waist he wore an old brass-buckled leather belt, the one solid thing in the whole rig of him.
“Three years!” I cried. “Were you shipwrecked?”
“Nay, mate,” said he; “marooned.”
The word I knew, and what it meant — a hideous punishment common among the buccaneers, where a man is dumped on some bare, far-off island with a pinch of powder and shot and abandoned there.

“Marooned three years gone,” he went on, “and lived on goats ever since, and berries, and oysters. Wherever a man is, says I, a man can shift for himself. But, mate, my heart aches for Christian food. You wouldn't happen to have a bit of cheese about you, now? No? Why, many's the long night I've dreamed of cheese — toasted, mostly — and woke up again, and here I was.”
“Once I'm aboard again,” said I, “you shall have cheese by the stoneful.”

All this time he had been fingering the stuff of my jacket, stroking my hands, looking at my boots, and, in the pauses of his talk, showing a child's delight at the sight of a fellow creature. But at my last words he started up into a kind of wary slyness.
“Once you're aboard again, is it?” he echoed. “And just who's to stop you?”
“Not you, I'm sure,” I answered.
“And right you are,” he cried. “Now — what do you call yourself, mate?”
“Jim,” I told him.
“Jim, Jim,” says he, quite pleased it seemed. “Well now, Jim, I've lived that rough you'd be ashamed to hear of it. To look at me now, you wouldn't think I'd had a pious mother, would you?” he asked.
“Why, no — not particularly,” I owned.

“Ah, well,” said he, “but I had — remarkable pious. And I was a civil, pious boy, and could reel off my catechism that fast you couldn't have told one word from the next. And here's what it came to, Jim — and it began with pitch-and-toss on the blessed gravestones! That's how it began, but it went further than that, and so my mother told me, and foretold the whole of it, she did, the pious woman. But it was Providence put me here. I've thought it all out, on this lonely island, and I'm back to being pious. You'll not catch me at the rum so much now — just a thimbleful for luck, of course, first chance I get. I'm set on being good, and I see the way to it. And, Jim” — looking all round and dropping his voice to a whisper — “I'm rich.”

By now I felt sure the poor fellow had gone cracked in his loneliness, and I suppose it showed in my face, for he repeated it hotly: “Rich! Rich, I tell you! And I'll tell you more — I'll make a man of you, Jim. Ah, Jim, you'll bless your stars you were the first to find me!”
And at this a sudden shadow came lowering over his face, and he gripped my hand the tighter and raised a warning forefinger before my eyes.
“Now, Jim, you tell me true — that's not Flint's ship?” he asked.
At that I had a happy thought. I began to believe I'd found an ally, and answered him straight off.
“It's not Flint's ship, and Flint is dead; but I'll tell you true, since you ask — there are some of Flint's old hands aboard, worse luck for the rest of us.”
“Not a man — with one — leg?” he gasped.
“Silver?” I asked.
“Ah, Silver!” says he. “That was the name.”
“He's the cook — and the ringleader too.”
He had hold of my wrist still, and at the word he fairly wrung it.
“If you were sent by Long John,” said he, “I'm as good as pork, and I know it. But where were you, do you suppose?”

I had made up my mind in a moment, and by way of answer told him the whole story of our voyage and the fix we were in. He listened with the keenest interest, and when I'd done he patted me on the head.

“You're a good lad, Jim,” said he; “and you're all in a clove hitch, aren't you? Well, you just put your trust in Ben Gunn — Ben Gunn's the man for it. Now, do you reckon it likely your squire would prove an open-handed gentleman, if he were helped — him being in a clove hitch, as you put it?”
I told him the squire was the most open-handed of men.

“Aye, but you see,” returned Ben Gunn, “I didn't mean a gate to keep and a suit of livery and the like; that's not my mark, Jim. What I mean is, would he be likely to come down to the tune of, say, one thousand pounds out of money that's as good as a man's own already?”
“I'm sure he would,” said I. “As things stood, every hand was to have a share.”
“And a passage home?” he added, with a look of great cunning.
“Why,” I cried, “the squire's a gentleman. And besides, if we were rid of the others, we'd need you to help work the ship home.”
“Ah,” said he, “so you would.” And he seemed mightily relieved.

“Now, I'll tell you what,” he went on. “This much I'll tell you, and no more. I was in Flint's ship when he buried the treasure — he and six along with him, six strong seamen. They were ashore the best part of a week, and us standing off and on in the old WALRUS. One fine day up went the signal, and here comes Flint by himself in a little boat, his head done up in a blue scarf. The sun was rising, and deadly white he looked across the bows. But there he was, mind you — and the six all dead; dead and buried. How he'd done it, not a man aboard could make out. It was battle, murder, and sudden death, at the least — him against six. Billy Bones was the mate; Long John, he was quartermaster; and they asked him where the treasure was. ‘Ah,' says he, ‘you can go ashore, if you like, and stay,' says he; ‘but as for the ship, she'll beat up for more, by thunder!' That's what he said.”

“Well, three years back I was in another ship, and we raised this island. ‘Boys,' said I, ‘here's Flint's treasure; let's land and find it.' The cap'n didn't like it, but my messmates were all of a mind, and we landed. Twelve days they searched, and every day they'd a worse word for me, till one fine morning all hands went back aboard. ‘As for you, Benjamin Gunn,' says they, ‘here's a musket,' they says, ‘and a spade, and a pickaxe. You can stop here and dig out Flint's money for yourself,' they says.”

“Well, Jim, three years I've been here, and not a bite of Christian food from that day to this. But now you look at me — do I look like a man before the mast? No, says you. Nor was I, neither, says I.”
And with that he winked and gave me a hard pinch.

“Just you say those very words to your squire, Jim,” he went on: “‘Nor was he, neither' — those are the words. Three years he was the man of this island, light and dark, fair weather and rain; and sometimes, maybe, he'd give a thought to a prayer (says you), and sometimes, maybe, he'd think of his old mother, so be as she's still living (you'll say); but the most of Gunn's time (and this is what you'll tell him) — the most of his time went on another matter. And then you'll give him a nip, the way I do you.”
And he pinched me again, in the most confidential way.

“Then,” he went on, “then you'll up and say this: Gunn's a good man (you'll say), and he puts a precious sight more trust — a precious sight, mind that — in a gentleman born than in these gentlemen of fortune, having been one of them himself.”
“Well,” I said, “I don't understand a word of all this. But that's neither here nor there, for how am I to get aboard?”

“Ah,” said he, “there's the rub, and no mistake. Well, there's my boat, that I made with my own two hands. I keep her under the white rock. If the worst comes to the worst, we might try her after dark. Hi!” he broke off. “What's that?”
For at that very moment — the sun yet an hour or two from setting — every echo on the island woke and roared back the boom of a cannon.
“They've begun to fight!” I cried. “Follow me.”
And I set off running toward the anchorage, my terrors all forgotten, while close at my side the marooned man trotted along easily and light in his goatskins.

“Left, left,” says he; “bear to your left hand, mate Jim! In under the trees with you! That's where I killed my first goat. They don't come down here now; they keep up on the mountains for fear of Benjamin Gunn. Ah, and there's the graveyard” — the cemetery, he must have meant. “You see the mounds? I came here and prayed, now and then, when I thought a Sunday was maybe about due. It wasn't quite a chapel, but it seemed more solemn-like; and then, says you, Ben Gunn was short-handed — no chaplain, nor so much as a Bible and a flag, you say.”
So he ran on as I ran, neither looking for nor getting any answer.
The cannon-shot was followed, after a good interval, by a volley of small arms.
Another pause; and then, not a quarter of a mile ahead, I saw the Union Jack flutter out above a wood.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: How the Ship Was Abandoned
paragraphs: It was about half past one — three bells, in sea talk — when the two boats put off from the HISPANIOLA and went ashore. The captain, the squire, and I were talking things over in the cabin. Had there been a breath of wind, we'd have fallen on the six mutineers left aboard with us, slipped our cable, and stood out to sea. But there was no wind; and, to crown our helplessness, down came Hunter with word that Jim Hawkins had slipped into a boat and gone ashore with the rest.

It never crossed our minds to doubt Jim Hawkins, but we feared for his safety. With the men in the temper they were in, it seemed an even chance whether we'd see the lad again. We hurried on deck. The pitch was bubbling in the seams; the foul stench of the place turned my stomach; if ever a man smelt fever and dysentery, it was in that vile anchorage. The six rogues sat grumbling under a sail in the forecastle; ashore we could see the gigs made fast, with a man sitting in each, close by where the river runs in. One of them was whistling “Lillibullero.”
Waiting told on the nerves, and it was settled that Hunter and I should go ashore in the jolly-boat to find out what we could.

The gigs had borne off to their right, but Hunter and I pulled straight in, toward the stockade marked on the chart. The two men left guarding the boats seemed thrown into a flurry at the sight of us; “Lillibullero” broke off, and I could see the pair arguing what they ought to do. Had they gone and told Silver, things might have fallen out quite otherwise; but they had their orders, I suppose, and chose to sit tight where they were and fall back on “Lillibullero.”

There was a slight bend in the coast, and I steered to put it between us, so that even before we landed the gigs were out of our sight. I jumped out and came as near a run as I dared, a big silk handkerchief under my hat against the heat, and a brace of pistols primed and ready for safety.
Not a hundred yards on, I had reached the stockade.

This is how it lay: a spring of clear water rose almost at the top of a knoll. On the knoll, and enclosing the spring, they had built a stout loghouse, big enough at a pinch to hold two-score people, and loopholed for musket-fire on every side. All round it they had cleared a wide open space, and the whole was finished off with a six-foot paling, with neither door nor gap — too strong to pull down without time and labour, too open to give the attackers any cover. The people inside had every advantage: they could stand quiet under shelter and pick the others off like partridges. All they needed was a careful watch and food enough; short of being utterly surprised, they could have held the place against a regiment.

What took my fancy above all was the spring. For though we were well enough placed in the cabin of the HISPANIOLA — plenty of arms and ammunition, food, excellent wines — one thing had been overlooked: we had no water. I was turning this over when there rang out across the island the cry of a man at the point of death. I am no stranger to violent death — I served his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, and took a wound myself at Fontenoy — but I know my pulse went all to pieces. “Jim Hawkins is done for,” was my first thought.

It is something to have been a soldier, but more still to have been a doctor. In our trade there's no time for dithering. So I made up my mind on the instant, and with no time lost went back to the shore and jumped into the jolly-boat.
Hunter, by good fortune, was a strong oar; we fairly made the water fly, and in no time the boat was alongside and I back aboard the schooner.
I found them all shaken, as was only natural. The squire was sitting down, white as a sheet, brooding on the harm he'd led us into — good soul; and one of the six forecastle hands was little better.

“There's a man,” says Captain Smollett, with a nod toward him, “new to this kind of work. He came near fainting, doctor, when he heard that cry. Another touch on the tiller and that fellow would come over to us.”
I laid my plan before the captain, and between us we worked out the particulars of carrying it through.

Old Redruth we stationed in the gallery between cabin and forecastle, with three or four loaded muskets and a mattress to shield him. Hunter worked the boat round under the stern-port, and Joyce and I fell to loading her — tins of powder, muskets, biscuit-bags, kegs of pork, a cask of brandy, and my precious medicine chest.
Meanwhile the squire and the captain stayed on deck, and the captain hailed the coxswain, the chief man left aboard.
“Mr. Hands,” said he, “here are two of us, with a brace of pistols each. If any one of you six makes a signal of any kind, that man's a dead man.”

They were taken aback, and after a little muttering together, the whole lot tumbled down the fore companion — meaning, no doubt, to take us in the rear. But when they found Redruth waiting for them in the railed gallery, they went about at once, and a single head popped up again on deck.
“Down, dog!” cries the captain.
And the head ducked back; and for the time we heard no more of these six very faint-hearted seamen.

By now, pitching things in as fast as they came, we had the jolly-boat loaded as deep as we dared. Joyce and I got out through the stern-port and pulled for shore again as hard as the oars would drive us.

This second trip fairly roused the watchers along the shore. “Lillibullero” stopped once more; and just before we lost sight of them behind the little point, one of them whipped ashore and was gone. I half thought of changing my plan and smashing their boats, but I feared Silver and the others might be close at hand, and that we might lose everything by reaching for too much.

We soon touched land in the same spot as before and set to stocking the blockhouse. All three of us made the first trip, heavily loaded, and pitched our stores over the palisade. Then, leaving Joyce to guard them — one man, true, but with half a dozen muskets — Hunter and I went back to the jolly-boat and loaded ourselves once more. So we kept on, never stopping for breath, until the whole cargo was stowed; whereupon the two servants took post in the blockhouse, and I, with all my strength, sculled back to the HISPANIOLA.

That we ventured a second boatload sounds bolder than it really was. They had the numbers, of course, but we had the arms. Not a man ashore carried a musket, and before they could come within pistol-range we flattered ourselves we could give a good account of half a dozen at least.

At the stern window the squire stood waiting, his faintness clean gone. He caught the painter, made it fast, and the two of us loaded the boat for dear life. The cargo was pork, powder, and biscuit, with no more than a musket and a cutlass each for the squire, myself, Redruth, and the captain. The rest of the arms and powder went over the side into two and a half fathoms, where we could see the bright steel glinting far down in the sun on the clean sand.

By now the tide had begun to ebb, and the ship was swinging round to her anchor. Voices could be heard faintly hallooing over toward the two gigs; and though that eased our minds for Joyce and Hunter, well to the eastward, it warned our own party to be gone.
Redruth quit his post in the gallery and let himself down into the boat, and we worked her round to the ship's counter, the handier for Captain Smollett.
“Now, men,” said he, “do you hear me?”
No answer came from the forecastle.
“It's to you, Abraham Gray — it's you I'm speaking to.”
Still no reply.

“Gray,” the captain went on, a little louder, “I'm leaving this ship, and I order you to follow your captain. I know you're a good man at bottom, and I dare say not one of the lot of you is as bad as he makes out. Here's my watch in my hand; I give you thirty seconds to come over to me.”
There was a pause.
“Come, my fine fellow,” the captain went on; “don't hang in stays so long. I'm risking my own life and these good gentlemen's every second of it.”
Then came a sudden scuffle, the sound of blows, and out burst Abraham Gray with a knife-cut down one cheek, and came running to the captain like a dog to the whistle.
“I'm with you, sir,” said he.
And in the next moment he and the captain were aboard with us, and we had pushed off and pulled away.
Out of the ship we were — but not yet safe ashore in the stockade.
