chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: The Jolly-boat’s Last Trip
paragraphs: This fifth trip was quite unlike any of the others. For one thing, the little cockleshell of a boat we were in was badly overloaded. Five grown men — three of them, Trelawney, Redruth, and the captain, over six feet tall — were already more than she was built to carry. Add to that the powder, the pork, the bread-bags. The gunwale was lipping water astern. Several times we shipped a little, and my breeches and coat-tails were soaked through before we'd gone a hundred yards.
The captain made us trim the boat, and we got her riding a little more evenly. Even so, we hardly dared breathe.

For another thing, the ebb was now setting — a strong rippling current running westward through the basin, then turning south and seaward down the straits we'd come in by that morning. The very ripples were a danger to our overloaded craft; but the worst of it was that the current swept us off our true course, away from the proper landing-place behind the point. Let it have its way, and we'd come ashore right beside the gigs, where the pirates might show up at any moment.

“I can't hold her head for the stockade, sir,” I told the captain. The tiller was mine, while he and Redruth, the two fresh hands, took the oars. “The tide keeps washing her down. Could you pull a bit harder?”
“Not without swamping her,” said he. “You must bear up, sir, if you please — bear up till you see you're gaining.”
I tried, and found by trial that the tide kept sweeping us westward until I'd laid her head due east — pretty near at right angles to the way we wanted to go.
“We'll never make the shore at this rate,” said I.

“If that's the only course we can lie, sir, then lie it we must,” returned the captain. “We've to keep upstream. You see, sir,” he went on, “once we dropped to leeward of the landing-place, there's no saying where we'd fetch up, besides the chance of being boarded by the gigs; whereas, the way we're heading, the current's bound to slacken, and then we can work back along the shore.”
“The current's easing already, sir,” said the man Gray, who sat in the bows; “you can let her off a bit.”
“Thank you, my man,” said I, just as if nothing had happened — for we'd all quietly made up our minds to treat him as one of ourselves.
Then suddenly the captain spoke again, and his voice, I thought, was a little altered.
“The gun!” said he.
“I've thought of that,” said I, supposing he meant a bombardment of the fort. “They could never get the gun ashore; and if they did, they'd never haul it through the woods.”
“Look astern, doctor,” the captain answered.

We'd clean forgotten the long nine; and there, to our horror, were the five rogues hard at work about her, stripping off her “jacket,” as they called the stout tarpaulin she sailed under. And in the same instant it flashed on me that the round-shot and the powder for the gun had been left behind, and that one stroke of an axe would put the whole of it into the villains' hands.
“Israel was Flint's gunner,” said Gray, hoarsely.

At any risk, we put the boat's head straight for the landing-place. By now we were so far out of the current's run that we kept steerage-way even at our slow, careful stroke, and I could hold her steady for the goal. But the worst of it was that the course I now had to steer turned our broadside, instead of our stern, to the HISPANIOLA, and made of us a target like a barn door.
I could hear, as well as see, that brandy-faced rascal Israel Hands thumping a round-shot down on the deck.
“Who's the best shot?” asked the captain.
“Mr. Trelawney, far and away,” said I.
“Mr. Trelawney, would you pick me off one of those men, sir? Hands, if you can,” said the captain.
Cool as steel, Trelawney looked to his priming.
“Now,” cried the captain, “easy with that gun, sir, or you'll swamp us. All hands stand ready to trim her as he aims.”
The squire raised his gun, the rowing stopped, and we leaned over to the other side to hold the balance; and it was all so neatly managed that we never shipped a drop.

By now they'd slewed the gun round on its swivel, and Hands, at the muzzle with the rammer, was the most exposed of them. Still, our luck was out, for just as Trelawney fired, Hands stooped down, the ball whistled over him, and it was one of the other four who fell.

The cry he gave was taken up not only by his mates aboard but by a great many voices from the shore; and looking that way I saw the other pirates pouring out from among the trees and tumbling into their places in the boats.
“Here come the gigs, sir,” said I.
“Give way, then,” cried the captain. “Never mind if we swamp her now. If we can't make the shore, it's all up with us.”
“Only one gig's being manned, sir,” I added; “the other crew are most likely going round by the shore to head us off.”

“They'll have a hot run of it, sir,” returned the captain. “Jack ashore is no great shakes. It's not them I mind; it's the round-shot. Carpet bowls! The squire's lady's-maid couldn't miss. Tell us when you see the match, squire, and we'll hold water.”

Meanwhile we'd been making fair headway for so loaded a boat, and had shipped only a little water doing it. We were close in now — thirty or forty strokes and we'd beach her, for the ebb had already bared a narrow belt of sand below the clustering trees. The gig was no longer to be feared; the little point had hidden it from us. The ebb-tide, that had used us so cruelly, was now making amends and holding back our pursuers. The one danger left was the gun.
“If I dared,” said the captain, “I'd lie to and pick off another man.”
But it was plain they meant to let nothing hold up their shot. They never so much as glanced at their fallen mate, though he wasn't dead — I could see him trying to crawl away.
“Ready!” cried the squire.
“Hold!” cried the captain, quick as an echo.

And he and Redruth backed with a great heave that drove her stern clean under water. The report came at the same instant. This was the first that Jim heard — the squire's shot hadn't carried to him. Where the ball went, none of us rightly knew; but I fancy it must have passed over our heads, and that the wind of it may have helped on our mishap.

In any case the boat settled by the stern, gently enough, in three feet of water, leaving the captain and me on our feet, face to face. The other three went clean under and came up streaming and gasping.

So far there was no great harm. No lives lost, and we could wade ashore safely enough. But all our stores were on the bottom; and, worse, only two of our five guns were fit to use. Mine I'd snatched from my knees and held over my head, by a sort of instinct. The captain had carried his slung over his shoulder by a bandoleer, and, like a wise man, lock uppermost. The other three had gone down with the boat.

To add to our worries, we could already hear voices drawing near in the woods along the shore; and we had not only the danger of being cut off from the stockade in our half-crippled state, but the fear of whether Hunter and Joyce, if a half-dozen fell on them, would have the sense and steadiness to hold firm. Hunter we could count on; Joyce was a doubtful case — a pleasant, polite fellow for a valet, good at brushing a coat, but hardly cut out for a man of war.
With all this in mind, we waded ashore as fast as we could, leaving the poor jolly-boat behind us, and a good half of all our powder and provisions with her.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: End of the First Day’s Fighting
paragraphs: We made what speed we could across the strip of wood that now lay between us and the stockade, and at every step the buccaneers' voices rang nearer. Soon we could hear their footfalls as they ran, and the cracking of the branches as they forced through a patch of thicket.
I began to see we'd have a real brush of it, and looked to my priming.
“Captain,” said I, “Trelawney's our dead shot. Give him your gun — his own's no good.”

They swapped guns, and Trelawney — silent and cool as he'd been since the trouble began — paused a moment on his heel to see all was fit for service. At the same time, noticing Gray had no weapon, I handed him my cutlass. It did all our hearts good to see him spit on his hand, knit his brows, and make the blade sing through the air. Every line of him showed that our new hand was worth his salt.

Forty paces more brought us to the edge of the wood, with the stockade before us. We struck the fence about the middle of the south side, and almost at the same instant seven mutineers — Job Anderson, the boatswain, at their head — broke into view, in full cry, at the southwestern corner.

They pulled up as if taken aback, and before they recovered, the squire and I, and Hunter and Joyce from the blockhouse, all had time to fire. The four shots went off in a rather ragged volley, but they did the work: one of the enemy dropped, and the rest, without a pause, turned and dived back into the trees.
Having reloaded, we walked down the outside of the palisade to see to the fallen man. He was stone dead — shot clean through the heart.

We were beginning to rejoice at our luck when, in that very moment, a pistol cracked in the bushes, a ball sang close past my ear, and poor Tom Redruth staggered and fell his full length on the ground. The squire and I both fired back, but having nothing to aim at, we likely only wasted powder. Then we reloaded and turned to poor Tom.
The captain and Gray were already over him, and I saw at half a glance that it was all up with him.

I believe the quickness of our return volley had scattered the mutineers once more, for we were let alone to lift the poor old gamekeeper over the stockade and carry him, groaning and bleeding, into the loghouse.

Poor old fellow — from the very first of our troubles down to this hour, when we laid him in the loghouse to die, he had never let fall one word of surprise, complaint, fear, or even of consent. He had lain like a Trojan behind his mattress in the gallery; he had obeyed every order silently, doggedly, and well; he was the oldest of our party by a score of years; and now it was he, the dour, old, faithful servant, who was to die.
The squire dropped on his knees beside him and kissed his hand, crying like a child.
“Am I going, doctor?” he asked.
“Tom, my man,” said I, “you're going home.”
“I wish I'd had a crack at them with the gun first,” he answered.
“Tom,” said the squire, “say you forgive me — won't you?”
“Would that be respectful-like, sir, from me to you?” came the answer. “But so be it — amen!”
After a short silence he said he thought somebody might read a prayer. “It's the custom, sir,” he added, as if apologizing. And not long after, without another word, he was gone.

Meanwhile the captain — whom I'd noticed to be wonderfully bulged about the chest and pockets — turned out a whole heap of odds and ends: the British colours, a Bible, a coil of stout rope, pen, ink, the log-book, and pounds of tobacco. He'd found a longish fir, felled and trimmed, lying in the enclosure, and with Hunter's help had set it up at the corner of the loghouse where the trunks crossed to make an angle. Then, climbing to the roof, he had with his own hands bent on and run up the colours.

This seemed a great relief to him. He came back into the loghouse and fell to counting up the stores, as if nothing else existed. But he kept an eye on Tom's passing all the same; and the moment it was over, he came forward with a second flag and reverently spread it over the body.
“Don't take on, sir,” he said, gripping the squire's hand. “All's well with him; no fear for a man shot down at his duty to captain and owner. It mayn't be sound divinity, but it's a fact.”
Then he drew me aside.
“Dr. Livesey,” said he, “in how many weeks do you and the squire look for the consort?”

I told him it was a matter not of weeks but of months: that if we weren't back by the end of August, Blandly was to send out to find us — but not before, and not after. “You can reckon it for yourself,” I said.
“Why, yes,” said the captain, scratching his head; “and making every allowance, sir, for the bounty of Providence, I'd call us pretty close-hauled.”
“How do you mean?” I asked.

“It's a pity, sir, we lost that second load — that's my meaning,” replied the captain. “For powder and shot, we'll do well enough. But the rations are short — very short; so short, Dr. Livesey, that we're maybe as well without that extra mouth.”
And he pointed to the dead body under the flag.
Just then, with a roar and a whistle, a round-shot flew high over the loghouse roof and came down far beyond us in the wood.
“Oho!” said the captain. “Blaze away! You've little enough powder as it is, my lads.”
At the next try the aim was truer, and the ball came down inside the stockade, throwing up a cloud of sand but doing no other harm.
“Captain,” said the squire, “the house is quite hidden from the ship. It must be the flag they're aiming at. Wouldn't it be wiser to haul it in?”

“Strike my colours?” cried the captain. “No, sir, not I.” And the moment he'd said it, I think we all agreed with him. For it wasn't only a piece of stout, seamanly good feeling; it was good policy too, and showed our enemies we cared nothing for their cannonade.

All through the evening they kept thundering away. Ball after ball flew over, or fell short, or kicked up the sand inside the enclosure; but they had to fire so high that the shot dropped spent and buried itself in the soft sand. We'd no ricochet to fear; and though one ball came in through the loghouse roof and out again through the floor, we soon grew used to that kind of rough play and minded it no more than a game of cricket.

“There's one good thing in all this,” said the captain. “The wood in front of us is likely clear. The ebb's been making a good while now; our stores should be uncovered. Volunteers to go and fetch in pork?”

Gray and Hunter were first to step forward. Well armed, they slipped out of the stockade — but the errand came to nothing. The mutineers were bolder than we'd reckoned, or trusted more to Israel's gunnery; for four or five of them were busy carrying off our stores and wading out with them to one of the gigs that lay close by, a man pulling an oar now and then to hold her against the current. Silver was in the stern-sheets, in command; and every one of them was now armed with a musket out of some secret store of their own.
The captain sat down to his log, and here is how the entry begins:

Alexander Smollett, master; David Livesey, ship's doctor; Abraham Gray, carpenter's mate; John Trelawney, owner; John Hunter and Richard Joyce, owner's servants and landsmen — being all that is left faithful of the ship's company — came ashore this day with stores for ten days at short rations, and flew the British colours over the loghouse on Treasure Island. Thomas Redruth, owner's servant and landsman, shot by the mutineers; James Hawkins, cabin-boy—
And at that very moment I was wondering what had become of poor Jim Hawkins.
A hail from the land side.
“Somebody hailing us,” said Hunter, who was on guard.
“Doctor! Squire! Captain! Hullo, Hunter — is that you?” came the cries.
And I reached the door just in time to see Jim Hawkins — safe and sound — come scrambling over the stockade.

chapters.title: Narrative Resumed by Jim Hawkins: The Garrison in the Stockade
paragraphs: The moment Ben Gunn caught sight of the colours, he stopped short, gripped my arm, and sat down.
“There,” he said. “Those are your friends, no mistake.”
“Far likelier it's the mutineers,” I said.

“Them?” he cried. “Why, in a spot like this, where nobody puts in but gentlemen of fortune, Silver would fly the Jolly Roger — you can be sure of that. No, those are your friends. There's been fighting, too, and I reckon your friends have had the better of it; and here they are ashore in the old stockade that Flint built years and years ago. Ah, Flint had a head on him, he did! Rum aside, there was never his match. Afraid of nobody, he wasn't — nobody but Silver. Silver was that genteel.”
“Well,” said I, “maybe that's how it is. All the more reason for me to hurry on and join them.”

“Not you, mate,” said Ben. “You're a good lad, or I'm much mistaken — but you're only a lad, when all's said. Now, Ben Gunn's a sharp one. Rum itself wouldn't carry me where you're headed — not rum — not till I've seen your born gentleman and have his word of honour. And don't forget what I told you: ‘A precious sight' — that's what you'll say — ‘a precious sight more confidence' — and then you nip him.”
And he pinched me a third time with the same knowing look.

“And when Ben Gunn's wanted, you know where to find him, Jim. Right where you found him today. And the one who comes must carry something white in his hand, and he must come alone. Oh — and you'll tell him this: ‘Ben Gunn,' says you, ‘has reasons of his own.'”
“Well,” said I, “I think I follow. You've a proposal to make, you want to see the squire or the doctor, and you're to be found where I found you. Is that the whole of it?”
“And when? says you,” he added. “Why, from about noon till around six bells.”
“Good,” said I. “Now may I go?”

“You won't forget?” he asked anxiously. “Precious sight, and reasons of his own, says you. Reasons of his own — that's the mainstay, as between man and man. Well then” — still holding on to me — “I reckon you can go, Jim. And Jim — if you was to run across Silver, you wouldn't go and sell out Ben Gunn? Wild horses wouldn't drag it out of you? No, says you. And if those pirates camp ashore, Jim — well, what would you say to there being widows by morning?”

Here he was cut off by a loud report, and a cannonball came tearing through the trees and buried itself in the sand not a hundred yards from where the two of us stood talking. The next instant we had each bolted in opposite directions.

For a good hour afterward the island shook with repeated reports, and balls kept crashing through the woods. I went from one hiding place to the next, forever pursued — or so it felt — by those terrifying missiles. But toward the end of the bombardment, though I still dared not head toward the stockade, where the balls fell thickest, I had begun to take heart a little, and after a long loop to the east I crept down among the trees along the shore.

The sun had just gone down, the sea breeze was rustling and tumbling through the woods and ruffling the grey surface of the anchorage; the tide was far out as well, and broad stretches of sand lay bare. After the heat of the day, the air chilled me through my jacket.

The Hispaniola still lay at her anchorage — but sure enough, the Jolly Roger, the black flag of piracy, now flew from her peak. Even as I watched, another red flash and report sent the echoes clattering, and one more round-shot whistled overhead. That was the last of the cannonade.

I lay a while watching the activity that followed the attack. Down on the beach near the stockade, men were hacking something to pieces with axes — the poor jolly-boat, I learned later. Off near the river mouth a great fire glowed among the trees, and one of the gigs kept shuttling between that point and the ship, the men — so grim before — now shouting at the oars like children. But there was a note in their voices that smelled of rum.

At last I judged I might start back toward the stockade. I was well down the low, sandy spit that closes the anchorage to the east and joins Skeleton Island at half-tide; and as I got to my feet, I saw, some way further along the spit, an isolated rock rising from the low bushes — fairly tall, and oddly white. It struck me this might be the white rock Ben Gunn had mentioned, and that one day a boat might be wanted and I would know where to look for one.
Then I worked my way through the woods until I had come round to the back — the shoreward side — of the stockade, and was soon given a warm welcome by the faithful party.

I quickly told my story and began to take stock of my surroundings. The log-house was built of unsquared pine trunks — roof, walls, and floor alike. The floor stood in places a foot or a foot and a half above the sand. There was a porch at the door, and under it the little spring welled up into an odd sort of basin — nothing but a great iron ship's kettle with its bottom knocked out, sunk ‘to her bearings,' as the captain put it, in the sand.
Little was left of the house but its frame, though in one corner a stone slab had been laid down for a hearth, and an old rusty iron basket stood ready to hold the fire.

The slopes of the knoll and the whole inside of the stockade had been stripped of timber to build the house, and the stumps showed what a fine, tall grove had been cut down. Most of the soil had washed away or buried itself in drift once the trees were gone; only where the stream ran down from the kettle did a thick bed of moss, with some ferns and little creeping bushes, stay green among the sand. Close around the stockade — too close for defence, the others said — the wood still grew tall and dense: all fir on the land side, but toward the sea mixed heavily with live-oaks.

The cold evening breeze I mentioned whistled through every chink of the rough building and sprinkled the floor with a steady fall of fine sand. There was sand in our eyes, sand in our teeth, sand in our supper, sand dancing in the spring at the bottom of the kettle for all the world like porridge coming to a boil. Our chimney was a square hole in the roof; only a little of the smoke found its way out, and the rest swirled about the house and kept us coughing and wiping our streaming eyes.

Add to all this that Gray, the new man, had his face tied up in a bandage over a cut he'd taken breaking away from the mutineers, and that poor old Tom Redruth, still unburied, lay stiff and stark along the wall under the Union Jack.

Had we been left to sit idle, we'd all have sunk into gloom, but Captain Smollett was never one for that. He called us all up before him and split us into watches: the doctor, Gray, and I on one; the squire, Hunter, and Joyce on the other. Tired as we were, two were sent out for firewood, two more set to dig Redruth's grave; the doctor was named cook, I was posted sentry at the door, and the captain went from man to man, keeping our spirits up and lending a hand wherever it was wanted.
Every so often the doctor stepped to the door for a breath of air and to rest his eyes, which were all but smoked out of his head; and each time he did, he'd a word for me.
“Smollett,” he told me once, “is a better man than I am — and coming from me, Jim, that's saying plenty.”
Another time he came and stood silent a while. Then he cocked his head and looked at me.
“Is this Ben Gunn a man?” he asked.
“I don't know, sir,” said I. “I'm not quite sure he's sane.”

“If there's any doubt about it, then he is,” said the doctor. “A man who's spent three years biting his nails on a desert island, Jim, can't be expected to seem as sane as you or me. It isn't in human nature. Cheese, you said — that was what he craved?”
“Yes, sir — cheese,” I answered.

“Well, Jim,” says he, “see now the good of being particular about your food. You've noticed my snuff-box? And you've never once seen me take snuff — the reason being that what I carry in it is a piece of Parmesan, a very nourishing cheese made in Italy. Well — that's for Ben Gunn!”

Before supper we buried old Tom in the sand and stood round him a while, bare-headed in the breeze. A fair amount of firewood had been brought in, but not enough to please the captain, who shook his head over it and told us we ‘must get back to this tomorrow a deal livelier.' Then, when we'd eaten our pork and each had a stiff glass of brandy grog, the three chiefs drew together in a corner to talk over our chances.

It seems they were at their wits' end. The stores were so low that we'd have been starved into surrender long before any help could arrive. Our best hope, they decided, was to pick off the buccaneers until they either struck their flag or made off with the Hispaniola. From nineteen they were already down to fifteen; two more were wounded, and one at least — the man shot beside the gun — badly, if he wasn't dead. Every time we got a clear shot at them we were to take it, while guarding our own lives with the utmost care. And besides that, we had two solid allies: rum and the climate.

As for the first, though we lay half a mile off, we could hear them roaring and singing far into the night; and as for the second, the doctor staked his wig that, camped where they were in the marsh and with no medicines, half of them would be flat on their backs within the week.
“So,” he added, “if we're not all shot down first, they'll be glad enough to clear out in the schooner. It's a ship, after all, and they can take up buccaneering again, I suppose.”
“The first ship I ever lost,” said Captain Smollett.
I was dead tired, as you can imagine; and when at last I dropped off — which wasn't until I'd tossed about a great deal — I slept like a log.
The others had long been up, had breakfasted, and had added half as much again to the woodpile by the time I was woken by a bustle and the sound of voices.
“A flag of truce!” I heard a voice call; and then, hard on it, an astonished cry — “Silver himself!”
At that I sprang up, rubbed my eyes, and ran to a loophole in the wall.

chapters.title: Silver’s Embassy
paragraphs: Sure enough, there were two men just beyond the stockade — one of them waving a white cloth, the other none other than Silver, standing calmly by.

It was still quite early, and the coldest morning I think I was ever out in — a chill that bored into the marrow. Overhead the sky was bright and cloudless, and the treetops glowed rosy in the sun. But where Silver stood with his lieutenant everything lay in shadow, and the two of them waded knee-deep in a low white vapour that had crept up overnight out of the swamp. The chill and the mist together told a sorry tale of the island: plainly a damp, feverish, unhealthy place.
“Keep inside, men,” said the captain. “Odds are this is a trick.”
Then he hailed the buccaneer.
“Who goes there? Stand, or we fire.”
“Flag of truce,” cried Silver.

The captain stood in the porch, keeping himself well clear of any treacherous shot. He turned and spoke to us: “Doctor's watch to the lookout. Dr. Livesey, take the north side, if you please; Jim, the east; Gray, the west. The watch below, all hands load muskets. Lively, men — and careful.”
Then he turned back to the mutineers.
“And what's your flag of truce for?” he called.
This time it was the other man who answered.
“Cap'n Silver, sir — come to make terms,” he shouted.
“Cap'n Silver? Don't know him. Who's he?” cried the captain. And we heard him mutter to himself, “Captain, is it? My heart — here's a promotion!”

Long John answered for himself. “Me, sir. These poor lads chose me captain after you deserted them, sir” — leaning hard on the word ‘deserted.' “We're willing to come to terms and have done with it, fair and square. All I ask is your word, Cap'n Smollett, to let me out of this stockade safe and sound, and one minute's grace to get out of range before a shot's fired.”
“My man,” said Captain Smollett, “I haven't the slightest wish to talk to you. If you want to talk to me, come ahead — that's all. Any treachery, it'll be on your side, and the Lord help you.”
“That's enough, Cap'n,” Long John called back cheerily. “One word from you's plenty. I know a gentleman when I see one, you may lay to that.”

We could see the man with the flag of truce trying to hold Silver back — small wonder, after so cool an answer from the captain. But Silver only laughed in his face and clapped him on the back, as if the very notion of danger were absurd. Then he came up to the stockade, tossed his crutch over, got a leg across, and with great strength and skill hauled himself over the fence and dropped safely down the other side.

I'll admit I was far too caught up in all this to be the least use as a sentry; in fact I had already abandoned my eastern loophole and crept up behind the captain, who had now settled himself on the threshold, elbows on knees, head in his hands, eyes fixed on the water bubbling up out of the old iron kettle in the sand. He was whistling “Come, Lasses and Lads.”

Silver had a terrible hard time getting up the knoll. What with the steep slope, the thick stumps, and the soft sand, he and his crutch were as helpless as a ship caught in stays. But he stuck at it without a word, like a man, and at last stood before the captain and saluted him in the handsomest style. He was got up in his best — a huge blue coat thick with brass buttons hanging to his knees, and a fine laced hat shoved back on his head.
“Here you are, my man,” said the captain, lifting his head. “You'd best sit down.”
“You ain't going to let me inside, Cap'n?” complained Long John. “It's a main cold morning, sir, to be sitting out here on the sand.”

“Why, Silver,” said the captain, “if you'd chosen to be an honest man, you might be sitting in your galley now. It's your own doing. You're either my ship's cook — and then you were treated handsomely — or you're Cap'n Silver, a common mutineer and pirate, and then you can go hang!”

“Well, well, Cap'n,” said the sea-cook, sitting down on the sand as he'd been told, “you'll just have to give me a hand up again afterward, that's all. A sweet pretty place you've got here. Ah — there's Jim! Top of the morning to you, Jim. Doctor, my service to you. Why, here you all are together like one happy family, in a manner of speaking.”
“If you've something to say, my man, you'd best say it,” said the captain.

“Right you are, Cap'n Smollett,” Silver replied. “Duty's duty, to be sure. Well now — that was a neat piece of work of yours last night. I'll not deny it: a neat piece of work. Some of you handy enough with the butt-end of a handspike. And I'll not deny some of my people were shaken — maybe all of them — maybe I was shaken myself; maybe that's why I'm here for terms. But mark me, Cap'n: it won't go twice, by thunder! We'll keep a sentry posted and ease off a point on the rum. Maybe you reckon we were all three sheets to the wind. Well, I'll tell you, I was sober — only dog-tired; and had I woken a second sooner I'd have caught you at it, I would. He weren't dead when I got to him, not him.”
“Well?” says Captain Smollett, cool as you please.

Everything Silver said was a riddle to him, but you'd never have known it from his voice. As for me, I was beginning to catch on. Ben Gunn's last words came back to me. I guessed he must have paid the buccaneers a visit while they lay drunk together round their fire, and I reckoned with glee that we now had only fourteen enemies to face.
“Here it is, then,” said Silver. “We want that treasure, and we'll have it — that's our side of it. You'd as soon keep your lives, I reckon — and that's yours. You've a chart, haven't you?”
“That's as may be,” the captain answered.

“Oh, you have, I know it,” said Long John. “No call to be so short with a man; there's not a ha'porth of good in it, you may lay to that. What I mean is, we want your chart. Now, I never meant you any harm myself.”
“None of that with me, my man,” the captain cut in. “We know exactly what you meant to do, and we don't care — because now, you see, you can't do it.”
And the captain looked at him coolly and set about filling a pipe.
“If Abe Gray—” Silver burst out.

“Belay there!” cried Mr. Smollett. “Gray told me nothing, and I asked him nothing; and what's more, I'd sooner see you and him and this whole island blown sky-high into blazes first. So there's my mind for you, my man, and you can chew on it.”
This little flash of temper seemed to cool Silver off. He'd been getting nettled, but now he gathered himself.
“Like enough,” said he. “I'll set no limits on what gentlemen may or mayn't think shipshape. And seeing as you're about to take a pipe, Cap'n, I'll make so bold as do the same.”
He filled a pipe and lit it, and the two men sat smoking in silence a good while — now eyeing each other, now tamping the tobacco, now leaning forward to spit. It was as good as a play to watch them.

“Now,” Silver went on, “here it is. You hand over the chart to get the treasure by, and you quit shooting poor seamen and staving in their heads while they sleep. Do that, and we'll give you a choice. Either you come aboard with us once the treasure's stowed, and I'll give you my affidavy, on my word of honour, to set you down somewhere safe ashore. Or, if that don't suit — some of my hands being rough, with old scores to settle over the hazing — then you can bide here. We'll share out the stores with you, man for man, and I'll give my affidavy, same as before, to hail the first ship I sight and send her back to take you off. Now there's talking for you. Handsomer than that you couldn't hope to get, not you. And I hope” — lifting his voice — “that every man in this here block house will weigh my words, for what's said to one is said to all.”
Captain Smollett rose and knocked the ashes out of his pipe into the palm of his left hand.
“Is that all?” he asked.
“Every last word, by thunder!” answered John. “Turn that down, and the next you'll see of me is musket-balls.”

“Very good,” said the captain. “Now hear me. Come up one at a time, unarmed, and I'll undertake to clap you all in irons and carry you home to a fair trial in England. Refuse, and — my name's Alexander Smollett, I've flown my sovereign's colours, and I'll see the lot of you down to Davy Jones. You can't find the treasure. You can't sail the ship — there's not a man among you fit to. You can't fight us — Gray there got clear of five of you. Your ship's in irons, Master Silver; you're on a lee shore, and so you'll find. I stand here and tell you so, and these are the last kind words you'll get from me, for by heaven I'll put a ball in your back the next time we meet. Now march, my lad. Out of this, and quick about it — hand over hand, on the double.”
Silver's face was a sight; his eyes started from his head with fury. He shook the fire out of his pipe.
“Give me a hand up!” he cried.
“Not I,” returned the captain.
“Who'll give me a hand up?” he roared.
Not one of us stirred. Snarling the vilest curses, he dragged himself along the sand until he reached the porch and could haul himself back onto his crutch. Then he spat into the spring.

“There!” he cried. “That's what I think of the lot of you. Inside the hour I'll stave in your old block house like a rum cask. Laugh away, by thunder — laugh! Inside the hour you'll be laughing the other side of your faces. The ones that die will be the lucky ones.”

And with a hideous oath he stumped off, floundering through the sand, was hauled over the stockade — after four or five tries — by the man with the flag of truce, and vanished among the trees an instant later.

chapters.title: The Attack
paragraphs: The moment Silver was gone, the captain, who had been watching him closely, turned back into the house and found not a man of us at his post but Gray. It was the first time we'd ever seen him angry.

“Quarters!” he roared. And as we all slunk back to our places: “Gray,” he said, “I'll put your name in the log; you stood by your duty like a seaman. Mr. Trelawney, I'm surprised at you, sir. Doctor — I thought you'd worn the king's coat! If that's how you served at Fontenoy, sir, you'd have done better to stay in your berth.”
The doctor's watch were all back at their loopholes, the rest busy loading the spare muskets, and every man red in the face, you may be sure, and with a flea in his ear, as the saying goes.
A while the captain watched in silence. Then he spoke.

“My lads,” said he, “I gave Silver a broadside. I poured it in red-hot on purpose; and before the hour's out, just as he said, we'll be boarded. We're outnumbered — I needn't tell you that — but we fight under cover; and a minute ago I'd have said we fought with discipline. I've no doubt at all we can beat them off, if you choose to.”
Then he made his rounds and saw, as he put it, that all was clear.

On the two short sides of the house, east and west, there were only two loopholes; on the south side, where the porch stood, two more; and on the north side, five. We had a round twenty muskets for the seven of us. The firewood had been stacked into four piles — tables, you might call them — one toward the middle of each wall, and on each lay some ammunition and four loaded muskets, ready to the defenders' hands. In the middle, the cutlasses were laid out in a row.
“Douse the fire,” said the captain. “The chill's past, and we can't have smoke in our eyes.”
Mr. Trelawney carried the whole iron fire-basket out bodily, and smothered the embers in sand.

“Hawkins hasn't had his breakfast. Hawkins, help yourself and take it back to your post,” the captain went on. “Lively, lad — you'll want it before you're through. Hunter, serve out a round of brandy to all hands.”
And while this went on, the captain finished working out, in his own mind, the plan of defence.

“Doctor, you'll take the door,” he resumed. “Mind you don't expose yourself; keep inside and fire through the porch. Hunter, the east side, there. Joyce, you stand by the west, my man. Mr. Trelawney, you're the best shot — you and Gray take this long north wall with its five loopholes; that's where the danger lies. If they can reach it and fire in on us through our own ports, things will turn ugly. Hawkins, neither you nor I count for much at the shooting; we'll stand by to load and lend a hand.”

As the captain had said, the chill was past. The moment the sun cleared our girdle of trees, it came down full force on the clearing and drank up the vapours at one draught. Soon the sand was baking and the resin sweating out of the logs of the block house. Jackets and coats were thrown off, shirts opened at the neck and rolled to the shoulder; and there we stood, each at his post, in a fever of heat and suspense.
An hour went by.
“Hang them!” said the captain. “Dull as the doldrums, this. Gray — whistle us up a wind.”
And just then came the first sign of the attack.
“Begging your pardon, sir,” said Joyce, “am I to fire if I see anyone?”
“I told you so!” cried the captain.
“Thank you, sir,” said Joyce, with the same quiet courtesy.

Nothing came of it for a time, but the question had put us all on edge, ears and eyes straining — the musketeers with their pieces balanced in their hands, the captain out in the middle of the block house, mouth set tight and a frown on his face.

So a few seconds passed, until all at once Joyce threw up his musket and fired. The report had hardly died when it was answered, again and again, by a scattering volley from outside — shot after shot, like a string of geese, from every side of the enclosure. Several bullets struck the log-house, but not one came through; and as the smoke thinned and cleared, the stockade and the woods around it looked as still and empty as before. Not a branch stirred, not the gleam of a barrel betrayed our enemies.
“Did you hit your man?” asked the captain.
“No, sir,” Joyce answered. “I believe not, sir.”
“Next best thing's to tell the truth,” muttered Captain Smollett. “Load his gun, Hawkins. How many on your side would you say there were, doctor?”
“I know exactly,” said Dr. Livesey. “Three shots from this side. I saw the three flashes — two close together, one further west.”
“Three!” the captain repeated. “And how many on yours, Mr. Trelawney?”

But that wasn't so easily answered. Many had come from the north — seven by the squire's count, eight or nine by Gray's. From east and west only a single shot each. Plainly, then, the real attack would come from the north, and on the other three sides we'd only be harried by a show of force. Still, Captain Smollett made no change in his arrangements. If the mutineers got over the stockade, he argued, they'd seize any unguarded loophole and shoot us down like rats in our own stronghold.

Nor had we much time left for thinking. Suddenly, with a loud hurrah, a little knot of pirates burst from the woods on the north side and rushed straight at the stockade. At the same instant fire opened again from the trees, and a rifle ball came singing through the doorway and smashed the doctor's musket to bits.

The boarders swarmed over the fence like monkeys. Squire and Gray fired again and again; three men dropped, one pitching forward into the enclosure, two falling back outside. But one of those was more frightened than hurt, for he was on his feet in a flash and gone among the trees.

Two were down for good, one had fled, and four had got a footing inside our defences, while from the cover of the woods seven or eight men, each plainly carrying several muskets, kept up a hot but useless fire on the log-house.

The four who had boarded made straight for the building, shouting as they came, and the men in the trees shouted back to cheer them on. Several shots were fired, but in their haste not one of the marksmen seems to have hit a thing. In a moment the four pirates had scrambled up the mound and were on us.
Job Anderson, the boatswain, showed his head at the middle loophole.
“At 'em, all hands — all hands!” he roared in a voice of thunder.

At the same moment another pirate seized Hunter's musket by the muzzle, wrenched it out of his hands, dragged it through the loophole, and with one stunning blow laid the poor fellow senseless on the floor. Meanwhile a third, running clear round the house unharmed, appeared all at once in the doorway and fell with his cutlass on the doctor.
Our whole position was reversed. A moment before we'd been firing, under cover, on an exposed enemy; now it was we who stood exposed and could not strike a blow in return.
The log-house was thick with smoke, and to that we owed our relative safety. Cries and confusion, the flashes and cracks of pistol-shots, and one loud groan rang in my ears.
“Out you go, lads — out and at them in the open! Cutlasses!” cried the captain.

I snatched a cutlass from the pile, and someone else, grabbing another at the same moment, gave me a cut across the knuckles that I scarcely felt. I dashed out the door into the bright sun. Someone was close at my heels, I didn't know who. Straight ahead, the doctor was driving his man down the hill, and just as my eyes fell on him he beat down the fellow's guard and sent him sprawling on his back with a great slash across the face.
“Round the house, lads — round the house!” cried the captain; and even through the din I caught the change in his voice.

Without thinking, I obeyed, turned east, and with my cutlass up ran round the corner of the house. The next moment I was face to face with Anderson. He gave a roar, and his hanger went up over his head, flashing in the sun. I had no time to be afraid, but as the blow still hung above me I sprang aside, missed my footing in the soft sand, and rolled headlong down the slope.

When I'd first burst from the door, the other mutineers had already been swarming up the palisade to finish us. One man, in a red night-cap, his cutlass between his teeth, had even got astride the top. Yet so short was the interval that when I found my feet again everything stood just as before — the fellow in the red night-cap still half over, another just showing his head above the stockade. And yet, in that single breath, the fight was over and the day was ours.

Gray, hard behind me, had cut down the big boatswain before he could recover from his last stroke. Another had been shot at a loophole in the very act of firing into the house, and now lay dying, the pistol still smoking in his hand. A third, as I'd seen, the doctor had dropped with one blow. Of the four who'd scaled the palisade, only one was left unaccounted for, and he — having dropped his cutlass on the field — was now scrambling back out with the fear of death on him.
“Fire — fire from the house!” cried the doctor. “And you, lads, back under cover.”

But no one heeded him; not a shot was fired, and the last boarder got clean away and vanished with the rest into the wood. In three seconds nothing was left of the attacking party but the five who had fallen — four inside the palisade and one without.
The doctor, Gray, and I ran for shelter at full speed. The survivors would soon be back where they'd left their muskets, and the firing might start up again at any moment.

By now the house was somewhat clear of smoke, and at a glance we saw the price of our victory. Hunter lay stunned beside his loophole; Joyce, by his, shot through the head, never to stir again; while right in the centre the squire was holding up the captain, the one as pale as the other.
“The captain's wounded,” said Mr. Trelawney.
“Have they run?” asked Mr. Smollett.
“Every man that could, you may be sure,” the doctor answered; “but there's five of them that'll never run again.”

“Five!” cried the captain. “Come, that's better. Five against three leaves us four to nine. That's better odds than we started with. Seven to nineteen we were then — or thought we were — and that's as hard to bear.” *

*The mutineers were soon down to only eight, for the man Mr. Trelawney had shot aboard the schooner died of his wound that same evening. But of course the faithful party did not learn this until later.

chapters.title: How I Began My Sea Adventure
paragraphs: There was no fresh attack from the mutineers — not so much as another shot from the woods. They had ‘got their rations for that day,' as the captain put it, and we had the place to ourselves and a quiet spell to tend the wounded and get dinner. The squire and I cooked outside, danger or no; and even out there we could hardly keep our minds on the work, for the horror of the loud groans that reached us from the doctor's patients.

Of the eight men who had fallen in the fight, only three still breathed — the pirate shot at the loophole, Hunter, and Captain Smollett; and of these the first two were as good as dead. The mutineer, indeed, died under the doctor's knife, and Hunter, for all we could do, never came back to his senses in this world. He lingered through the day, breathing heavily like the old buccaneer at home in his fit, but his ribs had been crushed by the blow and his skull cracked in the fall; and sometime in the night, without a sign or a sound, he went to his Maker.

As for the captain, his wounds were bad enough, but not dangerous. No vital organ had been struck. Anderson's ball — for it was Job who shot him first — had broken his shoulder-blade and grazed the lung, not seriously; the second had only torn and shifted some muscle in his calf. He would certainly recover, the doctor said; but in the meantime, and for weeks to come, he must not walk or move his arm, nor even speak if he could help it.
My own accidental cut across the knuckles was a flea-bite. Dr. Livesey patched it with plaster and tweaked my ears into the bargain.

After dinner the squire and the doctor sat a while by the captain's side in council; and when they had talked their fill — it being then a little past noon — the doctor took up his hat and pistols, buckled on a cutlass, slipped the chart into his pocket, and with a musket over his shoulder crossed the palisade on the north side and strode off briskly through the trees.

Gray and I sat together at the far end of the block house, to be out of earshot while our officers conferred; and Gray took the pipe from his mouth and clean forgot to put it back, so thunderstruck was he at the sight.
“Why, in the name of Davy Jones,” said he, “has Dr. Livesey gone mad?”
“Not he,” said I. “He's about the last of this crew I'd expect it of.”
“Well, shipmate,” said Gray, “mad he may not be — but if he isn't, then mark my words, I am.”
“My guess,” I replied, “is that the doctor has a notion of his own; and if I'm right, he's off now to see Ben Gunn.”

I was right, as it turned out; but in the meantime, the house being stifling hot and the little patch of sand inside the palisade blazing under the midday sun, another thought began to work in my head — one not nearly so sound. What I fell to was envying the doctor, walking in the cool shade of the woods with the birds about him and the sweet smell of the pines, while I sat grilling, my clothes glued to the hot resin, with so much blood around me and so many poor dead bodies lying about that I took a loathing of the place almost as strong as fear.

All the while I was swabbing out the block house and then washing up after dinner, this loathing and envy grew stronger and stronger, until at last, finding myself near a bread-bag with no one watching, I took the first step toward my escapade and stuffed both coat pockets with biscuit.

Call me a fool — and a fool I was, bent on a foolish, reckless act; but I meant to carry it out with every precaution I could. The biscuit, if anything went wrong, would at least keep me from starving well into the next day.
The next thing I laid hands on was a brace of pistols; and as I already had a powder-horn and bullets, I reckoned myself well armed.

The scheme in my head wasn't a bad one in itself. I meant to go down the sandy spit that divides the anchorage from the open sea on the east, find the white rock I'd marked the evening before, and see whether Ben Gunn had truly hidden his boat there — well worth doing, as I still believe. But certain I'd never be let out of the enclosure, my only plan was to take French leave and slip off when nobody was looking — and that bad way of going about it was just what made the thing itself wrong. But I was only a boy, and my mind was made up.

As it fell out, a fine chance came my way. The squire and Gray were busy helping the captain with his bandages; the coast was clear; I made a dash over the stockade into the thickest of the trees, and before anyone marked my absence I was beyond hail of my companions.
This was my second piece of folly, far worse than the first, since it left only two sound men to guard the house; but, like the first, it ended up helping to save us all.

I made straight for the east coast of the island, meaning to go down the seaward side of the spit and keep clear of any eyes at the anchorage. It was already late in the afternoon, though still warm and sunny. As I threaded the tall woods I could hear, far ahead, not only the steady thunder of the surf but a tossing of leaves and grinding of boughs that told me the sea breeze had got up stronger than usual. Soon cool draughts of air reached me, and a few steps more brought me out at the open edge of the grove, where the sea lay blue and sunlit to the horizon, the surf tumbling its foam along the beach.

I have never once seen the sea quiet around Treasure Island. The sun might blaze overhead, the air hang without a breath, the surface lie smooth and blue, and still these great rollers would be running all along the outer coast, thundering and thundering by day and by night; I scarcely believe there's a single spot on the island out of earshot of their noise.
I walked along beside the surf with great enjoyment until, judging I'd come far enough south, I took cover among some thick bushes and crept warily up to the ridge of the spit.

Behind me lay the sea, before me the anchorage. The sea breeze, as if it had blown itself out the sooner for its violence, had already died; in its place came light, shifting airs from the south and south-east, carrying great banks of fog. The anchorage, under the lee of Skeleton Island, lay as still and leaden as on the day we first entered it. The Hispaniola was mirrored there from truck to waterline, the Jolly Roger drooping from her peak.

Alongside lay one of the gigs, Silver in the stern-sheets — him I could always tell — while a couple of men leaned over the stern bulwarks, one in a red cap, the very rogue I'd seen astride the palisade some hours earlier. They seemed to be talking and laughing, though at that distance — over a mile — I could of course catch nothing of what passed. All at once a hideous, unearthly screaming broke out that gave me a bad start, until I recalled the voice of Captain Flint, and even fancied I could make out the bird by her bright plumage as she perched on her master's wrist.
Before long the jolly-boat pushed off and pulled for the beach, while the man in the red cap and his mate dropped below through the cabin companion.
About the same time the sun dropped behind the Spy-glass, and with the fog gathering fast it began to grow dark in earnest. I saw I had no time to lose if I meant to find the boat that evening.

The white rock, plain enough above the brush, stood still some eighth of a mile further down the spit, and it took me a good while to reach it, crawling, often on all fours, through the scrub. Night had all but come when I laid my hand on its rough side. Right below it lay a tiny hollow of green turf, screened by banks and a thick, knee-deep undergrowth that grew there in plenty; and in the middle of the dell, sure enough, stood a little tent of goat-skins, like the ones gipsies carry about in England.

I dropped into the hollow, lifted the flap of the tent, and there was Ben Gunn's boat — home-made if ever a thing was: a rough, lop-sided frame of tough wood with a goat-skin hide stretched over it, the hair turned inward. It was extremely small, even for me, and I can hardly think it would have floated under a full-grown man. There was a single thwart set as low as it would go, a sort of footrest in the bows, and a double paddle to drive her.

I had never then seen a coracle, of the kind the ancient Britons made; but I've seen one since, and I can give you no truer notion of Ben Gunn's boat than to say it was like the first and the worst coracle ever built by man. Yet it certainly had the coracle's great virtue, being very light and easy to carry.

Well, now that I'd found the boat, you'd think I had had enough of truancy for once; but by then another notion had taken hold of me, and I'd grown so stubbornly fond of it that I believe I'd have carried it out in the teeth of Captain Smollett himself. It was this: to slip out under cover of dark, cut the Hispaniola adrift, and let her run ashore wherever she chose. I'd quite convinced myself that the mutineers, after their repulse that morning, wanted nothing so much as to weigh anchor and put to sea; to stop that, I thought, would be a fine stroke, and now that I'd seen how they left their watchmen without a boat, it seemed it might be done at little risk.

Down I sat to wait for dark, and made a hearty meal of biscuit. It was a night in ten thousand for my purpose. The fog had now blotted out the whole sky. As the last of the daylight faded and went, utter blackness came down over Treasure Island. And when at last I shouldered the coracle and groped my stumbling way out of the hollow where I'd supped, just two points of light showed anywhere on the anchorage.

One was the great fire on shore, where the beaten pirates lay carousing in the swamp. The other, a mere smudge of light on the dark, marked where the ship lay at anchor. She had swung round to the ebb — her bow toward me now — and the only lights aboard were in the cabin; what I saw was just the glow of the strong rays from the stern window, thrown back off the fog.

The ebb had been running some time, and I had to wade through a long belt of swampy sand, sinking past my ankle more than once, before I reached the edge of the retreating water; then, wading a little way in, I managed with some strength and knack to set the coracle, keel down, on the surface.

chapters.title: The Ebb-tide Runs
paragraphs: The coracle — as I had every reason to learn before I was through with her — was a very safe boat for someone of my height and weight, buoyant and quick in a seaway; but she was the most contrary, lop-sided craft to handle. Do what you would, she made more leeway than anything afloat, and spinning round and round was the trick she did best. Even Ben Gunn himself owned that she was ‘queer to handle till you knew her ways.'

And know her ways I certainly did not. She turned every direction but the one I wanted; most of the time we went broadside on, and I'm quite sure I'd never have reached the ship at all but for the tide. By good luck, paddle as I might, the tide kept sweeping me down; and there lay the Hispaniola right in the fairway, hardly to be missed.

First she loomed up before me like a blot of something blacker than the dark; then her spars and hull took shape; and the next moment, it seemed (for the farther I went the brisker ran the ebb), I was alongside her hawser and had caught hold.

The hawser was as taut as a bowstring, so hard did the current drag her on her anchor. All round the hull, in the blackness, the rippling current bubbled and chattered like a little mountain stream. One cut of my sea-knife and the Hispaniola would go humming away down the tide.

So far so good — but then it came back to me that a taut hawser, cut all at once, is as dangerous as a kicking horse. Ten to one, if I were rash enough to part the Hispaniola from her anchor, the coracle and I would be flung clean out of the water.

That brought me up short, and had luck not once more stood my friend, I'd have had to give up the plan. But the light airs that had begun in the south-east and south had, after nightfall, hauled round into the south-west. Just as I sat pondering, a puff came, caught the Hispaniola, and pushed her up into the current; and to my great joy I felt the hawser go slack in my grip, and the hand I held it with dip a moment under water.

At that I made up my mind, took out my knife, opened it with my teeth, and cut one strand after another until the ship hung by only two. Then I lay still, waiting to part the last when a breath of wind should ease the strain once more.

All this while I'd been hearing loud voices from the cabin, but to tell the truth my mind had been so full of other things that I'd hardly listened. Now, with nothing else to do, I began to pay closer heed.

One voice I knew for the coxswain's — Israel Hands, who had been Flint's gunner in the old days. The other was my friend of the red night-cap. Both were plainly far gone in drink, and still at it, for even as I listened one of them, with a drunken shout, threw open the stern window and pitched something out — an empty bottle, I guessed. But they were more than tipsy: they were in a furious rage. Oaths flew like hail, and now and again came such an outburst that I felt sure it must end in blows. But each time the quarrel blew over and the voices grumbled lower for a spell, until the next flare-up came, and passed in its turn without result.

On shore I could see the glow of the great camp-fire burning warm through the trees along the beach. Someone was singing a dull, old, droning sailor's song with a dip and a quaver at the close of every verse, and seemingly no end to it but the singer's patience. I'd heard it more than once on the voyage, and these words came back to me:
“But one man of her crew alive, What put to sea with seventy-five.”

And I thought it a ditty rather too gloomily fitting for a company that had taken such cruel losses that very morning. But, from what I saw, all these buccaneers were as callous as the sea they sailed.
At last the breeze came; the schooner edged sidewise and loomed nearer in the dark; once more I felt the hawser ease, and with one good hard saw I parted the last fibres.

The breeze had little hold on the coracle, and almost at once I was swept up against the bows of the Hispaniola. At the same time the schooner began to turn on her heel, swinging slowly, end for end, across the current.

I worked like a fiend, for I looked every moment to be swamped; and finding I couldn't push the coracle straight off, I now shoved dead astern. At last I cleared my dangerous neighbour; and just as I gave the final shove, my hands fell on a light cord trailing overboard across the stern bulwarks. I grabbed it on the instant.
Why I did so I can hardly tell. At first it was mere instinct; but once I had it fast in my hands, curiosity got the better of me, and I made up my mind to have one look in at the cabin window.

I hauled in hand over hand on the cord, and when I judged myself near enough, raised myself — at huge risk — to about half my height, and so got a view of the cabin roof and a slice of what lay within.

By now the schooner and her little consort were slipping along quite fast through the water; indeed we had already drawn level with the camp-fire. The ship was ‘talking,' as sailors say — loudly — treading the countless ripples with a ceaseless weltering splash; and until I got my eye over the sill I couldn't make out why the watchmen had raised no alarm. One glance settled it — and one glance was all I dared take from that unsteady skiff. It showed me Hands and his companion locked in a deadly wrestle, each with a hand at the other's throat.

I dropped back onto the thwart, and none too soon, for I was near overboard. For a moment I could see nothing but those two furious, blood-red faces swaying together under the smoky lamp, and I shut my eyes to let them grow used to the dark again.
The endless ballad had come to its end at last, and the whole thinned company round the camp-fire had broken into the chorus I'd heard so often:
“Fifteen men on the dead man's chest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

I was just thinking how busy drink and the devil were at that very moment in the cabin of the Hispaniola, when I was startled by a sudden lurch of the coracle. At the same instant she yawed sharply and seemed to change her course. Her speed, meanwhile, had strangely increased.

I opened my eyes at once. All round me were little ripples, combing over with a sharp, bristling sound and faintly phosphorescent. The Hispaniola herself, a few yards in whose wake I was still being whirled along, seemed to stagger in her course; I saw her spars toss a little against the black of the night, and as I looked longer I felt sure she too was wheeling to the southward.

I glanced over my shoulder, and my heart leaped against my ribs. There, right behind me, was the glow of the camp-fire. The current had turned at a right angle, sweeping the tall schooner and the little dancing coracle along with it; ever quickening, ever bubbling higher, ever muttering louder, it went spinning through the narrows toward the open sea.

All at once the schooner ahead gave a violent yaw, turning perhaps twenty degrees; and almost in the same breath one shout followed another from her deck. I heard feet pounding up the companion ladder, and knew that the two drunkards had at last broken off their quarrel and waked to their disaster.

I lay down flat in the bottom of that wretched skiff and devoutly commended my soul to its Maker. At the end of the straits, I felt sure, we must run into some bar of raging breakers, where my troubles would soon be over; and though I think I could have borne to die, I could not bear to watch my fate come on.

So I must have lain for hours, tossed endlessly to and fro on the swell, now and then drenched with flying spray, and never ceasing to expect death at the next plunge. Little by little weariness crept over me; a numbness, with now and then a stupor, settled on my mind even amid my terrors, until at last sleep came, and there in my sea-tossed coracle I lay and dreamed of home and the old Admiral Benbow.

chapters.title: The Cruise of the Coracle
paragraphs: It was broad day when I woke and found myself tossing off the south-west end of Treasure Island. The sun was up, but still hidden from me behind the great bulk of the Spy-glass, which on this side dropped almost to the sea in fearsome cliffs.

Haulbowline Head and Mizzenmast Hill were close at my elbow — the hill bare and dark, the head ringed with cliffs forty or fifty feet high and skirted with great heaps of fallen rock. I was barely a quarter-mile to seaward, and my first thought was to paddle in and land.

That notion was soon dropped. Among the fallen rocks the breakers spouted and bellowed; loud booming echoes, heavy sprays flung up and falling, followed one another second by second; and I saw myself, if I dared go nearer, dashed to death on the rough shore or wearing out my strength for nothing trying to scale the overhanging crags.

Nor was that the worst, for crawling together on the flat slabs of rock, or dropping into the sea with loud reports, I saw huge, slimy monsters — soft snails, as it were, of unbelievable size — two or three score together, setting the rocks ringing with their barking.

I've learned since that they were sea lions, and quite harmless. But the look of them, with the difficult shore and the high surf, was more than enough to put me off that landing-place. I felt readier to starve at sea than to face such perils.

Meanwhile I had, as I supposed, a better chance ahead of me. North of Haulbowline Head the land runs a long way out, leaving at low tide a broad stretch of yellow sand. North of that again comes another cape — Cape of the Woods, as the chart had it — thick with tall green pines that ran right down to the water's edge.

I remembered what Silver had said about the current that sets northward along the whole west coast of Treasure Island; and seeing from where I lay that I was already in its grip, I chose to leave Haulbowline Head behind and save my strength for a try at the kindlier-looking Cape of the Woods.
A great smooth swell ran on the sea. With the wind holding steady and soft out of the south, it had no quarrel with the current, and the billows rose and fell without breaking.

Had it been otherwise, I must have perished long before; but as it was, it was wonderful how easily and safely my little light boat could ride. Often, while I still lay in the bottom with no more than an eye above the gunwale, I'd see a big blue summit heave up close above me; yet the coracle would only bob a little, dance as if on springs, and sink down the far side into the trough as lightly as a bird.

After a little I began to grow over-bold and sat up to try my hand at paddling. But even a small shift in the weight makes a violent change in how a coracle behaves. I had hardly moved before the boat gave up her gentle dancing all at once, ran straight down a slope of water so steep it turned me giddy, and drove her nose, with a spout of spray, deep into the side of the next wave.

I was drenched and terrified, and fell straight back into my old place, whereupon the coracle seemed to recover her head and carried me as softly as before among the billows. Plainly she was not to be meddled with; and at that rate, since I could in no way steer her, what hope was left of my ever reaching land?

A horrible fear began to take me, but I kept my wits in spite of it. First, working with great care, I baled the coracle dry bit by bit with my sea-cap; then, raising my eye over the gunwale again, I gave my mind to studying how she contrived to slip so quietly through the rollers.

I found that each wave — instead of the big, smooth, glassy mountain it looks from shore or a ship's deck — was for all the world like a stretch of hills on dry land, full of peaks and flats and valleys. The coracle, left to herself, turning this way and that, threaded her way, so to speak, through the lower ground and shunned the steep slopes and high, toppling crests of the wave.

“Well, then,” thought I, “it's plain I must lie where I am and not upset the balance; but it's plain too that I can put the paddle over the side now and again, in the smooth places, and give her a shove or two toward land.” No sooner thought than done. There I lay on my elbows in the most trying posture, and every so often gave a feeble stroke or two to turn her head shoreward.

It was tiring, slow work, yet I plainly gained ground; and as we neared the Cape of the Woods, though I saw I must surely miss the point itself, I had still made a hundred yards or so of easting. I was, in truth, close in. I could see the cool green tree-tops swaying together in the breeze, and felt sure I'd fetch the next headland without fail.

It was high time, for I now began to be tortured by thirst. The blaze of the sun overhead, its thousandfold glare off the waves, the sea-water that splashed me and dried caking my very lips with salt — all together set my throat burning and my head aching. The sight of the trees so near had almost sickened me with longing, but the current soon swept me past the point; and as the next reach of sea opened out, I saw a sight that turned my thoughts clean around.

Right in front of me, not half a mile off, lay the Hispaniola under sail. I made sure, of course, I'd be taken; but I was in such distress for want of water that I scarcely knew whether to be glad or sorry — and long before I'd settled it, sheer surprise took over my mind, and I could do nothing but stare and wonder.

The Hispaniola was under her mainsail and two jibs, the lovely white canvas shining in the sun like snow or silver. When I first sighted her all her sails were drawing; she lay on a course about north-west, and I supposed the men aboard were rounding the island to get back to the anchorage. Presently she began to fetch more and more to the west, so that I thought they'd spotted me and were coming about to chase. At last, though, she ran right up into the wind's eye, was taken flat aback, and hung there a while helpless, her sails shivering.
“Clumsy fools,” said I; “drunk as owls still, the lot of them.” And I pictured the dance Captain Smollett would have led them.

Meanwhile the schooner fell off and filled again on another tack, ran swiftly a minute or so, then brought up once more dead in the wind's eye. Over and over it went. To and fro, up and down, north, south, east, west, the Hispaniola sailed by swoops and dashes, each time ending as she'd begun, the canvas idly flapping. It grew plain to me that no one was at the helm. And if so — where were the men? Either dead drunk or fled, I thought; and maybe, if I could get aboard, I might hand the ship back to her captain.

The current was carrying coracle and schooner south at the same rate. As for the schooner's sailing, it was so wild and broken, and she hung so long in irons each time, that she certainly gained nothing — perhaps even lost. If only I dared sit up and paddle, I felt sure I could run her down. The scheme had an air of adventure that fired me, and the thought of the water-cask by the fore companion doubled my rising courage.

Up I got, and was greeted almost at once by another cloud of spray; but this time I held to my purpose and set myself, with all my strength and care, to paddle after the unsteered Hispaniola. Once I shipped so heavy a sea that I had to stop and bale, my heart fluttering like a bird's; but little by little I got the knack of it, and steered my coracle among the waves with only now and then a knock on her bows and a dash of foam in my face.

I was gaining fast on the schooner now; I could see the brass glinting on the tiller as it banged to and fro, and still not a soul showed on her decks. I couldn't but suppose her deserted. If not, the men must be lying drunk below, where I might batten them down, perhaps, and do as I pleased with the ship.

For some while she'd been doing the worst thing possible for me — standing still. She headed nearly due south, yawing, of course, all the time. Each time she fell off, her sails part-filled and brought her in a moment right up to the wind again. The worst thing possible, I say, for helpless as she looked, with the canvas cracking like guns and the blocks rattling and banging about the deck, she still kept running from me — not only with the speed of the current but by the whole of her leeway, which was naturally great.

But now, at last, my chance came. The breeze fell very low for a few seconds, and the current, slowly turning her, brought the Hispaniola round on her centre until she showed me her stern, the cabin window still gaping open and the lamp over the table still burning on into the day. The mainsail hung drooped like a banner. She was stock-still but for the current.
For the last little while I'd actually been losing ground; but now, redoubling my efforts, I began once more to gain on the chase.
I was within a hundred yards of her when the wind clapped down again; she filled on the port tack and went off afresh, dipping and skimming like a swallow.

My first impulse was despair, my second joy. Round she came, till she lay broadside to me — round still, till she had covered a half, then two-thirds, then three-quarters of the gap between us. I could see the water boiling white under her forefoot. Vastly tall she looked to me, down in my little coracle.

And then, all at once, I began to understand. I had scarce time to think — scarce time to act and save myself. I was on the crest of one swell as the schooner came stooping over the next. The bowsprit was right over my head. I sprang to my feet and leaped, stamping the coracle under water as I went. One hand caught the jib-boom, my foot lodged between the stay and the brace; and as I clung there panting, a dull blow told me the schooner had charged down and struck the coracle, and that I was left, with no way back, aboard the Hispaniola.

chapters.title: I Strike the Jolly Roger
paragraphs: I had barely got a footing on the bowsprit when the flying jib flapped and filled on the other tack, with a bang like a gun. The schooner shook to her keel under the reverse; but the next moment, the other sails still drawing, the jib flapped back and hung idle again.
That had nearly pitched me into the sea; so I lost no time, crawled back along the bowsprit, and tumbled head-first onto the deck.

I was on the lee side of the forecastle, and the mainsail, still drawing, hid a good part of the after-deck from me. Not a soul in sight. The planks, unswabbed since the mutiny, were trodden with the prints of many feet, and an empty bottle, its neck broken off, rolled to and fro in the scuppers like a living thing.

All at once the Hispaniola came right up into the wind. The jibs behind me cracked aloud, the rudder slammed over, the whole ship gave a sickening heave and shudder, and at the same moment the main-boom swung inboard, the sheet groaning in its blocks, and laid the lee after-deck bare to me.

And there were the two watchmen, sure enough: red-cap on his back, stiff as a handspike, his arms flung out like a crucifix and his teeth bared through his open lips; Israel Hands propped against the bulwarks, his chin sunk on his chest, his hands lying open before him on the deck, his face under its tan as white as a tallow candle.

For a while the ship kept bucking and sidling like a vicious horse, the sails filling now on one tack, now on the other, the boom swinging to and fro till the mast groaned aloud with the strain. Every so often a cloud of light spray came over the bulwark, and the bows struck the swell a heavy blow; this great rigged ship made far harder weather of it than my home-made, lop-sided coracle, now gone to the bottom of the sea.

At every plunge of the schooner, red-cap slid this way and that; but — ghastly to see — neither his posture nor that fixed, teeth-baring grin was in the least disturbed by the rough handling. At every plunge, too, Hands seemed to sink further into himself and settle lower on the deck, his feet sliding ever farther out and his whole body canting toward the stern, until little by little his face was hidden from me and at last I could make out nothing beyond his ear and one frayed ringlet of whisker.
At the same time I noticed, about them both, dark splashes of blood on the planks, and grew sure they had killed each other in their drunken fury.

While I stood there looking and wondering, in a calm moment when the ship lay still, Israel Hands turned half round and, with a low moan, writhed himself back into the position I'd first seen him in. That moan, telling of pain and deadly weakness, and the slack hang of his jaw, went to my heart. But when I remembered the talk I'd overheard from the apple barrel, all my pity drained away.
I walked aft as far as the mainmast.
“Come aboard, Mr. Hands,” I said, in mockery.
He rolled his eyes round heavily, but was too far gone to show surprise. All he could manage was a single word — “Brandy.”
I saw there was no time to waste, and dodging the boom as it lurched across the deck once more, I slipped aft and down the companion stairs into the cabin.

It was such a scene of wreckage as you can hardly imagine. Every lock-fast place had been broken open in the hunt for the chart. The floor was caked with mud where the ruffians had sat down to drink or confer after wading the marshes round their camp. The bulkheads, all painted clean white and beaded with gilt, were patterned with dirty handprints. Dozens of empty bottles clinked together in the corners with the roll of the ship. One of the doctor's medical books lay open on the table, half its leaves torn out — for pipe-lights, I suppose. And over it all the lamp still threw its smoky glow, dim and brown as umber.

I went down into the hold; every cask was gone, and a staggering number of the bottles had been drunk dry and flung away. Plainly, since the mutiny began, not one of them could ever once have been sober.

Rummaging about, I found a bottle with some brandy left in it for Hands; and for myself I dug out some biscuit, a few pickled fruits, a great bunch of raisins, and a lump of cheese. With these I came on deck, set my own store down behind the rudder-head, well out of the coxswain's reach, went forward to the water-cask, and took a long, deep drink of water; and then, and only then, did I give Hands the brandy.
He must have swallowed a gill before he took the bottle from his lips.
“Aye,” said he, “by thunder, I needed that!”
I had already settled in my own corner and fallen to eating.
“Hurt bad?” I asked him.
He grunted — barked, rather.

“If that doctor were aboard,” he said, “he'd put me right in a turn or two; but I never get a scrap of luck, you see, and that's what ails me. As for that swab, he's good and dead, he is” — nodding at the man in the red cap. “No seaman, him, anyhow. And where might you have sprung from?”
“Well,” said I, “I've come aboard to take possession of this ship, Mr. Hands; and you'll be so good as to consider me your captain until further notice.”
He gave me a sour enough look but said nothing. Some colour had crept back into his cheeks, though he still looked very sick and kept sliding and settling down as the ship knocked about.
“By the way,” I went on, “I'll not have these colours flying, Mr. Hands; so, by your leave, I'll strike them. Better none than these.”
And again dodging the boom, I ran to the flag-lines, hauled down their accursed black flag, and pitched it overboard.
“God save the king!” said I, waving my cap. “And there's the end of Captain Silver!”
He watched me close and sly, his chin all the while sunk on his breast.
“I reckon,” he said at last — “I reckon, Cap'n Hawkins, you'll be wanting to get ashore about now. Suppose we have a talk.”
“Why, gladly, Mr. Hands,” says I. “Say on.” And I fell to my meal again with a good appetite.

“This man,” he began, with a feeble nod at the corpse — “O'Brien his name was, a rank Irishman — this man and me got the canvas on her, meaning to sail her back. Well, he's dead now, dead as bilge-water; and who's to sail this ship, I don't see. Without I give you the word, you're not the lad to do it, far as I can tell.
