Now look here: you give me food and drink, and an old scarf or kerchief to bind up my wound, and I'll tell you how to sail her — and that's about fair all round, I take it.”
“I'll tell you one thing,” says I. “I'm not going back to Captain Kidd's anchorage. I mean to make North Inlet and beach her quietly there.”

“Of course you do!” he cried. “Why, I'm not such a born lubber after all. I can see, can't I? I've had my throw, I have, and lost, and it's you that has the weather of me. North Inlet? Why, I've no choice, not I! I'd help you sail her up to Execution Dock, by thunder — so I would!”

There seemed to me to be some sense in this. We struck our bargain on the spot. In three minutes I had the Hispaniola running easily before the wind along the coast of Treasure Island, with fair hopes of weathering the northern point by noon and beating down again as far as North Inlet before high water, when we might beach her safely and wait for the falling tide to let us land.

Then I lashed the tiller and went below to my own chest, where I got out a soft silk handkerchief of my mother's. With this, and with my help, Hands bound up the great bleeding stab in his thigh; and after he'd eaten a little and taken another swallow or two of the brandy, he visibly picked up — sat straighter, spoke louder and clearer, and looked in every way a different man.

The breeze served us beautifully. We skimmed before it like a bird, the island's coast flashing by and the view shifting every minute. Soon we were past the high ground and bowling along beside low, sandy country thinly dotted with dwarf pines; and soon past that too, and round the corner of the rocky hill that ends the island to the north.

I was greatly puffed up with my new command, delighted with the bright, sunny weather and the changing prospects of the coast. I had plenty of water now and good things to eat, and my conscience, which had punished me hard for deserting, was eased by the great prize I'd taken. I'd have had nothing left to wish for, I think, but for the coxswain's eyes following me mockingly about the deck, and the odd smile that never left his face. It was a smile with something of pain and weakness in it — a haggard old man's smile; but there was, besides, a grain of mockery in it, a shadow of treachery in his look as he slyly watched, and watched, and watched me at my work.

chapters.title: Israel Hands
paragraphs: The wind, as if to oblige us, now hauled into the west, so that we ran the easier from the north-east corner of the island to the mouth of North Inlet. Only, having no power to anchor, and not daring to beach her till the tide had risen a good deal further, we had time on our hands. The coxswain told me how to lay the ship to; after many tries I managed it, and we both sat in silence over another meal.

“Cap'n,” said he at length, with that same uneasy smile, “there's my old shipmate O'Brien; suppose you was to heave him overboard. I'm not over-particular as a rule, and I don't hold myself to blame for settling his account, but I don't reckon him much of an ornament now — do you?”
“I'm not strong enough, and I don't fancy the job; and there he stays, for me,” said I.

“This is an unlucky ship, this Hispaniola, Jim,” he ran on, blinking. “A power of men have been killed aboard her — a sight of poor seamen dead and gone since you and I shipped at Bristol. I never saw such dirty luck, not I. There was this O'Brien, now — he's dead, ain't he? Well, I'm no scholar, and you're a lad that can read and figure; so tell me straight: do you take it a dead man's dead for good, or does he come alive again?”
“A body you can kill, Mr. Hands, but not the soul — surely you know that much,” I replied. “O'Brien yonder has passed into another world, and may be watching us now.”

“Ah!” says he. “Well, that's unfortunate — looks as if killing a man were a waste of time, then. Still, spirits don't count for much, by what I've seen. I'll take my chance with the spirits, Jim. And now you've spoken up so free, I'll take it kindly if you'd step down to that cabin and fetch me a — a — shiver my timbers, I can't lay my tongue to the name of it; well, fetch me a bottle of wine, Jim — this brandy's too strong for my head.”

Now, the coxswain's stumbling seemed unnatural; and as for his preferring wine to brandy, I flatly disbelieved it. The whole tale was a pretext. He wanted me off the deck — that much was plain; but with what purpose I couldn't begin to guess. His eyes never once met mine; they kept roving up and down, this way and that, now glancing at the sky, now flitting to dead O'Brien. All the while he kept smiling and putting his tongue out in the most guilty, shamefaced way, so that a child could have seen he was bent on some trick. I was quick with my answer, though, for I saw where my advantage lay: with a fellow so thick-witted I could hide my suspicions to the very end.
“Some wine?” said I. “Much better. White or red?”
“Well, I reckon it's all one to me, shipmate,” he answered; “so long as it's strong, and plenty of it, what's the odds?”
“Right,” I said. “I'll bring you port, Mr. Hands. But I'll have to dig for it.”

With that I clattered down the companion, making all the noise I could, then slipped off my shoes, ran quietly along the planked gallery, climbed the forecastle ladder, and popped my head up out of the fore companion. He'd never look for me there; yet I took every care I could, and sure enough my worst suspicions proved true.

He had risen onto his hands and knees, and though his leg plainly hurt him sharply when he moved — I could hear him stifle a groan — still it was at a good, rattling pace that he dragged himself across the deck. In half a minute he had reached the port scuppers and picked out of a coil of rope a long knife, or rather a short dirk, stained to the hilt with blood. He looked at it a moment, thrusting out his lower jaw, tried the point on his hand, and then, hastily hiding it inside his jacket, trundled back to his old place against the bulwark.

That was all I needed to know. Israel could move about, he was armed now, and if he'd gone to so much trouble to be rid of me, plainly I was meant to be his victim. What he'd do afterward — whether he'd try to crawl clear across the island from North Inlet to the camp in the swamps, or fire Long Tom and trust his own comrades to reach him first — was more than I could say.

Still, in one matter I felt I could trust him, since there our interests ran together: the handling of the schooner. We both wanted her safely stranded, in some sheltered spot, so that when the time came she could be floated off again with as little work and risk as might be; and until that was done, I reckoned my life was safe enough.

While I was thus turning it over in my mind, I had not been idle with my hands. I had stolen back to the cabin, slipped my shoes on again, and laid hold at random of a bottle of wine; and now, with this for my excuse, I came back up on deck.

Hands lay as I had left him, all collapsed in a heap, his eyelids lowered as if he were too weak to bear the light. He looked up, though, as I came, knocked the neck off the bottle like a man who'd done it often, and took a good pull, with his favourite toast of “Here's luck!” Then he lay quiet a little; and then, fishing out a stick of tobacco, begged me to cut him a quid.

“Cut me a hunk of that,” says he, “for I've no knife, and hardly the strength if I had. Ah, Jim, Jim, I reckon I've missed stays! Cut me a quid — it'll likely be my last, lad, for I'm bound for my long home, and no mistake.”
“Well,” said I, “I'll cut you some tobacco; but if I were you, and thought myself so far gone, I'd go to my prayers like a Christian man.”
“Why?” said he. “Now you tell me why.”

“Why?” I cried. “You were asking me just now about the dead. You've broken your trust; you've lived in sin and lies and blood; there's a man you killed lying at your feet this very moment — and you ask me why! For God's mercy, Mr. Hands, that's why.”

I spoke with a touch of heat, thinking of the bloody dirk he had hidden in his pocket, meaning in his wicked heart to make an end of me. He, for his part, took a great draught of the wine and answered with the most unusual solemnity.

“For thirty years,” said he, “I've sailed the seas, and seen good and bad, better and worse, fair weather and foul, provisions running short, knives coming out, and what not besides. Well, I tell you, I never yet saw good come of goodness. The man that strikes first is the man for me; dead men don't bite; that's my way of it — amen, and so be it. And now” — changing his tone all at once — “we've had about enough of this nonsense. The tide's risen high enough now. You just take my orders, Cap'n Hawkins, and we'll run her straight in and have done.”

All told we had barely two miles to run; but the going was tricky, for the entrance to this northern anchorage was not only narrow and shoal but ran east and west, so the schooner had to be handled nicely to be brought in. I think I made a good, ready second; and I'm quite sure Hands was a first-rate pilot, for we went about and about and threaded our way in, shaving the banks, with a sureness and a neatness that were a pleasure to watch.

We were scarcely through the heads before the land closed round us. The shores of North Inlet were as thickly wooded as those of the southern anchorage, but the reach was longer and narrower, and more like what it really was — the mouth of a river. Right ahead, at the southern end, we saw the wreck of a ship in the last stages of decay. She had been a great three-masted vessel, but had lain so long open to the weather that she was draped in great hanging webs of dripping seaweed, and on her deck shore-bushes had taken root and now stood thick with flowers. It was a melancholy sight, yet it told us the anchorage was calm.
“Now,” said Hands, “look yonder; there's a sweet spot to beach a ship. Fine flat sand, never a cat's-paw of wind, trees all round, and flowers blowing like a garden on that old wreck.”
“And once she's beached,” I asked, “how do we get her off again?”

“Why, like this,” he answered. “You carry a line ashore yonder, on the far side, at low water; take a turn round one of those big pines; bring it back, take a turn round the capstan, and lie by for the tide. Come high water, all hands haul on the line, and off she comes as sweet as you please. And now, boy, stand by. We're near the spot, and she's carrying too much way. Starboard a little — so — steady — starboard — larboard a little — steady — steady!”

So he gave his orders, which I obeyed breathlessly, until all at once he cried, “Now, my hearty — luff!” I put the helm hard up, and the Hispaniola swung round smartly and ran stem-on for the low, wooded shore.

The excitement of these last manoeuvres had somewhat broken the close watch I'd kept till then on the coxswain. Even now I was so taken up, waiting for the ship to ground, that I'd clean forgotten the danger hanging over me, and stood craning over the starboard bulwark, watching the ripples spread wide before the bows. I might have fallen without a fight for my life, had not a sudden unease come over me and made me turn my head. Perhaps I'd caught a creak, or glimpsed his shadow shift from the tail of my eye; perhaps it was some instinct, like a cat's; but sure enough, when I looked round, there was Hands, already half-way to me, the dirk in his right hand.

We must both have cried out aloud when our eyes met; but while mine was the shrill cry of terror, his was a bellow of fury like a charging bull's. In the same instant he flung himself forward, and I leaped aside toward the bows. As I did, I let go the tiller, which sprang sharp to leeward; and this, I believe, saved my life, for it caught Hands across the chest and stopped him, for the moment, dead.

Before he could recover, I was clear of the corner he'd trapped me in, with the whole deck to dodge about. Just forward of the mainmast I stopped, drew a pistol from my pocket, took a cool aim though he had already turned and was coming straight at me again, and pulled the trigger. The hammer fell — but there came neither flash nor report; the priming was dead with sea-water. I cursed my own carelessness. Why hadn't I, long since, reprimed and reloaded my only weapons? Then I'd not now be a mere fleeing sheep before this butcher.

Wounded as he was, it was astonishing how fast he could move, his grizzled hair tumbling over his face, his face itself as red as a battle-flag with haste and rage. I'd no time to try my other pistol — nor much heart for it, being sure it too would fail. One thing I saw clearly: I must not simply back away from him, or he'd soon pin me in the bows as a moment ago he'd nearly pinned me in the stern. Once cornered, nine or ten inches of that blood-stained dirk would be my last experience on this side of eternity. I set my palms against the mainmast, which was of a good thickness, and waited, every nerve stretched tight.

Seeing that I meant to dodge, he too paused; and a moment or two went by in feints on his side and answering moves on mine. It was just such a game as I'd often played at home among the rocks of Black Hill Cove — though never, you may be sure, with such a wildly hammering heart as now. Still, a boy's game it was, and I reckoned I could hold my own at it against an elderly seaman with a wounded thigh. Indeed my courage had risen so high that I let myself dart a few thoughts toward how it would all end; and while I saw plainly I could spin it out a good while, I saw no hope of any final escape.

Well, while things stood so, all at once the Hispaniola struck, staggered, ground a moment in the sand, and then, quick as a blow, canted over to port till the deck stood at an angle of forty-five degrees and a great gush of water — a puncheon's worth — poured through the scupper-holes and lay in a pool between deck and bulwark.

We were both capsized in a second, and both rolled, almost together, into the scuppers — the dead red-cap, arms still spread, tumbling stiffly after us. So close were we that my head fetched up against the coxswain's foot with a crack that set my teeth rattling. Blow and all, I was first on my feet, for Hands had got tangled with the corpse. The sudden cant of the ship had made the deck no place for running; I had to find some new way out, and that on the instant, for my enemy was all but touching me. Quick as thought, I sprang into the mizzen shrouds, swarmed up hand over hand, and never drew breath till I sat astride the cross-trees.

It was my quickness that saved me; the dirk had struck not half a foot below me as I went up; and there stood Israel Hands, mouth open, face turned up to mine, the very picture of surprise and disappointment.

Now that I had a moment to myself, I lost no time repriming my pistol; and then, with one ready for use, and to make doubly sure, I set about drawing the charge of the other and loading it fresh from the start.

My new occupation struck Hands all of a heap; he saw the dice were turning against him, and after an obvious hesitation he too hauled himself heavily into the shrouds, and with the dirk in his teeth began slowly, painfully to climb. It cost him no end of time and groans to drag his wounded leg up after him, and I had finished my arrangements at leisure before he was more than a third of the way up. Then, a pistol in either hand, I spoke to him.
“One step more, Mr. Hands,” said I, “and I scatter your brains! Dead men don't bite — remember?” I added, with a chuckle.

He stopped on the instant. I could see by the working of his face that he was trying to think, and the process was so slow and laborious that, in my new-found safety, I laughed aloud. At last, after a swallow or two, he spoke, his face still wearing that look of utter bafflement. To speak, he had to take the dagger from his mouth, but in all else he never stirred.

“Jim,” says he, “I reckon we're fouled, you and me, and we'll have to sign articles. I'd have had you but for that lurch; but I never get any luck, not I; and I reckon I'll have to strike — which comes hard, you see, for a master mariner to strike to a ship's boy like you, Jim.”

I was drinking in his words and smiling away, as pleased with myself as a cock on a wall, when, all in one breath, back went his right hand over his shoulder. Something sang like an arrow through the air; I felt a blow, then a sharp pang, and there I was pinned by the shoulder to the mast. In the dreadful pain and shock of the moment — I can scarcely say it was by my own will, and I'm sure it was without any conscious aim — both my pistols went off, and both dropped from my hands. They did not fall alone: with a choked cry the coxswain let go his hold on the shrouds and plunged head-first into the water.

chapters.title: “Pieces of Eight”
paragraphs: Because of the ship's cant, the masts hung far out over the water, and from my perch on the cross-trees I had nothing below me but the surface of the bay. Hands, not so high up, was nearer the ship and fell between me and the bulwarks. He rose once to the surface in a lather of foam and blood, then sank again for good. As the water settled, I could see him lying huddled on the clean, bright sand in the shadow of the ship's side. A fish or two flicked past his body. Now and then, by the quiver of the water, he seemed to stir a little, as if trying to rise. But he was dead enough for all that — shot and drowned both — and food for fish in the very spot where he had meant to murder me.

No sooner was I sure of it than I began to feel sick, faint, and terrified. The hot blood was running down my back and chest. The dirk, where it pinned my shoulder to the mast, seemed to burn like a hot iron; yet it was not so much these real hurts that distressed me — those, it seemed to me, I could have borne without a murmur — as the horror in my mind of falling from the cross-trees into that still green water beside the coxswain's body.

I clung with both hands till my nails ached, and shut my eyes as if to blot out the danger. Little by little my wits came back, my pulse steadied to a more natural beat, and I was master of myself once more.

My first thought was to pull out the dirk; but either it stuck too fast, or my nerve failed, and I gave up with a violent shudder. Oddly enough, that very shudder did the trick. The knife, as it happened, had come within a hair of missing me altogether; it held me by no more than a pinch of skin, and the shudder tore that away. The blood ran the faster, to be sure, but I was my own man again, fastened to the mast now only by my coat and shirt.

These I broke through with a sudden wrench, and got back to the deck by the starboard shrouds. Nothing on earth would have tempted me, shaken as I was, to trust again to the overhanging port shrouds from which Israel had just fallen.

I went below and did what I could for my wound. It pained me a good deal and still bled freely, but it was neither deep nor dangerous, and did not much hamper me when I used the arm. Then I looked about me; and as the ship was now in a sense my own, I began to think of clearing her of her last passenger — the dead man, O'Brien.

He had pitched, as I've said, against the bulwarks, where he lay like some hideous, ungainly puppet — life-size, true, but how unlike the colour and comeliness of life! In that position I could manage him easily; and as the habit of tragic adventures had worn nearly all my fear of the dead away, I took him by the waist as if he'd been a sack of bran, and with one good heave tipped him overboard. He went in with a resounding splash; the red cap came off and floated on the surface; and as the splash died, I could see him and Israel lying side by side, both swaying with the tremulous movement of the water. O'Brien, though still quite a young man, was very bald. There he lay, his bald head across the knees of the man who had killed him, the quick fishes steering to and fro over them both.

I was alone on the ship now; the tide had just turned. The sun was within so few degrees of setting that already the shadow of the pines on the western shore reached right across the anchorage and fell in patterns on the deck. The evening breeze had sprung up, and though the two-peaked hill to the east warded it off well, the cordage had begun to sing softly to itself, and the idle sails to rattle to and fro.

I began to see the ship was in danger. The jibs I quickly doused and brought tumbling to the deck; but the mainsail was a harder matter. When the schooner canted over, the boom had of course swung outboard, and its cap, with a foot or two of sail, hung even under water. I thought this made things still more dangerous; yet the strain was so heavy that I half-feared to meddle. At last I got my knife and cut the halyards. The peak dropped at once, a great belly of loose canvas floated wide on the water, and since, pull as I might, I could not budge the down-haul, that was as much as I could do. For the rest, the Hispaniola must trust to luck, like myself.

By now the whole anchorage had fallen into shadow — the last rays, I remember, falling through a glade of the wood and shining bright as jewels on the flowery mantle of the wreck. It began to grow chill; the tide was running fast out to sea, and the schooner settled more and more on her beam-ends.

I scrambled forward and looked over. It seemed shallow enough, so, gripping the cut hawser in both hands for a last safeguard, I let myself drop softly overboard. The water scarcely reached my waist; the sand was firm and rippled, and I waded ashore in fine spirits, leaving the Hispaniola on her side, her mainsail trailing wide across the surface of the bay. About the same time the sun went fairly down, and the breeze whistled low in the dusk among the tossing pines.

At least, and at last, I was off the sea — and not empty-handed, either. There lay the schooner, clear at last of buccaneers and ready for our own men to board and put to sea again. I wanted nothing so much as to get home to the stockade and boast of what I'd done. I might be scolded a little for running off, perhaps; but the recapture of the Hispaniola was a clinching answer, and I hoped even Captain Smollett would own I'd not wasted my time.

So thinking, and in famous spirits, I set my face homeward for the block house and my companions. I remembered that the most easterly of the rivers draining into Captain Kidd's anchorage ran down from the two-peaked hill on my left, and I bent my course that way so as to cross the stream while it was still small. The wood was fairly open, and keeping to the lower slopes I soon rounded the shoulder of that hill, and not long after waded mid-calf across the watercourse.

This brought me near where I'd met Ben Gunn, the marooned man; and I went more warily now, keeping a sharp eye on every side. The dusk had almost wholly closed in, and as I opened out the cleft between the two peaks I saw a wavering glow against the sky, where, I judged, the man of the island was cooking his supper over a roaring fire. And yet in my heart I marvelled that he should be so careless. For if I could see this glare, might it not reach the eyes of Silver himself, camped on the shore among the marshes?

Little by little the night grew blacker; it was all I could do to steer myself even roughly toward my goal; the double hill behind me and the Spy-glass on my right loomed fainter and fainter; the stars were few and pale; and in the low ground where I wandered I kept tripping over bushes and tumbling into sandy pits.

Suddenly a kind of brightness fell around me. I looked up: a pale glimmer of moonlight had touched the summit of the Spy-glass; and soon after I saw something broad and silvery moving low behind the trees, and knew the moon had risen.

With this to help me, I made quick work of what remained of my journey; and, now walking, now running, drew impatiently near the stockade. Yet as I began to thread the grove before it, I had wit enough to slacken my pace and go a little warily. It would have been a sorry end to my adventures to be shot down by my own side in error.

The moon was climbing higher and higher, its light now falling here and there in patches through the more open parts of the wood; and right ahead a glow of a different colour showed among the trees. It was red and hot, and now and then a little darkened — the embers, as it were, of a bonfire dying down.
What it could be, I had not the least idea.

At last I came right down on the edge of the clearing. Its western end was already bathed in moonlight; the rest, and the block house itself, still lay in black shadow, criss-crossed with long silvery streaks. On the far side of the house an enormous fire had burned down to clear embers and threw a steady red glow, in sharp contrast with the soft paleness of the moon. Not a soul stirred; not a sound but the noises of the breeze.

I stopped, with great wonder in my heart, and perhaps a little fear as well. It had not been our way to build great fires; indeed, by the captain's orders we'd been rather sparing of firewood, and I began to dread that something had gone wrong while I was away.
I stole round by the eastern end, keeping close in the shadow, and at a convenient spot, where the dark lay thickest, climbed over the palisade.

To make doubly sure, I got down on my hands and knees and crawled, without a sound, toward the corner of the house. As I drew nearer, my heart all at once grew light. It's no pleasant noise in itself, and I've often grumbled at it at other times; but just then it was like music to hear my friends snoring together, so loud and peaceful, in their sleep. The watch's sea-cry, that lovely “All's well,” never fell more comfortingly on my ear.

Meanwhile one thing was beyond doubt: they kept a shamefully bad watch. Had it been Silver and his lads stealing in on them now, not a man would have seen daybreak. That was the cost, thought I, of having the captain wounded; and again I blamed myself bitterly for leaving them in such danger with so few to stand guard.

By this time I had reached the door and stood up. All was dark within, so that I could make out nothing by sight. As for sounds, there was the steady drone of the snorers, and a small, occasional noise — a flickering or pecking — that I could in no way account for.
Arms stretched out before me, I walked steadily in. I'd settle into my own place — I thought, with a silent chuckle — and relish their faces when they found me come morning.
My foot struck something yielding — a sleeper's leg; and he turned and groaned, but did not wake.
And then, all at once, a shrill voice broke out of the darkness:
“Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!” and so on, without pause or change, like the clacking of a tiny mill.
Silver's green parrot, Captain Flint! It was she I'd heard pecking at a piece of bark; it was she, keeping better watch than any human, who thus announced my arrival with her wearisome refrain.
I had no time to recover. At the sharp, clipping note of the parrot, the sleepers woke and sprang up; and with a mighty oath the voice of Silver cried, “Who goes there?”
I turned to run, crashed hard against one man, recoiled, and ran full into the arms of a second, who closed on me and held me fast.
“Bring a torch, Dick,” said Silver, once my capture was thus made sure.
And one of the men left the log-house and came back directly with a lighted brand.

chapters.title: In the Enemy’s Camp
paragraphs: The red glare of the torch, lighting up the inside of the block house, showed me the worst of my fears come true. The pirates held the house and the stores: there stood the cask of cognac, there were the pork and bread as before, and — what multiplied my horror tenfold — not a sign of any prisoner. I could only suppose they had all perished, and my heart smote me bitterly that I had not been there to perish with them.

Six buccaneers there were, all told; not another man left alive. Five of them were on their feet, flushed and bloated, just dragged out of the first sleep of drunkenness. The sixth had only raised himself on one elbow; he was deadly pale, and the blood-stained bandage round his head showed he'd lately been wounded, and more lately still bound up. I recalled the man shot and driven back into the woods during the great attack, and made no doubt this was he.

The parrot sat preening her feathers on Long John's shoulder. He himself, I thought, looked rather paler and grimmer than I was used to. He still wore the fine broadcloth suit he'd put on for his embassy, but it was sadly the worse for wear now, smeared with clay and torn by the sharp briars of the wood.
“So,” said he, “here's Jim Hawkins, shiver my timbers! Dropped in to call, eh? Well, come — I take that friendly.”
And with that he sat down astride the brandy cask and began to fill a pipe.

“Lend me the light, Dick,” said he; and then, once he'd a good glow going, “That'll do, lad,” he added. “Stick the torch in the wood-heap. And you, gentlemen, make yourselves easy — no call to stand up for Mr. Hawkins; he'll excuse you, you may lay to that. So, Jim” — pausing over the tobacco — “here you are, and a right pleasant surprise for poor old John. I saw you were sharp the first time I clapped eyes on you, but this here beats me clean, it does.”

To all this, as you may well suppose, I made no answer. They had set me with my back to the wall, and there I stood, looking Silver in the face — pluckily enough to all appearance, I hope — but with black despair in my heart.
With great composure Silver drew a whiff or two at his pipe, then went on again.

“Now, seeing as you are here, Jim,” says he, “I'll speak my mind to you. I've always had a liking for you, I have — a lad of spirit, the very picture of myself when I was young and handsome. I always wanted you to throw in with us, take your share, and die a gentleman; and now, my cock, you've got to. Cap'n Smollett's a fine seaman, as I'll grant any day, but a martinet for discipline. ‘Duty is duty,' says he, and right he is. So just you keep clear of the cap'n. The doctor himself's turned dead against you — ‘ungrateful scamp' was the word he used. And the long and short of it is this: you can't go back to your own lot, for they won't have you; and unless you'd start a third ship's company all by your lonesome — which might be lonely — you'll have to throw in with Cap'n Silver.”
So far so good. My friends, then, were still alive; and though I half-believed Silver's claim that the cabin party were furious at me for deserting, I was more relieved than wounded by what I heard.

“I'll say nothing about your being in our hands,” Silver went on, “though there you are, and you may lay to it. I'm all for reason; I never saw any good come of threats. If you like the service, well, you'll join; and if you don't, Jim, why, you're free to say no — free and welcome, shipmate; and if a mortal seaman can speak you fairer than that, shiver my sides!”

“Am I to answer, then?” I asked, my voice all atremble. Through all this jeering talk I was made to feel the threat of death hanging over me, and my cheeks burned and my heart beat painfully in my chest.
“Lad,” said Silver, “nobody's pressing you. Take your bearings. Not one of us'll hurry you, mate; time passes so pleasant in your company, you see.”
“Well,” says I, growing a little bolder, “if I'm to choose, I've a right to know how things stand, and why you're here, and where my friends are.”
“How things stand?” one of the buccaneers repeated, in a deep growl. “Ah, he'd be a lucky one that knew that!”

“You'll maybe batten down your hatches till you're spoken to, my friend,” Silver cried fiercely at this man. And then, in his first gracious tone, he answered me: “Yesterday morning, Mr. Hawkins,” said he, “in the dog-watch, down comes Dr. Livesey with a flag of truce. ‘Cap'n Silver,' says he, ‘you're sold out. The ship's gone.' Well, maybe we'd had a glass, and a song to wash it down — I won't deny it. Leastways, none of us had kept a lookout. We looked out — and by thunder, the old ship was gone! I never saw a pack of fools look more foolish; and you may lay to it I looked the foolishest. ‘Well,' says the doctor, ‘let's bargain.' We bargained, him and me, and here we are: stores, brandy, block house, the firewood you was kind enough to cut, and — in a manner of speaking — the whole blessed ship, from cross-trees to keelson. As for them, they've marched off; I don't know where they are.”
He drew quietly at his pipe again.

“And in case you take it into that head of yours,” he went on, “that you was let into the treaty — here's the last words that passed. ‘How many of you to leave?' says I. ‘Four,' says he; ‘four, and one of us wounded. As for that boy, I don't know where he is, confound him,' says he, ‘nor do I much care. We're about sick of him.' Those were his words.”
“Is that all?” I asked.
“It's all you're to hear, my son,” returned Silver.
“And now I'm to choose?”
“Choose you must, here and now — and you may lay to it,” said Silver.

“Well,” said I, “I'm not such a fool that I don't know pretty well what I've to look for. Let the worst come to the worst, it's little I care. I've seen too many die since I fell in with you. But there's a thing or two I've got to tell you,” I said — and by now I was thoroughly worked up — “and the first is this: here you are, in a bad way — ship lost, treasure lost, men lost, your whole venture wrecked; and if you want to know who did it — it was I! I was in the apple barrel the night we raised land, and I heard you, John, and you, Dick Johnson, and Hands, who's now at the bottom of the sea, and inside the hour I'd repeated every word you said. And as for the schooner, it was I who cut her cable, and I who killed the men you'd left aboard her, and I who brought her where none of you will ever set eyes on her again. The laugh's on my side; I've held the whip-hand of this whole business from the first; I no more fear you than I fear a fly. Kill me if you like, or spare me. But I'll say just one thing more: spare me, and bygones are bygones; and when you stand trial for piracy, I'll save you all I can. It's for you to choose. Kill another man and do yourselves no good — or spare me and keep a witness to save you from the gallows.”

I stopped, for — I tell you — I was out of breath; and to my amazement, not a man of them stirred, but all sat staring at me like so many sheep. And while they still stared, I broke out again: “And now, Mr. Silver,” I said, “I believe you're the best man here; and if things go to the worst, I'll take it kindly of you to let the doctor know how I bore it.”
“I'll bear it in mind,” said Silver, in an accent so strange that I could not, for the life of me, tell whether he was laughing at my request or had been won over by my courage.
“I'll add one to that,” cried the old mahogany-faced seaman — Morgan by name — whom I'd seen in Long John's tavern on the Bristol quays. “It was him that knew Black Dog.”
“And here's another, by thunder!” added the sea-cook. “It was this same boy that lifted the chart off Billy Bones. First and last, we've come to grief over Jim Hawkins!”
“Then here goes!” said Morgan, with an oath.
And he sprang up, whipping out his knife as nimbly as if he'd been twenty.

“Belay there!” cried Silver. “Who are you, Tom Morgan? Reckoned you were captain here, did you, perhaps? By the powers, I'll teach you better! Cross me, and you'll go where many a good man's gone before you these thirty years — some to the yard-arm, shiver my timbers, and some overboard, and all to feed the fishes. There's never a man yet looked me between the eyes and saw a good day afterward, Tom Morgan, you may lay to that.”
Morgan held off; but a hoarse muttering rose from the others.
“Tom's right,” said one.
“I took hazing enough from one man,” added another. “I'll be hanged if I'll take it from you, John Silver.”

“Did any of you gentlemen care to have it out with me?” roared Silver, leaning far forward from his seat on the keg, his pipe still glowing in his right hand. “Put a name to what you want; you're not dumb, I reckon. Let the man that wants it step up. Have I lived all these years only to have a son of a rum-cask cock his hat across my course at the end of it? You know the way of it; you're all gentlemen of fortune, by your own account. Well, I'm ready. Let him that dares take a cutlass, and I'll see the colour of his insides, crutch and all, before this pipe's burned out.”
Not a man stirred; not a man answered.

“That's your sort, is it?” he added, putting the pipe back to his lips. “Well, a gay lot you are to look at, anyhow. Not much use in a fight, you ain't. Maybe you can follow King George's English: I'm captain here by election. I'm captain here because I'm the best man by a long sea-mile. You won't fight, as gentlemen of fortune ought; then, by thunder, you'll obey — and you may lay to it! I like that boy, now; I never saw a better. He's more of a man than any two rats of you in this house, and what I say is this: let me see the man that'll lay a hand on him — that's what I say, and you may lay to it.”

A long silence followed. I stood straight against the wall, my heart still pounding like a sledge-hammer, but with a ray of hope now shining in me. Silver leaned back against the wall, arms folded, pipe in the corner of his mouth, as calm as if he'd been in church; yet his eye kept roving slyly, and he kept the tail of it on his unruly crew. They, for their part, drew gradually together toward the far end of the block house, and the low hiss of their whispering ran steadily in my ear, like a brook. One after another they'd glance up, and the red torchlight would fall a moment on their anxious faces; but it was not at me they looked — it was at Silver.
“You seem to have a deal to say,” remarked Silver, spitting far out into the air. “Pipe up and let me hear it, or hold your peace.”

“Asking your pardon, sir,” returned one of the men, “you're pretty free with some of the rules; maybe you'll be so good as to mind the rest. This crew's dissatisfied; this crew won't be bullied with a marlinspike; this crew has its rights like any other, I'll make so bold to say; and by your own rules, I take it we're free to talk it over. Asking your pardon, sir — owning you for captain at this present — I claim my right, and step outside for a council.”

And with an elaborate sea-salute, this fellow — a long, ill-favoured, yellow-eyed man of about thirty-five — stepped coolly to the door and out of the house. One after another the rest followed him, each saluting as he passed, each with some excuse. “According to rules,” said one. “Forecastle council,” said Morgan. And so, with one remark or another, they all filed out and left Silver and me alone with the torch.
The sea-cook took the pipe from his mouth on the instant.

“Now look you here, Jim Hawkins,” he said, in a steady whisper barely above a breath, “you're within half a plank of death — and, what's a deal worse, of torture. They're going to throw me over. But mind you, I stand by you through thick and thin. I didn't mean to — no, not till you spoke up. I was about desperate to lose all that money, and be hanged into the bargain. But I saw you were the right sort. Says I to myself: you stand by Hawkins, John, and Hawkins'll stand by you. You're his last card — and, by the living thunder, John, he's yours! Back to back, says I. You save your witness, and he'll save your neck!”
I began dimly to understand.
“You mean all's lost?” I asked.

“Aye, by gum, I do!” he answered. “Ship gone, neck gone — that's the size of it. Once I looked into that bay, Jim Hawkins, and saw no schooner — well, I'm tough, but I caved in. As for that lot and their council, mark me, they're rank fools and cowards. I'll save your life — if I can — from them. But see here, Jim, tit for tat: you save Long John from the rope.”
I was bewildered; it seemed so hopeless a thing he was asking — he, the old buccaneer, the ringleader of it all.
“What I can do, I'll do,” I said.
“It's a bargain!” cried Long John. “You speak up plucky, and by thunder, I've a chance!”
He hobbled over to the torch where it stood propped among the firewood, and lit his pipe afresh.

“Understand me, Jim,” he said, coming back. “I've a head on my shoulders, I have. I'm on the squire's side now. I know you've got that ship safe stowed somewhere. How you did it I don't know, but safe she is. Hands and O'Brien turned soft, I reckon; I never set much store by either of them. Now you mark me: I ask no questions, and I'll let no one else ask any. I know when a game's up, I do; and I know a staunch lad when I see one. Ah, you that's young — you and me might have done a power of good together!”
He drew some cognac from the cask into a tin pannikin.

“Will you taste, messmate?” he asked; and when I'd refused: “Well, I'll take a dram myself, Jim,” said he. “I need a stiffener, for there's trouble ahead. And speaking of trouble — why did that doctor hand me the chart, Jim?”
My face showed a wonder so plainly unfeigned that he saw it was useless to ask further.
“Ah, well — he did, though,” said he. “And there's something behind that, no doubt — something behind it, surely, Jim — for bad or good.”
And he swallowed another mouthful of brandy, shaking that great fair head of his like a man who looks for the worst.

chapters.title: The Black Spot Again
paragraphs: The buccaneers' council had run on some time when one of them came back into the house and, with a repetition of that same salute — which had, to my eye, a mocking air — begged the loan of the torch a moment. Silver agreed shortly, and the messenger withdrew again, leaving us together in the dark.
“There's a breeze coming, Jim,” said Silver, who had by now taken on quite a friendly, familiar tone.

I turned to the loophole nearest me and looked out. The embers of the great fire had burned so far down, glowing so low and dim, that I understood why the conspirators wanted a torch. About half-way down the slope toward the stockade they were gathered in a knot; one held the light, another knelt in their midst, and I saw the blade of an open knife shine in his hand, catching colours from moon and torch alike. The rest stood a little stooped, as if watching what he did. I could just make out that he had a book as well as a knife in his hand, and was still puzzling how anything so out of place had come among them, when the kneeling figure rose to his feet and the whole party began moving back toward the house.
“Here they come,” said I; and I went back to my old place, for it seemed beneath my dignity that they should catch me watching them.
“Well, let them come, lad — let them come,” said Silver cheerily. “I've still a shot in my locker.”

The door opened, and the five men, huddled together just inside, pushed one of their number forward. In any other circumstances it would have been comical to watch his slow advance, hesitating over each step he set down, yet holding his closed right hand out before him.
“Step up, lad,” cried Silver. “I won't eat you. Hand it over, lubber. I know the rules, I do; I'll not hurt a deputation.”
Thus heartened, the buccaneer stepped out more briskly, passed something to Silver from hand to hand, and slipped smartly back to his fellows.
The sea-cook looked at what he'd been given.

“The black spot! I thought as much,” he remarked. “And where might you have come by the paper? Why — hullo! Look here, now, this won't do! You've gone and cut this out of a Bible. What fool's been cutting up a Bible?”
“Ah, there!” said Morgan. “There! What did I say? No good'd come of that, I said.”
“Well, you've about settled it now, among you,” Silver went on. “You'll all swing now, I reckon. What soft-headed lubber owned a Bible?”
“It was Dick,” said one.
“Dick, was it? Then Dick had best get to his prayers,” said Silver. “He's seen the last of his luck, has Dick, and you may lay to that.”
But here the long man with the yellow eyes broke in.
“Stow that talk, John Silver,” he said. “This crew's handed you the black spot in full council, as duty bound; you just turn it over, as duty bound, and read what's written there. Then you can talk.”

“Thank'ee, George,” returned the sea-cook. “You always were a brisk one for business, and have the rules by heart, George, as I'm glad to see. Well — what is it, then? Ah! ‘Deposed' — that's it, is it? Very prettily written, to be sure; like print, I declare. Your hand of write, George? Why, you're getting to be quite a leading man in this crew. Captain next, I shouldn't wonder. Just oblige me with that torch again, will you? This pipe won't draw.”
“Come now,” said George, “you don't fool this crew any longer. You're a funny man, by your own account; but you're done now, and you'll maybe climb down off that barrel and help us vote.”

“I thought you said you knew the rules,” returned Silver scornfully. “Leastways, if you don't, I do; and I wait here — still your captain, mind — till you out with your grievances and I answer them. Till then, your black spot's not worth a biscuit. After that, we'll see.”

“Oh,” replied George, “you needn't fret yourself; we're all square, we are. First, you've made a hash of this cruise — you'll be a bold man to say no to that. Second, you let the enemy out of this here trap for nothing. Why did they want out? I don't know, but plain enough they did. Third, you wouldn't let us fall on them on the march. Oh, we see through you, John Silver; you mean to play both sides, that's what ails you. And fourth, there's this here boy.”
“Is that all?” asked Silver quietly.
“Enough, and to spare,” retorted George. “We'll all swing and dry in the sun for your bungling.”

“Well now, look here — I'll answer these four points; one by one I'll answer them. I made a hash of the cruise, did I? Well, you all know what I wanted; and you all know that had it been done, we'd be aboard the Hispaniola this very night, every man of us alive and well and full of good plum-duff, and the treasure in her hold, by thunder! And who crossed me? Who forced my hand, that was your lawful captain? Who handed me the black spot the day we landed and set this dance going? Ah, it's a fine dance — I'm with you there — and looks mighty like a hornpipe at the end of a rope on Execution Dock by London town. But who did it? Why, it was Anderson, and Hands, and you, George Merry! And you're the last left above board of that same meddling crew; and you've the brass — the Davy Jones's own insolence — to stand up for captain over me, you that sank the lot of us! By the powers! This beats the stiffest yarn I ever heard.”
Silver paused; and I could see by the faces of George and his late comrades that the words had not been wasted.

“That's for number one,” cried the accused, wiping the sweat from his face, for he had been speaking with a vehemence that shook the house. “Why, I give you my word, I'm sick to talk to you. You've neither sense nor memory, and I'll leave it to wonder where your mothers were that let you go to sea. Sea! Gentlemen of fortune! Tailors is more your trade, I reckon.”
“Go on, John,” said Morgan. “Speak up to the others.”

“Ah, the others!” returned John. “A nice lot they are, ain't they? You say this cruise is bungled. Ah! By gum, if you could only grasp how badly it's bungled, you'd see! We're that near the gibbet my neck's stiff with the thought of it. You've seen them, maybe — hanged in chains, the birds about them, seamen pointing them out as they drop down on the tide. ‘Who's that?' says one. ‘That? Why, that's John Silver. I knew him well,' says another. And you can hear the chains jangle as you tack about and reach for the next buoy. That's near enough where we stand, every mother's son of us, thanks to him, and Hands, and Anderson, and the rest of you ruination fools. And if you'd know about number four, and that boy — why, shiver my timbers, isn't he a hostage? Are we to throw away a hostage? Not us; he might be our last chance, and I shouldn't wonder. Kill that boy? Not me, mates! And number three? Ah, there's a deal to say to number three. Maybe you count it nothing to have a real college-bred doctor come see you every day — you, John, with your broken head; or you, George Merry, that had the ague-shakes on you not six hours back, and has eyes the colour of lemon-peel this very minute? And maybe you didn't know there's a consort coming, either? But there is, and not long now; and we'll see who's glad of a hostage when that day comes. And as for number two, and why I made a bargain — why, you came crawling on your knees to me to make it — on your knees you came, you were that downhearted — and you'd have starved too, if I hadn't. But that's a trifle. Look there — that's why!”

And he flung down on the floor a paper I knew at a glance — none other than the chart on yellow paper, with the three red crosses, that I had found in the oilskin at the bottom of the captain's chest. Why the doctor should have given it to him was beyond my fathoming.

But if it was a riddle to me, the sight of the chart was past belief to the surviving mutineers. They fell on it like cats on a mouse. It passed from hand to hand, each tearing it from the last; and by the oaths and cries and childish laughter that went with their poring over it, you'd have thought not only that they were fingering the very gold, but were safe at sea with it besides.
“Yes,” said one, “that's Flint, sure enough. ‘J. F.,' and a score under it, with a clove hitch — that was always his way.”
“Mighty pretty,” said George. “But how are we to make off with it, and never a ship?”

Silver sprang up of a sudden, steadying himself with a hand against the wall. “Now I give you warning, George,” he cried. “One more word of your sauce, and I'll call you down and fight you. How? Why, how should I know? You'd ought to tell me that — you and the rest, that lost me my schooner with your meddling, burn you! But not you — you can't; you haven't the wit of a cockroach. But civil you can speak, and shall, George Merry, you may lay to that.”
“That's fair enough,” said the old man Morgan.
“Fair! I reckon so,” said the sea-cook. “You lost the ship; I found the treasure. Who's the better man at that? And now I resign, by thunder! Elect whom you please for captain; I'm done with it.”
“Silver!” they cried. “Barbecue forever! Barbecue for captain!”

“So that's the tune now, is it?” cried the cook. “George, I reckon you'll have to wait another turn, friend; and lucky for you I'm not a vengeful man. That was never my way. And now, shipmates — this black spot? Not much good now, is it? Dick's crossed his own luck and spoiled his Bible, and that's about the whole of it.”
“It'll do to kiss the book on still, won't it?” growled Dick, plainly uneasy at the curse he'd brought down on himself.
“A Bible with a leaf cut out!” returned Silver mockingly. “Not it. It'll bind no more than a ballad-book.”
“Won't it, though?” cried Dick, with a kind of gladness. “Well, I reckon that's worth keeping too.”
“Here, Jim — here's a curiosity for you,” said Silver, and he tossed me the paper.

It was about the size of a crown piece. One side was blank, having been the last leaf; the other held a verse or two of Revelation — these words among them, that struck home sharp upon my mind: “Without are dogs and murderers.” The printed side had been blackened with wood-ash, which was already flaking off and dirtying my fingers; on the blank side was written, with the same ash, the single word “Depposed.” I have that curiosity by me as I write, but not a trace of the writing now remains beyond a single scratch, such as a man might make with his thumbnail.

That was the end of the night's business. Soon after, with a drink all round, we lay down to sleep; and the whole of Silver's revenge was to set George Merry up as sentinel and threaten him with death should he prove false.

It was long before I could close an eye, and heaven knows I had matter enough to think on — the man I had killed that afternoon, my own most perilous plight, and above all the remarkable game I now watched Silver play: holding the mutineers together with one hand while grasping with the other after every means, possible and impossible, to make his peace and save his wretched life. He himself slept peacefully and snored aloud; yet my heart was sore for him, villain though he was, to think of the dark perils that hemmed him in and the shameful gibbet that waited at the end.

chapters.title: On Parole
paragraphs: I was wakened — indeed, we were all wakened, for I could see even the sentinel pull himself together where he'd slumped against the door-post — by a clear, hearty voice hailing us from the edge of the wood:
“Block house, ahoy!” it cried. “Here's the doctor.”

And the doctor it was. Glad as I was to hear him, my gladness was not unmixed. I remembered with shame my disobedient, sneaking conduct; and seeing where it had landed me — among such companions, ringed with such dangers — I felt I could not look him in the face.
He must have risen in the dark, for the day had hardly broken; and when I ran to a loophole and looked out, I saw him standing, as Silver had once stood, knee-deep in creeping vapour.

“You, doctor! Top of the morning to you, sir!” cried Silver, wide awake and beaming with good humour in an instant. “Bright and early, to be sure; and it's the early bird, as they say, that gets the rations. George, rouse your timbers, son, and help Dr. Livesey over the ship's side. All doing well, your patients — all well and merry.”
So he rattled on, standing on the hilltop with his crutch under his arm and one hand against the wall of the log-house — quite the old John again in voice and manner and look.

“We've a little surprise for you too, sir,” he went on. “We've a small stranger here — he! he! A new boarder and lodger, sir, and looking trim and taut as a fiddle; slept like a supercargo, he did, right alongside of John — stem to stem the whole night through.”
Dr. Livesey was by now over the stockade and close to the cook, and I heard the change in his voice as he said, “Not Jim?”
“The very same Jim as ever was,” says Silver.
The doctor stopped dead, though he said nothing, and it was some seconds before he seemed able to go on.
“Well, well,” he said at last, “duty first and pleasure after, as you might say yourself, Silver. Let's overhaul these patients of yours.”

A moment later he had stepped into the block house and, with one grim nod to me, set about his work among the sick. He seemed under no fear at all, though he must have known that his life, among these treacherous fiends, hung by a hair; and he chattered on to his patients as if he were paying an everyday call on a quiet English household. His manner, I suppose, worked on the men, for they treated him as though nothing had happened — as though he were still ship's doctor and they still loyal hands before the mast.

“You're coming along, my friend,” he said to the man with the bandaged head. “If ever anyone had a narrow squeak, it was you; your skull must be as hard as iron. And George — how goes it? A pretty colour you are, to be sure; why, your liver, man, is clean upside down. Did you take that medicine? Did he take that medicine, men?”
“Aye, aye, sir, he took it, sure enough,” returned Morgan.

“Because, you see, being mutineers' doctor — or prison doctor, as I'd rather call it,” says Dr. Livesey, in his pleasantest way, “I make it a point of honour not to lose a single man for King George (God bless him!) and the gallows.”
The rogues glanced at one another, but swallowed the home-thrust in silence.
“Dick don't feel well, sir,” said one.
“Doesn't he?” replied the doctor. “Well, step up here, Dick, and let me see your tongue. No — I'd be astonished if he did! That tongue's fit to frighten the French. Another fever.”
“Ah, there,” said Morgan, “that comes of spoiling Bibles.”

“That comes — as you put it — of being arrant asses,” retorted the doctor, “and not having the wit to tell wholesome air from poison, or dry land from a foul, pestilent bog. I think it most likely — though it's only an opinion, of course — that you'll all have the devil to pay before you sweat that malaria out of your bones. Camp in a swamp, would you? Silver, I'm surprised at you. You're less of a fool than most, taken all round; but you don't seem to have the first notion of the rules of health.

“Well,” he added, once he'd dosed them all round and they'd taken their prescriptions with a humility really comical to see — more like charity-school children than blood-guilty mutineers and pirates — “well, that's enough for today. And now, if you please, I should like a word with that boy.”
And he nodded carelessly in my direction.
George Merry was at the door, spitting and grimacing over some foul-tasting medicine; but at the first word of the doctor's request he wheeled round, crimson, and cried “No!” with an oath.
Silver struck the barrel with his open hand.

“Si-lence!” he roared, and looked round him for all the world like a lion. “Doctor,” he went on in his usual tone, “I was thinking of that, knowing the fancy you've taken to the boy. We're all humbly grateful for your kindness, and, as you see, we put our faith in you and take your drugs down like so much grog. And I reckon I've hit on a way to suit everyone. Hawkins, will you give me your word of honour, as a young gentleman — for a young gentleman you are, though poor born — your word of honour not to slip your cable?”
I readily gave the pledge.

“Then, doctor,” said Silver, “you just step outside the stockade, and once you're there I'll bring the boy down on the inside, and I reckon you can yarn away through the spars. Good day to you, sir, and our duties to the squire and Cap'n Smollett.”

The storm of disapproval, which only Silver's black looks had held in, burst out the moment the doctor had left the house. Silver was roundly charged with playing double — with trying to patch up a separate peace for himself, with sacrificing the interests of his confederates and victims; in a word, with the exact thing he was doing. It seemed to me so plain, in this case, that I couldn't think how he'd turn aside their anger. But he was twice the man the rest of them were, and his victory of the night before had given him a vast hold over their minds. He called them every fool and dolt you can imagine, said it was necessary I should talk to the doctor, fluttered the chart in their faces, and asked them whether they could afford to break the treaty the very day they were bound off treasure-hunting.
“No, by thunder!” he cried. “It's us must break the treaty when the time's ripe; and till then I'll humour that doctor, if I have to grease his boots with brandy.”
And then he told them to get the fire lit, and stumped out on his crutch, his hand on my shoulder, leaving them in confusion — silenced by his flow of talk rather than convinced.
“Slow, lad, slow,” he said. “They might turn on us in the wink of an eye if they saw us hurry.”
Very deliberately, then, we crossed the sand to where the doctor waited on the far side of the stockade; and the moment we were within easy speaking distance, Silver stopped.

“You'll make a note of this too, doctor,” says he, “and the boy'll tell you how I saved his life, and was deposed for it into the bargain, you may lay to that. Doctor, when a man's steering as near the wind as me — playing pitch-and-toss with the last breath in his body — you wouldn't grudge him one good word, maybe? You'll bear in mind it's not my life only now — it's that boy's as well; and you'll speak me fair, doctor, and give me a scrap of hope to go on, for mercy's sake.”
Silver was a changed man now he was out there, his back to his crew and the block house; his cheeks seemed to have caved in, his voice shook; never was a soul more deadly in earnest.
“Why, John, you're not afraid?” asked Dr. Livesey.

“Doctor, I'm no coward; no, not I — not so much as that!” and he snapped his fingers. “If I were, I wouldn't say it. But I'll own up honest, I've the shakes on me for the gallows. You're a good man and a true; I never saw a better! And you'll not forget the good I've done, no more than you'll forget the bad — I know that. And I stand aside — see here — and leave you and Jim alone. And you'll set that down to my credit too, for it's a long reach, that is!”

So saying, he stepped back a little, till he was out of earshot, sat down on a tree-stump, and began to whistle, turning now and again on his seat to keep an eye now on me and the doctor, now on his unruly ruffians as they went to and fro on the sand between the fire — which they were busy rekindling — and the house, out of which they were fetching pork and bread for breakfast.

“So, Jim,” said the doctor sadly, “here you are. As you've brewed, so must you drink, my boy. Heaven knows I can't find it in my heart to blame you; but this much I'll say, kind or unkind: when Captain Smollett was well, you dared not have slipped off; and to do it when he was ill and couldn't stop you — by George, that was downright cowardly!”

I'll own that here I began to cry. “Doctor,” I said, “you might spare me. I've blamed myself enough; my life's forfeit anyhow, and I'd be dead by now if Silver hadn't stood up for me. And doctor — believe this — I can die, and I dare say I deserve it; but what I dread is torture. If they come to torture me—”
“Jim,” the doctor broke in, his voice quite altered, “Jim, I can't have this. Whip over the fence, and we'll run for it.”
“Doctor,” said I, “I gave my word.”

“I know, I know,” he cried. “We can't help that now, Jim. I'll take it all on my own shoulders, the whole load, blame and shame, my boy; but leave you here I cannot. Jump! One jump, and you're out, and we'll run like antelopes.”

“No,” I replied. “You know very well you'd not do it yourself — not you, nor the squire, nor the captain; and no more will I. Silver trusted me; I gave my word, and back I go. But, doctor, you didn't let me finish. If they come to torture me, I might let slip where the ship is; for I got the ship — part by luck, part by risk — and she lies in North Inlet, on the southern beach, just below high water. At half tide she must be high and dry.”
“The ship!” exclaimed the doctor.
Quickly I told him my adventures, and he heard me out in silence.

“There's a kind of fate in this,” he said when I'd done. “At every step it's you that saves our lives; and do you imagine for a moment we'll let you lose your own? That would be a poor return, my boy. You uncovered the plot; you found Ben Gunn — the best thing you ever did, or ever will do, though you live to ninety. Oh, by Jupiter — and speaking of Ben Gunn! Why, this is mischief itself. Silver!” he cried. “Silver! I'll give you a piece of advice,” he went on as the cook drew near again: “don't be in any great hurry after that treasure.”
“Why, sir, I do my best, which that ain't,” said Silver. “I can only — asking your pardon — save my life and the boy's by going after that treasure; and you may lay to that.”
“Well, Silver,” replied the doctor, “if that's how it is, I'll go one step further: look out for squalls when you find it.”

“Sir,” said Silver, “between man and man, that's too much and too little. What you're after, why you quit the block house, why you handed me that chart — I don't know, now, do I? And yet I did your bidding with my eyes shut, and never a word of hope! But no — this here's too much. If you won't tell me plain what you mean, just say so, and I'll let go the helm.”

“No,” said the doctor thoughtfully; “I've no right to say more; it's not my secret, you see, Silver, or I give you my word I'd tell it you. But I'll go as far with you as I dare, and a step beyond — for I'll have my wig dusted by the captain else, or I'm much mistaken! And first, I'll give you a scrap of hope: Silver, if we both come out of this wolf-trap alive, I'll do my best to save you, short of perjury.”
Silver's face shone. “You couldn't say more, I'm sure, sir — not if you was my own mother,” he cried.

“Well, that's my first concession,” added the doctor. “My second is a word of advice: keep the boy close at your side, and when you need help, sing out. I'm off to fetch it for you — and that alone will show you whether I speak at random. Good-bye, Jim.”
Dr. Livesey shook my hand through the palings, gave Silver a nod, and strode off briskly into the wood.

chapters.title: The Treasure-hunt--Flint’s Pointer
paragraphs: “Jim,” said Silver, once we were alone, “if I saved your life, you saved mine; and I'll not forget it. I saw the doctor wave you to make a run for it — out of the tail of my eye I saw it — and I saw you say no, as plain as if I'd heard you. Jim, that's a point to you. It's the first gleam of hope I've had since the attack went wrong, and I owe it to you. And now, Jim, we're to go after this treasure, under sealed orders too, and I don't like it; so you and me must stick close, back to back, and we'll save our necks in spite of fate and fortune both.”

Just then a man hailed us from the fire that breakfast was ready, and we were soon scattered here and there about the sand over biscuit and fried salt-meat. They had lit a fire fit to roast an ox, grown so hot now that they could only come at it from windward, and even there with care. In the same wasteful spirit they had cooked, I suppose, three times what we could eat; and one of them, with an empty laugh, pitched the leavings into the fire, which flared and roared again over the strange fuel. I never in my life saw men so heedless of tomorrow; hand to mouth is the only phrase for their way of going on; and between wasted food and sleeping sentries, bold enough as they were for a single brush, I could see how utterly unfit they were for anything like a long campaign.

Even Silver, eating away with Captain Flint on his shoulder, had not a word of blame for their recklessness — which surprised me the more, for I thought he had never shown himself so sly as he did just then.

“Aye, mates,” said he, “it's lucky for you you've got Barbecue to do your thinking with this head of mine. I got what I was after, I did. Sure enough, they've got the ship. Where they've stowed her I don't know yet; but once we've laid hands on the treasure, we'll have to scour about and find out. And then, mates, them of us as has the boats will hold the upper hand, I reckon.”
So he ran on, his mouth full of hot bacon; so he gave them back their hope and their confidence — and patched up his own, I more than suspect, at the same time.

“As for the hostage,” he went on, “that's his last talk, I guess, with them he loves so dear. I've had my bit of news, and thank him for it; but that's over and done. I'll lead him on a line when we go treasure-hunting, for we'll keep him safe as gold, in case of accidents, you mark me. Once we've got ship and treasure both, and put to sea like jolly companions, why, then we'll talk Mr. Hawkins over, and give him his fair share, to be sure, for all his kindness.”

No wonder the men were in good humour now. For my part, I was horribly cast down. Should the scheme he'd just sketched prove workable, Silver — twice a traitor already — would not scruple to take it up. He still had a foot in each camp, and no doubt he'd sooner have wealth and freedom with the pirates than the bare escape from hanging that was the best we could offer him.

And even if things fell out so that he was forced to keep faith with Dr. Livesey — even then, what danger lay before us! What a moment, when his followers' suspicions hardened into certainty, and he and I had to fight for dear life — he a cripple, I a boy — against five strong, active seamen!

Add to this double dread the mystery that still hung over my friends' conduct — their unexplained abandonment of the stockade, their inexplicable surrender of the chart, and, hardest of all to fathom, the doctor's last word to Silver, “Look out for squalls when you find it” — and you'll readily believe how little relish I found in my breakfast, and with how uneasy a heart I set off behind my captors on the hunt for treasure.

We made a curious figure, had there been anyone to see us — all in soiled sailor's clothes, and all but me armed to the teeth. Silver carried two guns slung about him, one before and one behind, besides the great cutlass at his waist and a pistol in each pocket of his square-tailed coat. To finish off his strange look, Captain Flint sat perched on his shoulder, gabbling scraps of aimless sea-talk. I had a line about my waist and followed obediently after the sea-cook, who held the loose end now in his free hand, now between his powerful teeth. For all the world, I was led like a dancing bear.

The rest were variously loaded, some with picks and shovels — the very first thing they'd brought ashore from the Hispaniola — others with pork, bread, and brandy for the midday meal. Every scrap of the stores, I noticed, came from our own; and I could see the truth of Silver's words the night before. Had he not struck his bargain with the doctor, he and his mutineers, left without a ship, must have fallen back on plain water and what their hunting brought in. Water would have been little to their taste; a sailor's no great marksman as a rule; and besides, short as they were of food, they were hardly likely to be flush of powder.

Thus equipped, off we all set — even the fellow with the broken head, who should by rights have stayed in the shade — and straggled, one behind another, down to the beach, where the two gigs lay waiting. Even these bore the marks of the pirates' drunken folly: one had a broken thwart, and both were muddy and unbailed. Both were to be taken along, for safety's sake; and so, our numbers split between them, we pushed off onto the bosom of the anchorage.

As we pulled across, there was some dispute over the chart. The red cross was, of course, far too big to serve as a guide, and the wording of the note on the back — as you'll hear — left some room for doubt. It ran, as the reader may recall, thus:
Tall tree, Spy-glass shoulder, bearing a point to the N. of N.N.E. Skeleton Island E.S.E. and by E. Ten feet.

A tall tree, then, was the chief mark. Now, right before us the anchorage was shut in by a plateau two or three hundred feet high, joining to the north the sloping southern shoulder of the Spy-glass, and rising again to the south into the rough, cliffy height called Mizzenmast Hill. The top of the plateau was thick with pines of every height. Here and there one of another kind rose forty or fifty feet clear above its neighbours, and which of these was Captain Flint's particular “tall tree” could only be settled on the spot, by the compass.
Yet, for all that, every man in the boats had picked out a favourite of his own before we were half-way across — Long John alone shrugging his shoulders and bidding them wait till they got there.

We pulled gently, by Silver's orders, so as not to tire the hands too soon; and after a fair long passage, landed at the mouth of the second river — the one that runs down a wooded cleft of the Spy-glass. From there, bearing to our left, we began to climb the slope toward the plateau.

At the start, heavy, miry ground and a tangled, marshy growth slowed us badly; but little by little the hill steepened, grew stony underfoot, and the wood changed its character, standing more open. It was, indeed, a most pleasant part of the island we were now coming into. A heavy-scented broom and many flowering shrubs had nearly ousted the grass. Thickets of green nutmeg-trees were dotted here and there with the red pillars and broad shade of the pines, the spice of the one mingling with the fragrance of the other. The air, too, was fresh and stirring, and this, under the straight rays of the sun, was a wonderful refreshment to the senses.

The party spread out, fan-wise, shouting and leaping to and fro. About the middle, and a good way behind the rest, Silver and I came on — I tethered by my rope, he labouring, with deep pants, among the sliding gravel. Now and then, indeed, I had to lend him a hand, or he'd have lost his footing and tumbled backward down the hill.

We'd gone about half a mile this way, and were nearing the brow of the plateau, when the man farthest to the left began to cry out, as if in terror. Shout after shout came from him, and the others started running his way.
“He can't have found the treasure,” said old Morgan, hurrying past us from the right, “for that's clean up top.”

And so, when we reached the spot ourselves, it proved to be something quite different. At the foot of a fair-sized pine, tangled in a green creeper that had even lifted some of the smaller bones, a human skeleton lay on the ground, with a few shreds of clothing about it. I believe a chill struck every heart for a moment.
“He was a seaman,” said George Merry, who, bolder than the rest, had gone right up and was fingering the rags. “Leastways, this is good sea-cloth.”
“Aye, aye,” said Silver; “likely enough; you'd not look to find a bishop up here, I reckon. But what kind of a way is that for bones to lie? It ain't natural.”

Indeed, at a second look, it seemed past believing the body lay so by chance. But for a little disarray — the work, maybe, of the birds that had fed on him, or of the slow creeper that had wound about his remains — the man lay perfectly straight, his feet pointing one way, his hands, raised over his head like a diver's, pointing dead opposite.

“I've taken a notion into this old numbskull of mine,” said Silver. “Here's the compass; there's the tip-top point of Skeleton Island, sticking up like a tooth. Just take a bearing, will you, along the line of those bones.”
It was done. The body pointed straight at the island, and the compass read duly E.S.E. and by E.

“I thought so,” cried the cook. “This here's a pointer. Right up yonder's our line for the Pole Star and the jolly dollars. But, by thunder! It turns me cold inside to think of Flint. This is one of his jokes, no mistake. Him and these six were alone here; he killed the lot, every man; and this one he dragged here and laid out by compass, shiver my timbers! Long bones, they are, and the hair's been yellow. Aye, that'd be Allardyce. You mind Allardyce, Tom Morgan?”
“Aye, aye,” said Morgan; “I mind him well — owed me money, he did, and carried off my knife ashore.”
“Speaking of knives,” said another, “why don't we find his lying about? Flint warn't the man to pick a seaman's pocket; and the birds, I reckon, would leave it be.”
“By the powers, and that's true!” cried Silver.
“There's nothing left here,” said Merry, still groping among the bones; “not a copper coin nor a tobacco-box. It don't look natural to me.”

“No, by gum, it don't,” agreed Silver; “not natural, nor not pretty, says you. Great guns, messmates — if Flint were living, this'd be a hot spot for you and me. Six they were, and six are we; and bones is all they are now.”
“I saw him dead with these here eyes,” said Morgan. “Billy took me in to him. There he lay, with pennies on his eyes.”
“Dead — aye, sure enough he's dead and gone below,” said the man with the bandage; “but if ever a spirit walked, it'd be Flint's. Lord, but he died hard, did Flint!”

“Aye, that he did,” said another; “now he raged, now he bawled for the rum, now he sang. ‘Fifteen Men' was his only song, mates; and I tell you true, I've never rightly cared to hear it since. It was main hot, and the window stood open, and I hear that old song come floating out as clear as clear — and the death-rattle already on the man.”
“Come, come,” said Silver; “stow this talk. He's dead, and he don't walk, that I know; leastways, he'll not walk by day, you may lay to that. Care killed the cat. Fetch ahead for the doubloons.”

We started, sure enough; but for all the hot sun and the broad daylight, the pirates no longer ran apart and shouting through the wood, but kept side by side and spoke under their breath. The terror of the dead buccaneer had come down upon their spirits.

chapters.title: The Treasure-hunt--The Voice Among the Trees
paragraphs: Partly from the damping effect of this fright, partly to rest Silver and the sick men, the whole party sat down as soon as they'd gained the top of the rise.

The plateau tilting somewhat to the west, the spot where we'd halted commanded a wide view both ways. Before us, over the treetops, we saw the Cape of the Woods fringed with surf; behind, we looked down not only on the anchorage and Skeleton Island but — clear across the spit and the eastern lowlands — on a great stretch of open sea to the east. Sheer above us rose the Spy-glass, here dotted with single pines, there black with precipices. There was no sound but the distant breakers, climbing up from every side, and the chirp of countless insects in the brush. Not a man, not a sail, on the sea; the sheer vastness of the view deepened the sense of solitude.
Silver, as he sat, took certain bearings with his compass.

“There are three ‘tall trees,'” said he, “about on the right line from Skeleton Island. ‘Spy-glass shoulder,' I take it, means that lower point yonder. It's child's play to find the stuff now. I've half a mind to dine first.”
“I don't feel sharp-set,” growled Morgan. “Thinking on Flint — that's what done it, I reckon.”
“Ah well, my son, you thank your stars he's dead,” said Silver.
“He were an ugly devil,” cried a third pirate, with a shudder; “that blue in the face, too!”
“That was the rum took him so,” put in Merry. “Blue! Well, I reckon he was blue. That's a true word.”

Ever since they'd found the skeleton and got onto this train of thought, they'd talked lower and lower, till by now they were almost whispering, so that the sound scarcely broke the silence of the wood. All at once, out of the trees right ahead of us, a thin, high, quavering voice struck up the well-known tune and words:
“Fifteen men on the dead man's chest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”
I never saw men more dreadfully shaken than the pirates. The colour drained from all six faces as if by witchcraft; some sprang up, some clutched at the others; Morgan grovelled on the ground.
“It's Flint, by ——!” cried Merry.

The song had broken off as sharply as it began — cut short, you'd have said, in the middle of a note, as though a hand had been clapped over the singer's mouth. Coming through the clear, sunny air among the green treetops, it had sounded to me airy and sweet; which made its effect on my companions the stranger.

“Come,” said Silver, fighting to force the word past his ashen lips; “this won't do. Stand by to go about. It's a queer start, and I can't put a name to the voice; but it's someone skylarking — someone of flesh and blood, you may lay to that.”

His courage had come back as he spoke, and some of the colour with it. The others were beginning to take heart at his words and come a little to themselves, when the same voice broke out again — not singing this time, but in a faint, far-off hail that echoed fainter yet among the clefts of the Spy-glass.
“Darby M'Graw,” it wailed — for wail is the nearest word — “Darby M'Graw! Darby M'Graw!” over and over and over; then, rising a little, and with an oath I leave out: “Fetch aft the rum, Darby!”
The buccaneers stood rooted, their eyes starting from their heads. Long after the voice had died they still stared, in dreadful silence, before them.
“That settles it!” gasped one. “Let's go.”
“Them was his last words,” moaned Morgan, “the last he spoke above board.”
