Dick had his Bible out and was praying away. He'd been well brought up, had Dick, before he came to sea and fell among bad company.
Still Silver was not beaten. I could hear his teeth chatter in his head, but he had not yet given in.

“Nobody on this island ever so much as heard of Darby,” he muttered; “not a soul but us that's here.” And then, with a great effort: “Shipmates,” he cried, “I'm here to get that stuff, and I'll not be beat by man or devil. I never feared Flint in his life, and, by the powers, I'll face him dead. There's seven hundred thousand pound not a quarter-mile from here. When did ever a gentleman of fortune turn his stern on that much money for a boozy old seaman with a blue mug — and him dead, too?”
But there was no sign of waking courage in his followers — rather, indeed, a growing terror at the irreverence of his words.
“Belay there, John!” said Merry. “Don't you cross a spirit.”

And the rest were too terrified to answer at all. They'd have run off, each his own way, had they dared; but fear held them together, and held them close to John, as if his daring lent them some. He, for his part, had pretty well fought his own weakness down.

“A spirit? Well, maybe,” said he. “But there's one thing I can't make square. There was an echo. Now, no man ever yet saw a spirit with a shadow; so what's it doing with an echo to it, I'd like to know? That ain't natural, surely?”
The argument seemed feeble enough to me. But there's no telling what will work on the superstitious, and to my astonishment George Merry was much relieved.

“Well, that's so,” he said. “You've a head on your shoulders, John, no mistake. 'Bout ship, mates! This crew's on the wrong tack, I do believe. And come to think on it, it was like Flint's voice, I grant you — but not quite so clear-cut, after all. It was liker somebody else's, now — it was liker—”
“By the powers — Ben Gunn!” roared Silver.
“Aye — that it were,” cried Morgan, springing up on his knees. “Ben Gunn, sure enough!”
“It don't make much odds, do it, now?” asked Dick. “Ben Gunn's no more here in the body than Flint.”
But the older hands met this with scorn.
“Why, who heeds Ben Gunn?” cried Merry. “Dead or alive, not a soul heeds him.”

It was extraordinary how their spirits came back, and the natural colour with them. Soon they were chatting together, with spells of listening; and before long, hearing nothing more, they shouldered the tools and set off again, Merry leading with Silver's compass to hold them on the right line for Skeleton Island. He'd spoken true: dead or alive, nobody minded Ben Gunn.
Dick alone still clutched his Bible, casting fearful glances about him as he went; but he got no sympathy, and Silver even mocked him over his precautions.

“I told you,” said he — “I told you you'd spoiled your Bible. If it's no good to swear on, what do you suppose a spirit would give for it? Not that!” And he snapped his big fingers, pausing a moment on his crutch.

But Dick was past comforting; indeed, it was soon plain to me the lad was sickening: hurried on by heat, weariness, and the shock of his fright, the fever the doctor had foretold was plainly mounting fast.

It was fine open walking up here on the summit; our way ran a little downhill, for, as I've said, the plateau tilted west. The pines, great and small, stood well apart; and even between the clumps of nutmeg and azalea, wide open spaces baked in the hot sun. Striking, as we did, near north-west across the island, we drew ever nearer on the one hand under the shoulders of the Spy-glass, and looked ever wider on the other over that western bay where I'd once tossed and trembled in the coracle.

The first of the tall trees was reached, and the bearings proved it the wrong one. So with the second. The third rose near two hundred feet into the air above a clump of underwood — a giant of a tree, with a red trunk as thick as a cottage and a shade wide enough for a company to drill in. It showed up far out to sea, both east and west, and might well have been marked on the chart as a sailing-mark.

But it was not its size that struck my companions now; it was the knowledge that seven hundred thousand pounds in gold lay buried somewhere beneath its spreading shade. The thought of the money, as they came nearer, swallowed up their late terrors. Their eyes blazed; their feet went faster and lighter; their whole souls were bound up in that fortune, that whole lifetime of waste and pleasure, lying there and waiting for each of them.

Silver hobbled on, grunting, on his crutch; his nostrils stood out and quivered; he cursed like a madman when the flies lit on his hot, shining face; he tore furiously at the line that held me, and from time to time turned on me a deadly look. He took no pains now to hide his thoughts, and I read them plain as print. With the gold so near, all else had gone clean out of his head: his promise and the doctor's warning were both things of the past; and I could not doubt he meant to seize the treasure, hunt out and board the Hispaniola under cover of night, cut every honest throat on the island, and sail away laden with crimes and riches, just as he'd meant from the first.

Shaken as I was by these fears, it was hard to keep pace with the treasure-hunters' rush. Now and again I stumbled, and then Silver would wrench at the rope and shoot me his murderous glances. Dick, who had dropped behind and now brought up the rear, was babbling to himself, prayers and curses both, as his fever climbed. This too added to my misery; and to crown it all, I was haunted by the thought of the tragedy once played out on this plateau — when that godless buccaneer with the blue face, the one who died at Savannah singing and roaring for drink, had here, with his own hand, cut down his six companions. This grove, so peaceful now, must then have rung with cries, I thought; and with the very thought I could fancy I heard it ringing still.
We were now at the edge of the thicket.
“Huzza, mates — all together!” shouted Merry; and the foremost broke into a run.

And then, not ten yards on, we saw them stop short. A low cry went up. Silver doubled his pace, stabbing away with the foot of his crutch like one possessed; and the next moment he and I too came to a dead stop.

Before us was a great pit, dug some time since, for the sides had fallen in and grass had sprung on the bottom. In it lay the shaft of a pick, broken in two, and the boards of several packing-cases scattered about. On one of these boards I saw, branded with a hot iron, the name WALRUS — the name of Flint's ship.
It was all clear beyond doubt. The cache had been found and emptied; the seven hundred thousand pounds were gone!

chapters.title: The Fall of a Chieftain
paragraphs: There never was such a reversal in this world. Each of these six men stood as if struck by lightning. But with Silver the shock passed almost at once. Every thought of his soul had been straining, like a racer, toward that money; and now, in a single second, he was pulled up dead — yet he kept his head, mastered his temper, and changed his plan before the others had time to take in their disappointment.
“Jim,” he whispered, “take that, and stand by for trouble.”
And he slipped me a double-barrelled pistol.

At the same time he began quietly edging northward, and in a few steps had put the pit between us two and the other five. Then he looked at me and nodded, as much as to say, “Here's a tight corner” — as, indeed, I thought it was. His look was none too friendly, and I was so sickened by these endless turns of his that I could not help whispering, “So you've changed sides again.”

There was no time for him to answer. The buccaneers, with oaths and cries, began leaping one after another into the pit, clawing at the ground with their fingers and flinging the boards aside. Morgan turned up a piece of gold. He held it aloft amid a perfect fountain of oaths. It was a two-guinea piece, and it passed from hand to hand among them for a quarter of a minute.

“Two guineas!” roared Merry, shaking it at Silver. “That's your seven hundred thousand pounds, is it? You're the man for a bargain, ain't you? You that never bungled nothing, you wooden-headed lubber!”
“Dig away, boys,” said Silver, with the coolest insolence; “you'll turn up a few pig-nuts, I shouldn't wonder.”
“Pig-nuts!” shrieked Merry. “Mates, do you hear that? I tell you now, that man there knew it all along. Look in his face and you'll see it written there.”
“Ah, Merry,” remarked Silver, “standing for captain again? You're a pushing lad, to be sure.”

But this time the whole crew was for Merry. They began scrambling out of the pit, shooting furious looks behind them. One thing I marked, which boded well for us: they all came out on the side away from Silver.

Well, there we stood, two on one side, five on the other, the pit between, and not a man keyed up enough to strike the first blow. Silver never stirred; he watched them, very straight on his crutch, and looked as cool as ever I saw him. He was brave, and no mistake.
At last Merry seemed to think a speech might serve.
“Mates,” says he, “there's the two of them alone there: one's the old cripple that brought us all out here and blundered us into this; the other's that cub whose heart I mean to have. Now, mates—”

He was lifting his arm and his voice, plainly about to lead a rush. But just then — crack! crack! crack! — three musket-shots flashed out of the thicket. Merry pitched head-first into the pit; the man with the bandage spun round like a top and dropped full length on his side, where he lay dead but still twitching; and the other three turned and ran for their lives.

Before you could wink, Long John had emptied both barrels of his pistol into the struggling Merry; and as the man rolled up his eyes at him in his last agony, “George,” said he, “I reckon I've settled you.”
At that moment the doctor, Gray, and Ben Gunn came up to us from among the nutmeg-trees, their muskets smoking.
“Forward!” cried the doctor. “Quick march, my lads. We must cut them off from the boats.”
And off we set at a great pace, sometimes plunging breast-high through the bushes.

I tell you, Silver was set on keeping up with us. The work that man did, leaping on his crutch till the muscles of his chest seemed near to bursting, was such as no sound man ever matched — and so says the doctor. Even so, he was a good thirty yards behind us and on the point of choking when we reached the brow of the slope.
“Doctor,” he hailed, “look there! No call to hurry!”

Sure enough there was none. In an opener part of the plateau we could see the three survivors still running the way they'd started, straight for Mizzenmast Hill. We were already between them and the boats; so we four sat down to get our breath, while Long John, mopping his face, came slowly up to us.
“Thank ye kindly, doctor,” says he. “You came in about the nick, I reckon, for me and Hawkins. And so it's you, Ben Gunn!” he added. “Well, you're a fine one, to be sure.”
“I'm Ben Gunn, I am,” replied the maroon, writhing like an eel in his confusion. “And,” he added, after a long pause, “how do, Mr. Silver? Pretty well, thank ye, says you.”
“Ben, Ben,” murmured Silver, “to think it's you that's done me!”

The doctor sent Gray back for one of the pick-axes the mutineers had thrown down in their flight; and then, as we went leisurely downhill toward the boats, he told us in a few words what had happened. It was a tale that gripped Silver mightily; and Ben Gunn, the half-witted maroon, was the hero of it from first to last.

Ben, in his long, lonely ramblings about the island, had found the skeleton — it was he that had stripped it; he had found the treasure; he had dug it up (his was the pick-haft that lay broken in the pit); he had carried it on his back, in many a weary journey, from the foot of the tall pine to a cave he had on the two-pointed hill at the north-east corner of the island; and there it had lain, safely stored, since two months before the Hispaniola arrived.

When the doctor had wormed this secret out of him on the afternoon of the attack, and saw next morning that the anchorage was deserted, he had gone to Silver, made him a present of the chart — now worthless — and of the stores, for Ben Gunn's cave was well found with goat-meat salted by his own hand; given anything and everything, in short, for the chance of shifting in safety from the stockade to the two-pointed hill, clear of the malaria and within guard of the money.
“As for you, Jim,” he said, “it went against my heart, but I did what I judged best for those who'd stood by their duty; and if you weren't one of them, whose fault was that?”

That morning, finding I was to be caught up in the cruel disappointment he'd laid for the mutineers, he had run the whole way to the cave, and, leaving the squire to guard the captain, had taken Gray and the maroon and set out, cutting the diagonal across the island to be near the pine. Soon, though, he saw our party had the start of him; so Ben Gunn, being fleet of foot, was sent ahead to do what he could alone. And it had struck him to play on the superstitions of his old shipmates — so well that Gray and the doctor were up and lying in ambush before the treasure-hunters arrived.
“Ah,” said Silver, “it was a lucky thing for me I had Hawkins here. You'd have let old John be cut to ribbons, doctor, and never spared it a thought.”
“Not a thought,” replied Dr. Livesey cheerily.
And by this time we'd reached the gigs. The doctor smashed one of them with the pick-axe, and then we all got aboard the other to go round by sea to North Inlet.

It was a run of eight or nine miles. Silver, though near dead with fatigue already, was set to an oar like the rest of us, and soon we were skimming briskly over a smooth sea. Before long we were out of the straits and round the south-east corner of the island — the corner round which, four days back, we had towed the Hispaniola.

Passing the two-pointed hill, we caught sight of the black mouth of Ben Gunn's cave, with a figure beside it leaning on a musket. It was the squire; we waved a handkerchief and gave him three cheers, and Silver's voice joined in as heartily as any.

Three miles farther on, just inside the mouth of North Inlet, what should we meet but the Hispaniola, sailing free by herself? The last flood had floated her; and had there been much wind, or a strong tide-current as in the southern anchorage, we should never have found her, or found her stranded past help. As it was, little was amiss beyond the wreck of the mainsail. We got another anchor ready and let it go in a fathom and a half of water. Then we all pulled round again to Rum Cove, the nearest point to Ben Gunn's treasure-house; and Gray, single-handed, took the gig back to the Hispaniola, where he was to keep watch through the night.

A gentle slope ran up from the beach to the cave mouth. At the top the squire met us. To me he was warm and kind, saying nothing of my escapade, in blame or in praise. At Silver's polite salute he coloured a little.

“John Silver,” he said, “you're a prodigious villain and impostor — a monstrous impostor, sir. I'm told I'm not to prosecute you. Well, then, I won't. But the dead men, sir, hang round your neck like millstones.”
“Thank you kindly, sir,” replied Long John, saluting again.
“I dare you to thank me!” cried the squire. “It's a gross neglect of my duty. Stand back.”

And with that we all went into the cave. It was a large, airy place, with a little spring and a pool of clear water, overhung with ferns. The floor was sand. Before a great fire lay Captain Smollett; and in a far corner, only dimly touched by the blaze, I saw great heaps of coin and stacks built four-square of bars of gold. That was Flint's treasure, that we had come so far to find, and that had already cost the lives of seventeen men off the Hispaniola. What it had cost in the gathering — what blood and sorrow, what good ships sunk, what brave men sent blindfold off the plank, what roar of cannon, what shame and lies and cruelty — perhaps no living man could tell. Yet there were still three upon that island — Silver, old Morgan, and Ben Gunn — who had each taken a share in those crimes, as each had hoped, in vain, to take his share of the reward.

“Come in, Jim,” said the captain. “You're a good boy in your way, Jim, but I don't think you and me'll go to sea again. You're too much of the born favourite for my liking. Is that you, John Silver? What brings you here, man?”
“Come back to my duty, sir,” returned Silver.
“Ah!” said the captain; and that was all he said.

What a supper I had of it that night, with all my friends about me; and what a meal, with Ben Gunn's salt goat, and some dainties, and a bottle of old wine from the Hispaniola. Never, I'm sure, were people merrier or happier. And there sat Silver, well back almost out of the firelight, but eating heartily, quick to spring up when anything was wanted, and even joining quietly in our laughter — the same smooth, polite, fawning seaman of the voyage out.

chapters.title: And Last
paragraphs: Next morning we fell to work early, for the shifting of this great mass of gold — near a mile by land to the beach, and thence three miles by boat to the Hispaniola — was a heavy task for so few hands. The three fellows still loose on the island gave us little concern; a single sentry on the shoulder of the hill was enough to guard against any sudden rush, and we reckoned, besides, they'd had more than their fill of fighting.

So the work was pushed on briskly. Gray and Ben Gunn came and went with the boat, while the rest, in their absence, piled the treasure on the beach. Two bars, slung in a rope's end, made a fair load for a grown man — one he was glad to carry slowly. For my part, being not much use at the carrying, I was kept busy all day in the cave, packing the minted money into bread-bags.

It was a strange hoard, like Billy Bones's for the mixture of coinage, but so much greater and so much more varied that I think I never had more pleasure than in sorting it. English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese coins, georges and louis-d'or, doubloons and double-guineas and moidores and sequins, the heads of all the kings of Europe for the last hundred years, strange Eastern pieces stamped with what looked like wisps of string or scraps of spider's web, round coins and square coins, and coins bored through the middle as if to be worn round the neck — pretty nearly every kind of money in the world must, I think, have come together in that pile; and for number, they were like autumn leaves, so that my back ached with stooping and my fingers with sorting them out.
Day after day the work went on; every evening a fortune had been stowed aboard, and another fortune waited for the morrow; and all this while we heard nothing of the three surviving mutineers.

At last — the third night, I think it was — the doctor and I were strolling on the shoulder of the hill, where it looks down over the lowlands of the isle, when, out of the thick darkness below, the wind brought us a sound between a shriek and a song. It was only a snatch that reached us, and then the old silence again.
“Heaven forgive them,” said the doctor; “it's the mutineers!”
“All drunk, sir,” said the voice of Silver, just behind us.

Silver, I should say, was allowed his full liberty, and, in spite of daily snubs, seemed to count himself once more quite a privileged and friendly hanger-on. Indeed it was remarkable how well he took these slights, and with what tireless politeness he kept trying to win us all over. Yet I think none of us treated him better than a dog — unless it were Ben Gunn, still in deadly fear of his old quartermaster, or myself, who had something real to thank him for; though for that matter I had cause to think worse of him than anyone, having seen him plotting fresh treachery on the plateau. So it was gruffly enough that the doctor answered him.
“Drunk, or raving,” said he.
“True for you, sir,” replied Silver; “and mighty little odds which it is, to you or me.”

“I suppose you'd scarcely ask me to call you a humane man,” returned the doctor, with a sneer, “so my feelings may surprise you, Master Silver. But if I were sure they were raving — and I'm morally certain one at least is down with fever — I'd leave this camp and, whatever the risk to my own hide, carry them the help of my skill.”

“Asking your pardon, sir, you'd be very wrong,” said Silver. “You'd throw away your precious life, and you may lay to that. I'm on your side now, hand and glove; I'd not wish to see the party weakened — least of all yourself, knowing what I owe you. But those men down there, they couldn't keep their word — no, not if they wished to; and what's more, they couldn't believe that you'd keep yours.”
“No,” said the doctor. “Keeping your word's your specialty — we know that much.”

Well, that was about the last we heard of the three pirates. Once only we caught a gunshot a long way off, and supposed them hunting. A council was held, and it was settled we must leave them on the island — to the huge delight, I must say, of Ben Gunn, and with Gray's hearty approval. We left them a good store of powder and shot, the bulk of the salt goat, a few medicines and other necessaries, tools, clothing, a spare sail, a fathom or two of rope, and — by the doctor's particular wish — a handsome present of tobacco.

That was about our last act on the island. Before it, we'd got the treasure stowed and shipped enough water, and the last of the goat-meat too, against any hardship; and at last, one fine morning, we weighed anchor — which was about all we could manage — and stood out of North Inlet, the very colours flying that the captain had flown and fought under at the stockade.

The three men must have watched us closer than we knew, as we were soon to learn. For coming through the narrows we had to hug the southern point, and there we saw all three of them kneeling together on a spit of sand, their arms raised to us in supplication. It went to all our hearts, I think, to leave them in that wretched plight; but we dared not risk another mutiny, and to carry them home to the gallows would have been a cruel sort of mercy. The doctor hailed them, telling them of the stores we'd left and where to find them. But they only went on calling us by name and begging us, for God's sake, to be merciful and not leave them to die in such a place.

At last, seeing the ship still held her course and was fast running out of hail, one of them — which, I don't know — leaped to his feet with a hoarse cry, threw his musket to his shoulder, and sent a shot whistling over Silver's head and through the mainsail.

After that we kept under cover of the bulwarks; and when next I looked out, they were gone from the spit, and the spit itself had all but melted from sight in the widening distance. That, at least, was the end of them; and before noon, to my unspeakable joy, the highest rock of Treasure Island had sunk into the blue round of the sea.

We were so short-handed that everyone aboard had to lend a hand — all but the captain, who lay on a mattress in the stern and gave his orders; for though much mended, he still needed quiet. We laid her head for the nearest port in Spanish America, not daring the voyage home without fresh hands; and even so, what with baffling winds and a couple of fresh gales, we were all worn out before we made it.

It was just at sundown when we dropped anchor in a most lovely land-locked gulf, and were at once surrounded by shore-boats full of people selling fruit and vegetables and offering to dive for coins. The sight of so many cheerful faces, the taste of the tropical fruits, and above all the lights beginning to shine in the town, made the most charming contrast to our dark and bloody stay on the island; and the doctor and the squire, taking me with them, went ashore to pass the early part of the night. There they fell in with the captain of an English man-of-war, got into talk, went aboard his ship, and, in short, had so pleasant a time that day was breaking before we came back alongside the Hispaniola.

Ben Gunn was alone on deck, and the moment we came aboard he began, with wonderful writhings, to make us a confession. Silver was gone. The maroon had a hand in his escape in a shore-boat some hours before, and now assured us he'd done it only to save our lives, which would surely have been forfeit had “that man with the one leg stayed aboard.” But that was not all. The sea-cook had not gone empty-handed. He'd cut through a bulkhead unseen and carried off one of the sacks of coin — worth, perhaps, three or four hundred guineas — to help him on his further wanderings.
I think we were all glad to be so cheaply rid of him.

Well, to make a long story short, we shipped a few hands, made a good cruise home, and the Hispaniola came into Bristol just as Mr. Blandly was beginning to think of fitting out her consort. Only five of those who'd sailed came back in her. “Drink and the devil had done for the rest,” with a vengeance — though, to be sure, we were not quite so badly off as that other ship they sang about:
With one man of her crew alive, What put to sea with seventy-five.

Every one of us had a good share of the treasure, and used it wisely or foolishly, after our natures. Captain Smollett is now retired from the sea. Gray not only saved his money but, seized of a sudden with the wish to better himself, studied his calling too; and he's now mate and part-owner of a fine full-rigged ship, married into the bargain, and the father of a family. As for Ben Gunn, he got a thousand pounds, which he spent or lost in three weeks — or, to be exact, in nineteen days, for he was back begging on the twentieth. Then they gave him a lodge to keep, just as he'd dreaded on the island; and he lives there still, a great favourite, though something of a butt, with the country boys, and a noted singer in church on Sundays and feast-days.

Of Silver we have heard no more. That formidable one-legged seafarer has gone at last clean out of my life; but I dare say he found his old wife again, and perhaps lives still in comfort with her and Captain Flint. It is to be hoped so, I suppose, for his chances of comfort in the next world are very small.

The bars of silver and the weapons still lie, for all I know, where Flint buried them; and there, for me, they may lie till doomsday. Not oxen and cart-ropes would drag me back to that accursed island; and the worst dreams I ever have are when I hear the surf booming about its shores, or start bolt upright in bed with the sharp voice of Captain Flint still ringing in my ears: “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!”
